title: Native CLI command table (cmd/stow-s3)
summary: cmd/stow-s3 is the native binary's only entry point, and its interface is the command line plus the environment rather than a Go API. A five-word command table (serve, doctor, mcp, workspace, prewarm) sits on top of a second-level table of seventeen workspace verbs. The module owns four decisions a caller cannot make for it: the reconciliation of flags with the STOW_*/S3_*/AWS_* environment, the choice of storage backend, the choice of operational mode, and the refusal set (--backend workspace, a run-through live write on the memory backend, any upstream client in local mode). It then builds the store the S3 server serves, publishes the readiness record on an inherited file descriptor, and owns the shutdown path. Two independent clients, the TypeScript package and the Python package, drive it as a child process and depend on its flag spellings and on the readiness record it writes.

trace.scope: The command table dispatches argv[1] to one of five commands; --version and the usage text are handled before dispatch.
parseServeFlags parses the whole serve flag set into a serveFlags struct on a flag.ExitOnError FlagSet.
serveRunThroughConfig reconciles the parsed flags with the environment into the one runthrough.Config the server runs on.
resolveMode turns the --mode flag and STOW_MODE into one Mode; an empty flag defers to runthrough.DetectMode.
parseBackend turns --backend into a typed runtime.Backend, refusing the workspace backend and any unrecognised value.
buildStore opens the local store and, only in run-through mode, the upstream client, the outbox and the run-through adapter.
bindNativeRuntimeStore wraps that store in a runtime instance under the granted authority and reports the runtime's own capabilities.
s3api.New takes the bound store as the S3 server's Store, which is where every CLI decision about backend and mode lands.
announceStartup prints the banner and, when a readiness descriptor was given, writes the readiness object instead of the legacy stdout line.

One JSON readiness object is written to the inherited descriptor, carrying the endpoint that was bound, the region, the credentials, the mode, the backend and the runtime's capabilities; this is the bytes the client reads.

evidence.detail: The command table: serve, doctor, mcp, workspace and prewarm, with usage and exit 1 for anything else.
parseBackend is the only place --backend becomes a typed backend; 'workspace' is refused with 'not selectable from the CLI yet' and an unknown value is refused as invalid.
openLocalStore opens fs.NewFilesystemStore for the filesystem backend and storage.NewMemoryStore for the memory backend, and treats a failed open as fatal.
resolveMode maps 'local' and 'run-through' explicitly and delegates '' and 'auto' to runthrough.DetectMode; anything else is a fatal invalid --mode.
validateLiveWriteBackend refuses run-through plus memory backend plus upstream propagation, on the grounds that the combination cannot work rather than that the policy is wrong.
The live-write validation runs after rtCfg.Authority is assigned at :328 and before buildStore at :343, so it sees the narrowed authority and precedes the construction of the run-through adapter.
In run-through mode the CLI refuses to start without a complete upstream endpoint, access key and secret key, naming the STOW_*/S3_*/AWS_* sources.
announceStartup writes the readiness object to the descriptor when one was given and prints the legacy STOW_READY line with credentials only when it was not.
readyMessage builds the capabilities block from details.capabilities, the runtime's own answers rather than a re-derivation (:78-92), with only Upstream derived from the mode (:84).
parseServeFlags declares the entire serve flag surface on one ExitOnError FlagSet, which is why an unreadable flag has already printed why and exited before any configuration exists.

serveRunThroughConfig is the single reconciliation point: the flag beats the environment for the cache limits, offline and cache directory, the environment fills the rest, and --allow-live-writes only ever adds consent.
applyOfflineFlag leaves the config alone when the flag was absent, so an exported STOW_OFFLINE survives and only an explicit value overrides it.
buildStore returns the plain local store and a nil adapter before it reaches runthrough.NewS3Client, which is the mechanical form of the local-mode safety argument.
awaitShutdown drains the outbox worker with a 2s bound before a 10s server shutdown, and treats a serve error other than http.ErrServerClosed as fatal.
Two distinct doctor exit statuses: 1 for a failed required check and 2 for a doctor that could not run.
The workspace verb table of 17 verbs, with the usage line derived from it so a verb cannot be added to the dispatcher without appearing in the usage text.
validateMCPMode selects the storage mode by which flags were visited, not by their values, and refuses a flag belonging to the other mode.
runPrewarm never consults the mode switch: it constructs an upstream client from the environment whenever credentials resolve, so the local-mode guarantee is a property of serve, not of the CLI.
UpstreamConfig.FromEnv resolves endpoint, keys, token, region and bucket with the precedence STOW_* > S3_* > AWS_* through envFirst; the CLI's own surface names none of the S3_* or AWS_* names.
DetectMode reads only STOW_MODE and returns local for 'local', 'auto', unset and every unrecognised value.
Config.effectiveAuthority folds the consent flag into the one authority the adapter gates on, so consent is consulted once and never re-derived.
ready.WriteToFd writes exactly one JSON object to the inherited descriptor and leaves the descriptor open for the client.
The TypeScript client assembles the serve argv by hand, including --ready-fd 3, and strips STOW_*/S3_*/AWS_* from an isolated session's environment.
The Python client independently assembles the same serve argv with --mode local and --ready-fd, so the flag spellings are a cross-language contract.
TestBuildStoreIgnoresUpstreamConfigInLocalMode asserts that even with live-write consent the local path builds no adapter and no upstream client.
The package's own end-to-end test launches the built binary with --ready-fd 3 and asserts the record carries the bound port, the credentials, the region and protocolVersion 1.

interface.types: The interface is not a Go type; it is a command line plus an environment. argv[1] selects one of five command words (serve, doctor, mcp, workspace, prewarm) at cmd/stow-s3/main.go:165; the workspace command adds a second-level table of seventeen verbs at cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:119 (adopt, apply, checkpoint, collect, delta, destroy, diff, export, handoff, import, list, prepare, preview, prune, restore, resume, serve), each with its own flag set and each writing one JSON document (to stdout, or to a file at mode 0600 where the verb takes an output path), except the serve verb, which writes a readiness JSON (to the descriptor when --ready-fd is given) and then serves until shutdown (cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go:21-81). serve accepts 28 flags, declared in one place at cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:52-85: --max-concurrent-requests, --max-request-bytes, --allow-insecure-upstream, --port (default 9000, 0 means ephemeral), --data-dir (default .stow), --backend (default filesystem), --access-key, --secret-key, --host (default 127.0.0.1), --base-host, --allow-public-admin (deprecated and ignored), --admin-token, --cors-origin (repeatable), --mode (default empty, never 'auto'), --region (default us-east-1), --allow-live-writes, --read-only, --cache-dir, --cache-max-bytes (default -1), --cache-max-objects (default -1), --cache-ttl (default -1), --offline (a tri-state bool), --version/-v, --max-bytes (default 0), --max-objects (default 0), --ready-fd (default -1), --parent-pid (default 0). The second half of the interface is the environment: STOW_LOCAL_ACCESS_KEY_ID and STOW_LOCAL_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:210-218) for the server's own credentials, STOW_ADMIN_TOKEN (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:57-59) for the admin routes, STOW_MODE (internal/runthrough/config.go:324) for the mode, and the upstream set STOW_ENDPOINT/S3_ENDPOINT/AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3/AWS_ENDPOINT_URL/AWS_ENDPOINT, STOW_ACCESS_KEY_ID/S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, STOW_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY/S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, STOW_SESSION_TOKEN/S3_SESSION_TOKEN/AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, STOW_REGION/S3_REGION/AWS_REGION/AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, STOW_BUCKET/S3_BUCKET, STOW_UPSTREAM_ADDRESSING, STOW_POLICY, STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES, STOW_OFFLINE, STOW_REVALIDATE, STOW_CACHE, STOW_CACHE_DIR, STOW_CACHE_MAX_BYTES, STOW_CACHE_MAX_OBJECTS and STOW_CACHE_TTL (internal/runthrough/config.go:128-302).
invariants: No explicit request, no upstream: run-through is selected only by --mode run-through or STOW_MODE=run-through, and an unrecognised STOW_MODE value is local rather than an error or a fallback (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:243-255; internal/runthrough/config.go:324-344; docs/adr/0011-local-is-the-default-mode.md:16-19).

Local mode constructs no upstream client at all, whatever the environment says: buildStore returns the plain local store and a nil adapter before it reaches runthrough.NewS3Client (cmd/stow-s3/store.go:24-34; asserted at cmd/stow-s3/local_mode_test.go:268-286).

Live-write consent is a separate mechanism from the routing policy, and is folded exactly once into the authority: STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES or --allow-live-writes withholds or grants authority.UpstreamWrite, and a mirrorWrites policy alone propagates nothing (internal/runthrough/config.go:114-123, 217; internal/runthrough/writepolicy.go:30-42).

The --backend value becomes a typed backend in exactly one place, and only memory and filesystem are constructible: 'workspace' is a recognised runtime.Backend that the CLI refuses because it needs options the command does not carry (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:99-112; internal/runtime/types.go:19-25).

The readiness record is published exactly once, on the inherited descriptor, and when a descriptor is given the legacy STOW_READY line is deliberately not printed, so credentials stay off stdout (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:47-61; internal/ready/ready.go:102-118).

The published capabilities are the runtime instance's own answers rather than a re-derivation, so a capability published in the record and a capability the runtime reports cannot quietly diverge (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:78-92; cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:52-54).
A run-through server whose writes would propagate to upstream cannot use the memory backend; the combination is refused at startup rather than half-honoured (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:257-265, 329-331).

The command table is total: an unrecognised word prints usage and exits 1, and the workspace usage line is derived from the verb table so a verb cannot be added without appearing in it (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:165-186; cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:119-144).

The server's signing region comes from --region alone; STOW_REGION and AWS_REGION configure the upstream client, not the local server, and the readiness record is the only place the server's region is published (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:370, 445-450; internal/runthrough/config.go:159-164).
error_modes: Startup problems are fatal log.Fatal calls rather than recoverable errors: an unrecognised --backend (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:110, 312-315), an invalid --mode (:252), non-positive request limits (:300-302; cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:115-117), missing upstream credentials in run-through (:338-340), a run-through live write on the memory backend (:329-331), and a store that will not open (:120-123).
serve's flag set is flag.ExitOnError, so a flag the package cannot read has already printed why and exited before any configuration exists (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:51, 83-85).
doctor is the one command that separates outcomes by exit status: 1 for a required check that failed, 2 for a doctor that could not run (cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:62-65, 84-96).

workspace, mcp and prewarm return errors to main, which turns them into log.Fatal, so their exit status is 1 with a log line; 'workspace' with no verb returns the usage line as an error (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:171-181; cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:157-159).

An unknown workspace verb is an error that still names the alternatives, and the mcp command refuses a flag belonging to the other storage mode rather than ignoring it (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:176-181; cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:82-86).
prewarm refuses to run without a bucket, without at least one key, and without an upstream unless --offline was given (cmd/stow-s3/prewarm.go:73-78, 111-113).
ordering: --version is answered before anything is built, so it needs no writable data directory, no authority and no upstream (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:156-158, 296-299).
The mode is resolved before the backend, and the authority is decided before buildStore, which is what constructs the run-through adapter (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:311-343).
rtCfg.Authority is assigned before validateLiveWriteBackend runs, so the validation sees the narrowed authority rather than the default (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:328-331).
The readiness record is written only after the listener has bound and reported a non-empty address, and after the parent-death watch is armed (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:406-420).
On SIGINT or SIGTERM the outbox retry worker is drained with a two-second bound before the server is asked to stop with a ten-second budget (cmd/stow-s3/shutdown.go:21-24, 43-58).
The workspace verb table is consulted only after --version and the five help spellings, because a caller asking for help has not named a verb (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:151-183).
configuration: The flag beats the environment inside the CLI: the flag wins over the environment for the cache limits, the offline flag, the cache directory and the admin token, and the environment fills what the flag did not state (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:41-67).

An absent --offline defers to STOW_OFFLINE and an explicit --offline=false contradicts it, because STOW_OFFLINE is a safety property an operator needs a one-command way out of (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:117-132; internal/runthrough/config.go:204-211).

--allow-live-writes can only grant consent, never withdraw it: the flag sets cfg.AllowLiveWrites to true and there is no flag that sets it false, so an inherited STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES=true cannot be revoked from the command line except by --read-only, which withholds upstream reads as well (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:60-62; internal/authority/authority.go:72-80).

The upstream half of the environment is resolved in one place, internal/runthrough, with the precedence STOW_* > S3_* > AWS_*; the CLI's own flag help and usage text name none of the S3_* or AWS_* names (internal/runthrough/config.go:128-173, 346-353; cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:52-85; cmd/stow-s3/main.go:190-206).

--backend accepts memory and filesystem only; 'workspace' is refused at startup with a message that points at the embedded API, a fact the flag help does not state (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:103-108; cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:57).

The two limit families use the same non-positive numbers for different meanings: --cache-max-bytes/--cache-max-objects/--cache-ttl default to -1 meaning 'use the environment' and treat 0 as 'no limit', while --max-bytes and --max-objects treat any value at or below zero as unlimited; a negative cache limit below -1 is a fatal error while a negative --max-bytes is silently unlimited (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:71-73, 79-80; cmd/stow-s3/main.go:220-234; cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:23-35).
The registry-scoped workspace verbs take --registry-dir and --team as a pair, and a handoff document's team partition overrides the flagged one (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:93-97, 76-82).

The workspace command writes a JSON result to stdout (or to a file at mode 0600 when a path is given); the mcp command speaks MCP over stdio instead and takes no output file (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:390-403; cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:41-51).

implementation: The module is a thin dispatcher over decisions that live in a handful of named functions, each of which owns one rule. parseServeFlags (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:50) declares the whole serve surface in one FlagSet and returns a struct, deliberately keeping twenty-eight flag pointers out of serve's body. serveRunThroughConfig (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:41) is the reconciliation point: it resolves the local credentials, calls runthrough.ConfigFromEnvChecked, applies the cache-limit flags, applies the tri-state offline flag, falls back to STOW_ADMIN_TOKEN, applies the live-write flag and the cache directory. resolveMode (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:243) maps the flag and defers to runthrough.DetectMode, whose whole rule is that an unrecognised STOW_MODE is local rather than an error. parseBackend (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:99) is the only place --backend becomes a typed backend and refuses the workspace backend by name rather than by omission. buildStore (cmd/stow-s3/store.go:24) opens the local store and returns it with a nil adapter unless the mode is run-through, so the upstream client is constructed inside one visible branch. validateLiveWriteBackend (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:257) refuses run-through plus memory backend plus propagation, keyed on consent rather than on policy. bindNativeRuntimeStore (cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:37) wraps the store in a runtime instance under the one granted authority, so the run-through adapter and the runtime cannot disagree about what was granted, and reports the runtime's capabilities back to the caller. serve then builds the s3api server, waits for a non-empty address, and hands the readiness details to announceStartup, which writes the versioned JSON record to the inherited descriptor. awaitShutdown (cmd/stow-s3/shutdown.go:43) drains the outbox worker before the server. doctor (cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:68) runs six in-process checks plus a live loopback server probe, marking each check required or optional. The workspace verbs are a map of seventeen names to functions (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:119) whose usage line is derived from the map, and each verb delegates to pkg/stow and writes one JSON result.

callers.scope: buildServeArgs assembles the serve argv for the TypeScript client, including --ready-fd 3, --parent-pid, --backend, --mode, --allow-live-writes and the cache limits; buildChildEnv strips STOW_*/S3_*/AWS_* from an isolated session's environment.

_server_args assembles the serve argv for the Python client independently, with --mode local, --backend, --ready-fd and --parent-pid; the two clients duplicate the invocation contract rather than sharing it.
waitForReady reads the readiness object from descriptor 3 and falls back to parsing the legacy STOW_READY line, so the client's expectations of the record's fields are a contract with this module.
The benchmark harness spawns serve with --backend, --data-dir, --ready-fd 3 and --parent-pid, and asserts that the published mode and backend match the scenario it asked for.

The TypeScript client spawns the second-level command as 'workspace serve --id ... --ready-fd 3 --parent-pid', so the workspace verb spellings and its readiness descriptor are also a cross-language contract.
The Python client independently spawns 'workspace serve --id ... --ready-fd ... --parent-pid' with a pipe descriptor, duplicating the same second-level invocation contract.
The module's own end-to-end test builds the binary and launches it as a child process, asserting the readiness record's port, credentials, region and protocolVersion.
The module's own test asserts that local mode constructs no upstream client even with live-write consent and a complete upstream configuration.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Two halves, and the deletion test goes different ways for each. Delete the command table itself (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:165-186 and the workspace verb map at cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:119-137) and the complexity vanishes rather than concentrates: the verbs still exist and simply need some dispatcher, so the table is a thin entry point, not a module of its own. Delete the module's decisions instead, and the complexity reappears in every caller: the flag-beats-environment reconciliation, the mode rule, the backend refusal, the live-write consent fold and the readiness record would have to be reimplemented in the TypeScript client and again in the Python client, and they would drift, which is the failure mode the two clients already show by each carrying its own copy of the invocation contract (packages/stow-s3/src/start.ts:128-181 against packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/session.py:254-274, and packages/stow-s3/src/workspace-serve.ts:30 against packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/workspace_serve.py:61). So the interface is deep where it decides and shallow where it dispatches: deep in the reconciliation and selection rules, shallow as a routing table. The one qualification is that the upstream precedence and the consent fold themselves live one package away in internal/runthrough/config.go, so deleting cmd/stow-s3 would not remove those; what the CLI uniquely owns is the flag-versus-environment precedence, the mode wrapper, the backend refusal and the readiness publication.

leverage: A caller states intent once, as flags and environment, and gets back one decided configuration: a typed backend, one mode, one effective write policy, one authority, and a readiness record that reports the runtime's own capabilities rather than a re-derivation. Because the rules live in the binary rather than in each client, the TypeScript and Python packages get the same answers without reimplementing the precedence, and the three safety properties that matter most (local is the default, no upstream client exists in local mode, live-write consent is separate from policy) are asserted once in cmd/stow-s3's own tests instead of once per language. The clients also get credentials off stdout by asking for a descriptor, and a machine-readable capability set that reports the limit actually being enforced.
locality: Change, bugs and knowledge about the native surface concentrate in cmd/stow-s3: the flag declarations (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go), the reconciliation rules (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go), the store and mode decisions (cmd/stow-s3/main.go, cmd/stow-s3/store.go), the shutdown contract (cmd/stow-s3/shutdown.go) and the two dispatch tables (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:165, cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:119). The seventeen workspace verbs are spread over six files in the same package (workspace.go, workspace_lifecycle.go, workspace_archive.go, workspace_delta.go, workspace_handoff.go, workspace_serve.go), and each of them is a straight call into pkg/stow, so a change to the public library surface lands in cmd/stow-s3 too. The environment half of the contract lives one package away in internal/runthrough (config.go:128-302), so renaming an environment variable is a two-package edit with no compiler to catch it, and each client keeps its own copy of the invocation contract, making a spelling change a three-place edit with no type checker either.
risks: The upstream half of the interface is invisible from the CLI: no flag help string and no usage line names any of the S3_* or AWS_* variables or states the STOW_* > S3_* > AWS_* precedence, and the consent variable STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES is unnamed too (the --allow-live-writes help says only 'Propagate writes to upstream S3'). The mode, offline and admin-token variables are the exception: STOW_MODE (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:66), STOW_OFFLINE (:81) and STOW_ADMIN_TOKEN (:63) are each named in their own flag's help string, so the precedence and the consent variable are the parts learnable only by reading internal/runthrough/config.go (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:52-85; cmd/stow-s3/main.go:190-206; internal/runthrough/config.go:128-173).

prewarm ignores the mode switch entirely: it resolves upstream credentials from the environment and constructs an upstream client whenever they are present, even with STOW_MODE=local, so the 'local mode never constructs an upstream client' property is a property of serve and not of the binary (cmd/stow-s3/prewarm.go:111-117 against cmd/stow-s3/store.go:24-28).

--allow-live-writes can only grant consent, never withdraw it, and --offline, which is a tri-state precisely so an operator can contradict an exported safety variable, has no counterpart here; an inherited STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES=true therefore cannot be revoked from the command line (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:60-62 against cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:127-132).

The two limit families give the same non-positive numbers different meanings: --cache-max-bytes -1 means 'use the environment' and 0 means 'no limit', while --max-bytes at or below zero means unlimited, and a cache limit below -1 is fatal while a negative --max-bytes is silently unlimited (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:71-80; cmd/stow-s3/main.go:220-234; cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:23-35).

Two different regions exist and only one is published: --region sets the region the server verifies signatures against and reports in the readiness record, while STOW_REGION and AWS_REGION configure the upstream client, so a caller that assumes they are the same region signs against the wrong one until it reads the readiness record (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:370, 445-450; internal/runthrough/config.go:159-164).

--backend workspace is refused with a message that names the embedded API as the alternative, but the flag help only says 'filesystem or memory', so the refusal and its reason are discoverable only by trying the value or reading the source (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:103-108; cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:57).

The mcp command chooses its storage mode by which flags were visited rather than by their values, so --object-dir with an empty value still selects object mode, and no flag value states the mode (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:74-88).

doctor's two exit statuses, 1 for a failed required check and 2 for a doctor that could not run, appear in no help text and in no usage line, so a script that treats any non-zero exit as the same failure cannot distinguish a broken machine from an unrunnable diagnostic (cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:62-65, 84-96).

The two clients strip the child's environment with a prefix set over STOW_*, S3_* and AWS_*, so the CLI's environment contract is duplicated as a string pattern in TypeScript and Python with no shared source and no compiler check (packages/stow-s3/src/start.ts:190-194; packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/session.py:50, 61-70).

The comment in parseBackend cites docs/architecture/environment-implementation.md M1.2 as the authority for the workspace refusal, and that path does not exist in the tree; the file is at docs/history/architecture/environment-implementation.md, so the code's own justification points at a document that has been moved (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:103-108).

priority.rationale: Blast radius: the CLI is the only entry point to the native server, and its flag spellings, its --ready-fd contract and the shape of its readiness record are consumed by two independent client packages and by the benchmark harness (packages/stow-s3/src/start.ts:128-181; packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/session.py:254-274; packages/stow-s3/scripts/performance/server.mjs:12-20), so a rename breaks all three with no compiler to catch it. Unclear seam: the upstream half of the interface lives in internal/runthrough and no CLI surface states the precedence or the consent variable, so the rules a caller must know are only in prose comments and in a package the help text never names. Hidden coupling: the clients strip the child's environment with a prefix set that must match the CLI's variable names, and the readiness protocol's version field is the only guard against a client and a binary disagreeing. Impact is P1 because the rules the CLI owns are the safety-critical ones, where a wrong answer sends writes to a live provider or refuses a legitimate upstream; overall is P2 because the rules are stated in CONTEXT.md (Mode Selection and Live-Write Consent) and ADR 0011 and are asserted densely in the package's own tests, so a divergence is caught by the suite rather than by a customer.

next_action: Make the interface carry the contract it already enforces. Publish one artefact and have the help text point at it: extend cmd/stow-s3/main.go:190 usageTo and the serve flag help strings (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:52-85) so that every flag states the environment variable it shadows (STOW_LOCAL_ACCESS_KEY_ID, STOW_LOCAL_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, STOW_ADMIN_TOKEN, STOW_MODE, STOW_OFFLINE, STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES, STOW_POLICY) and every refusal is stated where it is enforced (parseBackend at cmd/stow-s3/main.go:99-112, validateLiveWriteBackend at :257-265); and add a `stow-s3 contract --json` verb that prints the command table, the workspace verb table, the flag defaults, the environment variable list with its STOW_* > S3_* > AWS_* precedence, the exit statuses and the refusal list, so the TypeScript and Python clients generate their invocation from it instead of copying it. The concrete interface that should change is the CLI's own: one machine-readable description of the command line plus the environment, replacing the three hand-written copies that exist today.

title: Workspace readiness record (`workspace serve` -> fd/stdout -> TS and Python readers)
summary: A second, distinct readiness value flows from `stow-s3 workspace serve` to the clients, and it is not the session readiness record. Its writer is cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go, which JSON-encodes a workspaceServeResult — the workspaceResult plus the embedded WorkspaceFacade endpoint/credentials — to an inherited descriptor, or to stdout when --ready-fd is unset. It identifies itself with a top-level `version` field (value 1) and carries workspace_id, root, bucket, endpoint, region, access_key_id and secret_access_key. The TypeScript reader packages/stow-s3/src/workspace-serve.ts and the Python reader packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/workspace_serve.py each require version==1 and the same seven string fields. A reader tells it apart from the session record by the identity key name — `version` versus `protocolVersion` — and by the snake_case field vocabulary, not by the number, which is 1 in both, and not by the presence of a capabilities object, which both records carry in different shapes.

trace.scope: serveWorkspaceCommand calls writeWorkspaceReady(*readyFD, result) after building the facade
writeWorkspaceReady json.NewEncoder's the result to the fd (defer Close), or to stdout when fd<0
TypeScript readWorkspaceReady decodes one newline-terminated record and checks version===1 plus seven string fields
Python _parse_ready json.loads's the line, requires version==1 and the same seven string fields
the decoded WorkspaceJSON becomes ServedWorkspace.ready; Python lands the same dict in ServedWorkspace (workspace_serve.py:74-75)

evidence.detail: workspaceResult's identity key is `version` (workspace.go:20) and makeWorkspaceResult sets it to 1 (workspace.go:377)
writeWorkspaceReady is the publication point: json.NewEncoder to the fd, or stdout when fd<0, closing the fd on the fd path
WorkspaceFacade supplies the record's endpoint, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key and the three limit fields under snake_case json tags
the TypeScript reader validates workspace_id, root, bucket, endpoint, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key and requires version 1
_parse_ready requires ready['version']==1 and the same seven string fields, and rejects a record over 256 KiB
TypeScript spawns `workspace serve` with --ready-fd 3, while Python passes its own pipe fd (workspace_serve.py:56,61-62)

the session record's identity key is protocolVersion (value 1); the session record also carries a capabilities object, so neither the number nor the presence of capabilities distinguishes the two records

with no ready descriptor the session `serve` path falls back to the legacy STOW_READY line, which prints access_key and secret_key on stdout, so stdout suppression is a descriptor-channel property, not a session-versus-workspace difference

interface.types: One newline-terminated JSON object. Identity key: version (int, must be 1). Validated string fields: workspace_id, root, bucket, endpoint, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key. Also present from workspaceResult: working_directory, checkpoint_id, registry_dir, team, seeded_bytes, seeded_objects, base_identity, repositories, capabilities (backend, max_bytes, max_objects, persistent, multipart, upstream, checkpoint_limits, registry_bound) and authority; and from the embedded *stow.WorkspaceFacade: max_multipart_uploads, max_concurrent_requests, max_request_bytes. Go: workspaceResult (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:19-34), workspaceServeResult (cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go:16-19), WorkspaceFacade (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:16-24). TypeScript: WorkspaceJSON (workspace.ts:8), ServedWorkspace.ready (workspace-serve.ts:19-23). Python: ServedWorkspace.ready (workspace_serve.py:17-22). The session record is a different object: protocolVersion plus binaryVersion, endpoint, region, accessKeyId, secretAccessKey, mode, backend and a camelCase capabilities object (internal/ready/ready.go:21-53).
invariants: The record is one newline-terminated JSON object, sized under 256 KiB; TypeScript and Python both reject a larger buffer (workspace-serve.ts:69, workspace_serve.py:90-91).
version must equal 1 and the seven string fields must be non-empty; otherwise the client rejects the child's readiness (workspace-serve.ts:74-77, workspace_serve.py:93-97).

When --ready-fd is unset (fd<0) the workspace record is written to stdout (workspace_serve.go:72-73). The session `serve` path likewise falls back to stdout when no descriptor is given, but with the legacy STOW_READY line rather than the JSON object (main.go:50-60), so neither writer keeps credentials off stdout unless a descriptor was supplied.

The workspace's credentials and loopback endpoint come from the embedded WorkspaceFacade, so the caller can sign against the workspace server (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:16-24, workspace_serve.go:58-62).

The record carries a `capabilities` object of its own (workspaceCapabilities, snake_case), distinct from the session record's ready.Capabilities (camelCase); the two are not interchangeable and their presence is not a discriminator (workspace.go:36-49, internal/ready/ready.go:21-40).
error_modes: Go writer: an invalid fd (os.NewFile returns nil) or an encode error is returned to serveWorkspaceCommand and surfaces as the command's error (workspace_serve.go:71-81).

TypeScript reader: a buffer over 256 KiB, a decode failure, a missing/empty field, or version!==1 rejects the startup promise (workspace-serve.ts:69,73-79); the child exiting or the stream ending first rejects with captured stderr (workspace-serve.ts:64-65); a 15 s timeout rejects (workspace-serve.ts:81); an abort rejects (workspace-serve.ts:66).

Python reader: a buffer over 256 KiB, invalid JSON, a non-dict, version!=1, or a missing/empty field raises ValueError (workspace_serve.py:89-98); _read_ready_line can raise TimeoutError or StowProtocolError first (workspace_serve.py:73).
ordering: The record is written after the workspace is resumed and the facade server is started, so the endpoint in it is bound (workspace_serve.go:53-64).
The reader waits for a newline before decoding; a partial record is not parsed (workspace-serve.ts:70-73, workspace_serve.py:73 via _read_ready_line's readline).
On any parse or spawn failure the client stops the child before re-raising (workspace-serve.ts:41-43, workspace_serve.py:76-80).
configuration: workspace serve's --ready-fd defaults to -1, meaning write to stdout (cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go:26).
TypeScript passes --ready-fd 3 and spawns with a 4-entry stdio (workspace-serve.ts:30,35); Python allocates an os.pipe fd and passes it in pass_fds (workspace_serve.py:56,61-62,68-69).
--parent-pid is passed by both clients so the served workspace stops with the launcher (workspace_serve.go:27, workspace-serve.ts:30, workspace_serve.py:62).

implementation: serveWorkspaceCommand resumes the workspace, builds the facade and a workspaceServeResult (workspace_serve.go:53-62), then calls writeWorkspaceReady, which json.NewEncoder-encodes the result to the descriptor or to stdout and closes the descriptor on the fd path (workspace_serve.go:71-81). The record's shape is workspaceResult (workspace.go:19-34) with version=1 from makeWorkspaceResult (workspace.go:374-388) plus the embedded *stow.WorkspaceFacade (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:16-24); it therefore carries its own `capabilities` object (workspaceCapabilities, snake_case), which is not the session record's ready.Capabilities. Both clients read it with their own separate parsers: TypeScript's readWorkspaceReady decodes one newline-terminated record and validates version and the seven string fields (workspace-serve.ts:47-88,73-77), and Python's _parse_ready does the same with json.loads (workspace_serve.py:89-98). This path never touches internal/ready: it has no protocolVersion key, no ready.ProtocolVersion constant and no protocol_mismatch error code.

callers.scope: the CLI command table dispatches `workspace`, whose serve verb writes the record
serveWorkspace awaits readWorkspaceReady(child, options) and returns ServedWorkspace
serve_workspace reads and parses the record into ServedWorkspace.ready
serve_workspace and ServedWorkspace are part of the published Python surface
agentDirectory(ready) consumes the record's working_directory and root fields, so the in-repo examples are a downstream reader reached through the TypeScript entry point

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting writeWorkspaceReady would not remove the record: the workspaceResult value is also written by the prepare/resume/handoff/archive verbs through writeWorkspaceJSON (workspace.go:390-399, workspace_archive.go:282, workspace_handoff.go:172), and the workspace serve subcommand would still have to publish some readiness value to a launcher. The function itself is thin, but the complexity (which fields, which version key, credential placement) reappears in whatever replaces it and is already restated in the two client parsers, so the depth is in the contract and it is duplicated rather than factored.

leverage: A launcher gets the workspace's loopback endpoint and credentials plus its identity and limits from one descriptor, so it can drive a persistent workspace's server without parsing logs, and it can reject a shape it does not understand via the version field.
locality: The writer is a forty-line block in cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go over a value defined in cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go and pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go. The consumer contract is duplicated across packages/stow-s3/src/workspace-serve.ts and packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/workspace_serve.py, each restating the same seven field names and the version check.
risks: The workspace record and the session record both travel over an inherited descriptor as one newline-terminated JSON object and both report version 1; they are told apart only by the identity key name (`version` versus `protocolVersion`) and by the field vocabulary (snake_case versus camelCase), so documentation or a launcher that keys on the number or on the fd convention conflates them (workspace.go:20, internal/ready/ready.go:44).

Both records carry a `capabilities` object, so its presence is not a discriminator as the record once claimed; the workspace one (backend, max_bytes, max_objects, persistent, multipart, upstream, checkpoint_limits, registry_bound) and the session one (persistent, multipart, upstream, conditionalWrites, presignedUrls, maxBytes, maxObjects, maxRequestBytes, maxConcurrentRequests) share field names in a different case and a reader must not treat them as the same shape (workspace.go:36-49, internal/ready/ready.go:21-40).

The workspace record is written to stdout when --ready-fd is unset and carries credentials (workspace_serve.go:72-73); the session path also puts credentials on stdout in that case, through the legacy STOW_READY line rather than the JSON object (main.go:54-60), so the workspace record is not an exposure the session path avoids, but it is a larger credential-bearing body on stdout than the one-line fallback.

TypeScript validates the version after the field loop (workspace-serve.ts:74-77) so a mismatched-version record with the right fields is only rejected at the end; the error is still raised, but the order means a field error masks a version error.

The field list is restated in three places (the Go struct tags, the TypeScript loop, the Python loop) with no shared definition, so adding a required field to the Go record silently breaks one or both clients.

priority.rationale: The record's blast radius is the workspace serve path in both published clients, and the two-record ambiguity plus the handwritten field lists are hidden coupling that a launcher or the docs can get wrong; the current parsers fail loudly rather than silently on the wrong record, so the impact stays at P2 and does not reach the S3 request path or the default session.

next_action: Give the two readiness records distinct, self-describing identity keys and write both down together (for example docs/session-protocol.md covering the `serve` and `workspace serve` records side by side, including the fact that both carry a capabilities object of a different shape), then reuse one validator per language instead of two inline field loops. The concrete interfaces to change are writeWorkspaceReady (cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go:71) and its readers readWorkspaceReady (packages/stow-s3/src/workspace-serve.ts:47) and _parse_ready (packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/workspace_serve.py:89).

title: The WASM host bridge (cmd/stow-wasm): JS global, two request protocols, a handle table and a JS-host-backed store
summary: cmd/stow-wasm is the package that lets a JavaScript host run stow's object model inside a WebAssembly isolate. It publishes exactly one global, globalThis.stow, with five members - call, callBinary, callBinaryAsync, openHost and exit (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:125). call is the v1 JSON protocol: one JSON string in, one JSON string out, with object bytes base64-encoded inside it (main.go:16, :129; decoded at cmd/stow-wasm/operations.go:65). callBinary/callBinaryAsync/openHost are the v2 binary protocol, discriminated by the request's version field equalling 2 (cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:10, :22): the payload crosses as a separate Uint8Array argument and returns as a separate Uint8Array, async dispatch becomes available, and a JS-supplied store can back the runtime. Runtimes are addressed by an integer handle from a monotonic counter (main.go:105-114), valid from open until close, and host-backed handles must be driven asynchronously (main.go:151-153). For host-backed storage the bridge builds a hostStore that implements the PUBLIC embedded.Store (internal/embedded/store.go:15), not internal/storage.Store, and reaches the internal seam only through embedded.adaptStore (internal/embedded/store.go:120); a store without multipart means the host runtime reports multipart=false. The bridge imports internal/embedded directly and bypasses pkg/stow, so the WASM surface is not covered by the public package's alias layer and exposes none of its workspace, checkpoint, delta or handoff verbs. Its Go-facing callers are the TypeScript client - the Node loader (packages/stow-s3/src/node-wasm-host.ts:41), the browser loader (packages/stow-s3/src/browser-wasm-host.ts:39), the browser worker (packages/stow-s3/src/browser-wasm-worker.ts:8), the persistent content worker (packages/stow-s3/src/browser-content-worker.ts:15) and the client's embedded/async facades - plus the Node isolate harness and probe (scripts/wasm-isolate-host.mjs:121, scripts/wasm-isolate-probe.mjs:119); the isolate probe test asserts the published global keeps its exact shape (scripts/wasm-isolate-probe.test.mjs:88).

trace.scope: the published global: globalThis.stow = {call, callBinary, callBinaryAsync, openHost, exit}; this one line is the entire surface a JS host calls
parseBinaryRequest discriminates protocol v2 by the JSON version field and copies the Uint8Array payload into Go memory
dispatch looks the handle up in the table, refuses a host handle on a synchronous call, and refuses an unknown handle
the 21-entry operationHandlers table maps the request op to its handler

the behaviour lands in the internal runtime instance the embedded facade bound: OpenWithStore for host-backed, Open for memory; the host store reaches it only through embedded.adaptStore (internal/embedded/store.go:120)

evidence.detail: the published global and its five members; scripts/wasm-isolate-probe.test.mjs:88 pins the key set.
protocolVersion = 1; call (:129) accepts one JSON string and rejects any other version at :137-139.
binaryProtocolVersion = 2; parseBinaryRequest (:14-31) validates the version, forbids encoded data in the metadata, and copies the payload in.
callBinaryAsync sets req.async and returns a Promise; openHost (:20-32) parses a JSON metadata string plus a host store object.
the handle allocator: handle = state.next++, stored in state.instances; close deletes it at cmd/stow-wasm/operations.go:141-143.
openHostRuntime builds hostStore, installs it as options.Store with BackendHost, records the handle in hostHandles, and calls stow.Open.
hostStore.invoke is the reverse protocol: it marshals a hostRequest, copies bytes to a Uint8Array, awaits the host's call promise, and copies the reply bytes back.
hostCheckConditions is the callback the bridge installs on the host store object; it evaluates IfMatch/IfNoneMatch with storage.CheckWritePreconditions.
streamToken allocates read/write stream tokens and caps a runtime handle at 16 concurrent streams with stow.ErrQuotaExceeded (:52-70).
errorResponse is the Go-to-wire error translation table; host_store_js.go:126-150 is the reverse direction.
the public embedded.Store hostStore implements; the file's comment at :13-14 states multipart and conditional writes need separate optional interfaces.
adaptStore is the only route from the public store to the internal storage.Store, and it carries multipart only when the caller's store does.
embedded.Open routes a supplied store to stowruntime.OpenWithStore with a nil reset hook, so a host-backed runtime cannot Reset.
Reset returns ErrExternalResetUnsupported when the reset hook is nil - the difference a host-backed WASM runtime shows against a native memory runtime.
pkg/stow.Open re-exports internal/embedded.Open; the WASM bridge does not go through it.
the TS client hand-declares EMBEDDED_PROTOCOL_VERSION=1 and EMBEDDED_BINARY_PROTOCOL_VERSION=2, duplicating the Go constants.

ContentObjectHost.call is the JS host store the bridge expects: it validates the v2 envelope, dispatches 15 ops (startPut, writePut, commitPut, abortPut, readObject, closeObject, close, openObject, listBuckets, createBucket, deleteBucket, listObjects, headObject, deleteObject, copyObject), and consults checkConditions for conditional writes (:119-123).
a real round trip over callBinary proving the v2 payload/return split and that the returned bytes are a copy (:34-36).

interface.types: The bridge's surface is one JS global, globalThis.stow, with five members. call(json: string) -> string is the v1 synchronous protocol. callBinary(metadata: string, data: Uint8Array) -> {metadata: string, data?: Uint8Array} is the v2 synchronous binary protocol. callBinaryAsync(metadata: string, data?: Uint8Array) -> Promise<{metadata: string, data?: Uint8Array}> is v2 asynchronous dispatch. openHost(metadata: string, store: HostObjectStoreBridge) -> Promise<{metadata, data?}> opens a runtime backed by a JS store. exit() shuts the Go runtime down. A request is JSON {version, op, handle, ...} (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:18-43) plus, for v2, the separate Uint8Array payload; a response is JSON {version, ok, error?: {code, message}, result?} (main.go:45-55). The host store object must provide call(metadata: string, data: Uint8Array) -> Promise<{metadata, data?}>; the bridge itself installs an optional checkConditions(metadata) -> string callback on that object (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:39-40). Backends are selected by options.backend: "memory" (bridge-created) or "host" (the supplied store). The op set is 21 operations (cmd/stow-wasm/operations.go:14-36), including the streaming openObjectRead/readObjectChunk/closeObjectRead and openObjectWrite/writeObjectChunk/commitObjectWrite/abortObjectWrite. For host-backed storage the bridge hands its hostStore to embedded.Open as options.Store (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:42-44), so the Go-side contract is the PUBLIC embedded.Store method set and not internal/storage.Store: CreateBucket(ctx, name string) error, DeleteBucket(ctx, name string) error, ListBuckets(ctx) ([]stow.Bucket, error), PutObject(ctx, bucket, key string, data []byte, options stow.PutOptions) (stow.Object, error), GetObject(ctx, bucket, key string) (stow.Object, error), HeadObject(ctx, bucket, key string) (stow.Object, error), DeleteObject(ctx, bucket, key string) error, ListObjects(ctx, bucket string, options stow.ListOptions) (stow.ObjectPage, error), Close() error (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:162-304, cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_io_js.go:21-111). internal/storage.Store is the incompatible internal contract (io.Reader bodies, storage.PutOptions, *storage.ObjectMeta results), reached only because internal/embedded.Open calls adaptStore. hostStore additionally opts into embedded.ConditionalWriteStore (SupportsConditionalWrites), embedded.StagedWriteStore (StageObject), embedded.StreamingStore (OpenObject/OpenObjectRange) and embedded.StreamingWriteStore (PutObjectStream); it does not implement embedded.MultipartStore.
invariants: A request's version must match the entry point: 1 for call, 2 for callBinary/callBinaryAsync/openHost; a mismatch is unsupported_protocol on call or invalid_request on the binary entries (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:137-139, cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:22-24).
A v2 binary request must not carry base64 object data in its metadata (cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:25-27).

A handle is allocated from a monotonic counter starting at 1 (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:112-114) and is valid only between a successful open and its close; a second close fails with "runtime handle N is not open" (main.go:155-159).
A host-backed handle is refused on a synchronous call: host-backed runtimes require asynchronous dispatch (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:151-153).

No single chunk may exceed 256 KiB (hostChunkLimit, cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:15): range reads (cmd/stow-wasm/host-store-range.go:15-17), stream chunks (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_sessions_js.go:120) and host replies (host_store_js.go:117-119) are all bounded by it.
Host-store staged writes are sequential: the offset of each writePut must equal the bytes accepted so far, or the host rejects it (packages/stow-s3/src/content-object-host.ts:102-109).
Bytes returned to JS are copies: mutating the returned Uint8Array does not change stored state (packages/stow-s3/test/node-wasm-host.test.ts:34-36).
At most 16 streams (reads, writes and pending combined) may be open per runtime handle (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_sessions_js.go:52-70).
error_modes: unsupported_protocol / invalid_request when the request shape or version is wrong (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:131-139, cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:16-27).
runtime_error "runtime handle N is not open" for an unknown or already-closed handle (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:158).
runtime_error "host-backed runtime requires asynchronous calls" for a synchronous call against a host handle (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:152).

The twelve mapped codes: quota_exceeded, closed, invalid_list_limit, unsupported_backend, bucket_not_found, bucket_exists, bucket_not_empty, object_not_found, invalid_bucket, invalid_key, precondition_failed, conditional_write_unsupported; anything unmapped is runtime_error (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:196-225).
Host store codes are translated back to embedded sentinels; an unknown code becomes a plain error and then runtime_error (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:126-150).
response_encoding when a response cannot be marshalled (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:233).
ordering: Open first to obtain a handle; every other operation names that handle; close last (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:148, :155-156; cmd/stow-wasm/operations.go:138-146).
For a host-backed runtime, use openHost (or the async binary entry) before any operation, because a synchronous call is refused (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:151-153).

Stream operations must be opened before their chunk operations and closed afterwards; openObjectWrite additionally requires an asynchronous call and a declared non-negative size (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_sessions_js.go:91-93, :176-178).
A stream write must commit or abort; abort is what an uncommitted StageObject invokes, and commit waits for the write goroutine to finish (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_sessions_js.go:246-272).
Close tears down stream sessions and the JS checkConditions callback, then calls the host store's close op (cmd/stow-wasm/operations.go:139, cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:283-304).
configuration: The protocol version is the discriminator: request.version 1 selects JSON, 2 selects binary (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:16, cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:10).
The backend is selected per open request: options.backend "memory" or, through openHost, "host" (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:43; packages/stow-s3/src/async-embedded.ts:39, :45).
Quotas come from options.maxBytes / options.maxObjects / options.maxMultipartUploads, decoded from the request options (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:22, internal/embedded/types.go:22-27).
The bridge reads no environment variables; unlike the native CLI's run-through path (cmd/stow-s3/store.go:24-51), there is no upstream, cache, outbox or mode configuration in this package.

implementation: main.go owns the published global (main.go:111-127), the request/response envelopes and their JSON shapes (main.go:18-101), the process-wide handle table (main.go:105-109), dispatch with the host-async guard (main.go:147-165), openRuntime (main.go:167-178), the capability projection (main.go:180-190) and the Go-to-wire error table (main.go:196-225). binary_js.go owns v2 parsing, the payload copy and the {metadata,data} response, plus a sync.Pool of read buffers (binary_js.go:10-67). async_js.go wraps a run in a JS Promise and parses the openHost arguments including the host store's call method (async_js.go:9-61). operations.go is the 21-op table and the marshalling of buckets, objects, pages, usage and capabilities, including the out-of-band object-data path (operations.go:14-180). host_store_js.go is the hostStore adapter: the embedded.Store method set, the reverse invoke protocol, hostStoreError and Close; host_store_io_js.go adds streaming reads/writes and staged writes with an MD5 ETag; host_store_sessions_js.go adds the runtime-side read/write session table used by the streaming operations; host_conditions_js.go evaluates conditional writes through storage.CheckWritePreconditions; host_store_await_js.go turns the JS promise into a Go channel with context cancellation; host-store-range.go bounds a ranged read. The decisions the package holds are: which serialization a request gets, how long a handle lives, when a call must be asynchronous, what a chunk may be, and how each side's errors are named.

callers.scope: the Node loader: instantiates the wasm_exec runtime, reads globalThis.stow (shape at :19-25) and exposes call/callBinary/callBinaryAsync/openHost/close.

the browser loader: instantiates Go in the current realm, reads globalThis.stow (:39, shape at :15-18) and exposes call/callBinary/callBinaryAsync/openHost/exit/close; the browser analogue of the Node loader and the parent of both worker entries.
the browser worker: serves the wasm bridge's callBinaryAsync over the worker transport.
the persistent content worker: routes openHost to ContentObjectHost and forwards everything else to callBinaryAsync.
AsyncEmbeddedStow.invoke: builds the v2 request metadata and calls host.callBinary, decoding the {metadata,data} reply.
the synchronous embedded client: chooses v1 or v2 by whether the host exposes callBinary, and calls host.call or host.callBinary.
the packaged-runtime test: opens a memory runtime through the bridge and exercises createBucket/putObject/getObject and a raw callBinary round trip.
the host-backed test: opens a runtime through openHost with ContentObjectHost and drives streams, preconditions and the 16-stream cap.
the isolate probe test: runs the probe and asserts the published global's exact key set (:88) and the isolate host surface.
the isolate harness: boots wasm_exec in a vm sandbox with no Node APIs, waits for sandbox.stow (:121), then calls sandbox.stow.call/exit and reads Object.keys(sandbox.stow).
the isolate probe: same sandbox boot; drives the whole op set through sandbox.stow.call (:119) and reports stowKeys and the exit settlement.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Delete cmd/stow-wasm and the whole isolate surface vanishes: no JS host can run the object model in a browser, worker or isolate, and nothing else in the repository adapts embedded to a JS caller. The complexity does not reappear dispersed across callers because the callers are TypeScript and Node scripts - there is no Go code to absorb a handle table, a two-version wire format, bidirectional byte copying, a host-store adapter, runtime-side stream sessions, a reverse error vocabulary and a promise-to-channel bridge. All of it concentrates in this package (branching, validation, state and translation across ten files) and would have to be rebuilt, in a different language on the other side of the boundary, if the package were removed. It is a leaf entry-point module whose interface is genuinely deep: five global functions hide a protocol, a lifetime model, an ownership model and a runtime binding.

leverage: A JS host gets stow's full object model - buckets, objects, conditional writes, ranged and streamed reads and writes, usage and capabilities - through five global functions and one optional store callback, with no Go toolchain and no Node APIs (scripts/wasm-isolate-probe.test.mjs:40-90). The bridge absorbs the awkward parts of the boundary: it picks the serialization per call, copies bytes so neither heap aliases the other, bounds every chunk to 256 KiB, translates both error vocabularies, and turns a JS promise into a Go call the runtime can block on.
locality: Change concentrates in cmd/stow-wasm: the protocol envelope and handle table in main.go, v2 parsing in binary_js.go, async and openHost in async_js.go, the op set in operations.go, the host-store adapter across host_store*.go and host-store-range.go. Knowledge of the wire format is duplicated out of the package into packages/stow-s3/src/embedded.ts and wasm-bridge.ts, so a protocol change is a change in at least two languages; the only automated pin on the global's shape is scripts/wasm-isolate-probe.test.mjs:88, and there is no Go test in the package.
risks: The wire contract is hand-duplicated across the language boundary: the Go constants (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:16, cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:10) and the TS constants (packages/stow-s3/src/embedded.ts:1-2) are independent declarations, and the op names and field names are re-stated in TypeScript (packages/stow-s3/src/content-object-host.ts:44-55, async-embedded.ts:83-132). A rename or field change compiles on both sides and fails only at runtime, and the probe pins the global key set, not field-level parity.

hostStore advertises SupportsConditionalWrites() unconditionally true (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:281) while enforcement is delegated to a JS callback the bridge installs (cmd/stow-wasm/host_conditions_js.go:10). A host store that does not consult checkConditions fails mid-commit with conditional_write_unsupported (packages/stow-s3/src/content-object-host.ts:120) rather than before the write, so the capability the runtime reports and the guarantee the store gives can disagree.

The bridge bypasses pkg/stow: it imports internal/embedded (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:13 and five sibling files), so its Go-side contract has no public alias and no version story, and the WASM surface exposes none of pkg/stow's workspace, checkpoint, delta or handoff verbs (pkg/stow/runtime.go:9 is only the alias the bridge does not use). A caller of the TypeScript client cannot tell from the API which of the public library's behaviours are missing.

Stream and handle state are paired by integer handle and by token across two maps with a closing flag (cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_sessions_js.go:33-39, :274-310); a JS host that abandons readers or writers without the close ops holds stream slots until the runtime handle closes, and the 16-stream cap turns that into quota_exceeded for later callers (packages/stow-s3/test/host-backed-streams.test.ts:64-67, :100-113).

priority.rationale: The blast radius is every browser, worker and isolate consumer of @chester-hill-solutions/stow-s3, because the published global and the wire protocol are the only way into the object model there, and the protocol is hand-mirrored in TypeScript with no shared schema (cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:125 vs packages/stow-s3/src/embedded.ts:1-2). The coupling is hidden rather than absent: hostStore claims conditional-write support unconditionally while delegating the predicate to a JS callback, and the package reaches internal/embedded directly so there is no public alias layer to absorb or document a change. It is not P1 because the module is a leaf with a small surface, the two versions and their discriminator are explicit in source, and the host-backed and isolate tests exercise the real protocol.

next_action: Give the protocol one source of truth and make the host capability honest. Concretely: derive the TypeScript request/response declarations and the two version constants from the Go envelope (or add a parity test that round-trips the Go request/response structs against the TS shapes) so packages/stow-s3/src/embedded.ts:1-2 and cmd/stow-wasm/main.go:16 / cmd/stow-wasm/binary_js.go:10 cannot drift silently; and change the interface hostStore exposes to the runtime - SupportsConditionalWrites at cmd/stow-wasm/host_store_js.go:281 - from a hardcoded true into a declared property of the host store object checked at openHost time (cmd/stow-wasm/async_js.go:34-50), so a host that cannot evaluate conditions is refused when it is bound rather than when a conditional write commits.

title: SigV4 request verification (internal/auth)
summary: internal/auth is the S3 request authentication boundary: the one place a request is authenticated before s3api dispatch. It parses and validates AWS Signature Version 4 in both of its forms — a header Authorization (AWS4-HMAC-SHA256) and a presigned query string — rebuilds the SigV4 canonical request, derives the signing key, and compares the resulting HMAC to the client's signature. It owns the canonical URI/query/header construction, the required signed-header rules, clock-skew and presigned-expiry validation, payload-hash validation, strict parsing of the authentication material (refusing any ambiguity rather than repairing it), the SigV2 refusal, and the local credential generation that hosts such as the CLI and the Workspace facade use to produce the access key and secret the verifier checks against. Its only production callers are internal/s3api (through s3api.SigV4Auth), cmd/stow-s3 serve and pkg/stow's Workspace facade; its own tests and the conformance harness drive it with hand-built and real-SDK signatures.

trace.scope: SigV4Auth wraps auth.Verifier.Authenticate as the s3api.AuthFunc the server holds
ServeHTTP's auth stage calls s.auth(r) after prepareRequestForAuth makes the body replayable
AuthenticateAt parses the query, refuses unconfigured server credentials, and applies Region/MaxSkew defaults
verifySignedRequest runs detect -> credential scope -> amz headers -> time -> payload -> signature
canonicalQueryString encodes names and values, then sorts by the encoded names
hmac.Equal compares the computed signature to the presented one and the verifier returns nil or *auth.Error

evidence.detail: encodedKey := uriEncode(key, true) captures the encoded key, and the sort comparator at lines 66-71 compares those encoded keys (then encoded values), so the canonical query is ordered by the encoded, not decoded, parameter names.

TestCanonicalQueryOrderFollowsTheEncodedNames asserts that 'z=last&%C3%A9=first' canonicalizes to '%C3%A9=first&z=last' — the encoded name %C3%A9 (0x25) sorts before z, which the decoded name would not.

The pinned @smithy/signature-v4 5.7.4 fixture records a request whose query carries the encoded name %C3%A9; node_signer_test.go:19-49 requires every fixture to authenticate, so the encoded ordering is the SDK-compatible one.
The signature comparison is hmac.Equal over the two hex strings (constant time); the comment at 291-292 states the hex is deliberately not case-folded.
DefaultMaxSkew is 15 minutes, applied by NewVerifier (auth.go:28-31) and re-applied in AuthenticateAt when MaxSkew is zero (auth.go:56-59).
Header-auth skew is checked in both directions against maxSkew and returns RequestTimeTooSkewed; a missing/malformed date is refused earlier via parseAmzTime (sigv4.go:419-427).
The presigned branch checks only the future edge (requestTime after now+maxSkew) plus its own expiry, so a URL signed in the past but not yet expired is accepted.
Presigned authentication accepts only GET, PUT and HEAD; any other method is AccessDenied 'unsupported presigned method'.
A header Authorization must supply a Credential, a non-empty SignedHeaders list and a Signature, or it is refused.
parseSignedHeaders refuses a list that is not already ascending, so a client must emit SignedHeaders lower-case, duplicate-free and sorted.
validateCredentialScope requires 'host' in SignedHeaders and, for header auth, the date header (x-amz-date when present, else date).
Every x-amz-* header present on the request must appear in SignedHeaders, except x-amz-content-sha256 for non-presigned requests.

authQueryValue refuses a presigned authentication parameter that appears more than once or under a differently-cased spelling; parsePresignedQuery requires X-Amz-Algorithm, X-Amz-Credential, X-Amz-Date, X-Amz-Expires, X-Amz-SignedHeaders and X-Amz-Signature (lines 32-72).
refuseLegacyScheme names Signature Version 2 in both its presigned and Authorization-header forms and tells the caller to sign with SigV4.
GenerateCredentials issues a 20-character access key and a 40-character secret from a crypto/rand-backed alphabet.
An empty server AccessKeyID or SecretAccessKey refuses every request with 'server credentials are not configured'.

resolveLocalCredentials falls back to STOW_LOCAL_ACCESS_KEY_ID / STOW_LOCAL_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; the flags win and are written back through serveRunThroughConfig (offline.go:42), and main.go:358-368 either uses them or generates a pair.
The Workspace facade generates credentials and wires s3api.SigV4Auth(auth.NewVerifier("us-east-1"), credentials), so the library surface authenticates through this module too.
prepareRequestForAuth supplies http.Request.GetBody so hashRequestBody can read the body for signed-payload verification.

hashRequestBody refuses with 'cannot verify signed payload without request body' when GetBody is nil and a payload hash was signed; verifyPayloadHash skips hashing only for presigned requests or the UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD marker (lines 378-396).

interface.types: A Verifier{Region string; MaxSkew time.Duration} plus two constructor paths: NewVerifier(region) and the package-level Authenticate(r, creds) helper, both defaulting Region to us-east-1 and MaxSkew to 15 minutes. The decision entry points are (v *Verifier).Authenticate(r *http.Request, creds Credentials) error and (v *Verifier).AuthenticateAt(r *http.Request, creds Credentials, now time.Time) error; AuthenticateAt exists so a caller can fix the reference clock. Credentials{AccessKeyID, SecretAccessKey string} is the single server-side pair; GenerateCredentials() (Credentials, error) mints an ephemeral pair. Failure is always *auth.Error{Code, Message string}. Callers pass a *http.Request and receive either nil (authenticated) or an *auth.Error; internal/s3api converts that into an S3 XML error through authError (internal/s3api/auth.go:25-42).
invariants: There is exactly one server-side access key per verifier and no keyring or lookup: sr.credential.accessKeyID must equal creds.AccessKeyID exactly (internal/auth/sigv4.go:313).
The credential service must be 's3' and the credential region must equal Verifier.Region; the credential date stamp must be a prefix of the request date (internal/auth/sigv4.go:316-336).
'host' must always be in SignedHeaders, and for header auth the date header must be too (internal/auth/sigv4.go:322-332).
Every x-amz-* header carried by the request must appear in SignedHeaders, except x-amz-content-sha256 when the request is not presigned (internal/auth/sigv4.go:299-308).
The canonical query percent-encodes names and values and orders them by the encoded key then the encoded value, and drops X-Amz-Signature case-insensitively (internal/auth/sigv4_canonical.go:48-85).
The canonical URI is built from the decoded path, encoded once per segment, so a literal '+' in a path signs as %2B (internal/auth/sigv4_canonical.go:11-23; internal/auth/sigv4.go:439-446).

The canonical header value is the header's full value set: each value trimmed and inner whitespace collapsed to one space, multiple values joined with a comma (internal/auth/sigv4_canonical.go:111-140).

The payload hash defaults to the empty-body SHA-256 when X-Amz-Content-Sha256 is absent; UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD (case-insensitive) skips body hashing; otherwise it must be 64 hex characters and match the body read through GetBody (internal/auth/sigv4.go:237-240, 378-417).

Presigned auth is recognised by X-Amz-Algorithm or X-Amz-Signature in the query and fixes the payload hash to UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD (internal/auth/sigv4.go:214-218; internal/auth/sigv4_presigned_query.go:62-71).
Only SigV4 is implemented; SigV2 is refused by name in both forms (internal/auth/scheme.go:9-38).
A failed decision is always *auth.Error with Code one of AccessDenied, SignatureDoesNotMatch or RequestTimeTooSkewed (internal/auth/errors.go).
error_modes: AccessDenied 'missing Authorization header' — no header and no presigned parameters (internal/auth/sigv4.go:49-51; scheme.go:33-35).
AccessDenied 'malformed Authorization header' — algorithm is not AWS4-HMAC-SHA256, a component repeats or is unknown, or Credential/SignedHeaders/Signature is empty (internal/auth/sigv4.go:53-125).
AccessDenied 'malformed credential scope' — not five slash-separated parts ending aws4_request (internal/auth/sigv4.go:139-150).
AccessDenied 'unknown access key' / 'region mismatch' / 'unsupported service in credential scope' / 'credential date mismatch' (internal/auth/sigv4.go:313-336).
AccessDenied 'host must be signed' / 'date must be signed' (internal/auth/sigv4.go:322-332).
AccessDenied 'malformed SignedHeaders' — empty entry, non-token, uppercase, duplicate or unsorted name (internal/auth/sigv4.go:161-188).
AccessDenied 'missing x-amz-date' / 'malformed request date' when neither X-Amz-Date nor Date is usable (internal/auth/sigv4.go:229-235, 419-427).
RequestTimeTooSkewed 'request time skew too large' — header auth outside MaxSkew in either direction, or a presigned signing time more than MaxSkew ahead (internal/auth/sigv4.go:348-350, 368-370).
AccessDenied 'request has expired' — presigned URL past requestTime + X-Amz-Expires (internal/auth/sigv4.go:371-374).
AccessDenied 'unsupported presigned method' — a presigned request that is not GET, PUT or HEAD (internal/auth/sigv4.go:355-357).
AccessDenied 'invalid X-Amz-Expires' — non-integer, zero, negative, or greater than 604800 seconds (internal/auth/sigv4_presigned_query.go:101-110).
AccessDenied 'ambiguous/repeated/missing presigned authentication parameter' for the X-Amz-* parameters (internal/auth/sigv4_presigned_query.go:32-160).
AccessDenied 'malformed query string' when the RawQuery does not parse (internal/auth/auth.go:46-48).
AccessDenied 'server credentials are not configured' when the host supplied no credential pair (internal/auth/auth.go:49-51).
AccessDenied '%s must be signed' for an unsigned x-amz-* header, and 'missing signed header %q' for a signed name absent from the request (internal/auth/sigv4.go:305-306; sigv4_canonical.go:127-130).
AccessDenied 'invalid x-amz-content-sha256', 'cannot verify signed payload without request body', 'cannot read request body' (internal/auth/sigv4.go:385-416).
SignatureDoesNotMatch 'payload hash mismatch' and SignatureDoesNotMatch 'signature mismatch' (internal/auth/sigv4.go:293-294, 392-394).
ordering: Scheme detection runs first: a query bearing X-Amz-Algorithm or X-Amz-Signature is treated as presigned, otherwise the SigV2 refusal runs, otherwise the Authorization header is parsed (internal/auth/sigv4.go:214-224).
The Authorization header grammar is exactly Credential, SignedHeaders, Signature, each appearing once, parsed by hand (internal/auth/sigv4.go:61-128).
SignedHeaders must arrive lower-case, ascending and duplicate-free; the list is embedded in the canonical request exactly as sent (internal/auth/sigv4.go:152-188, 452-454).
Validation order is: detect scheme, validate credential scope, validate x-amz-* signing, validate time, verify payload hash, then compute and compare the signature (internal/auth/sigv4.go:270-296).

Presigned parameters are read one name at a time and each exactly once; the canonical query separate from them still canonicalizes ordinary repeated parameters by sorting (internal/auth/sigv4_presigned_query.go:20-31).
configuration: Verifier.Region (default us-east-1) and Verifier.MaxSkew (default 15 minutes) are the only verifier configuration (internal/auth/auth.go:10-32).

CLI: --region (default auth.DefaultRegion), --access-key, --secret-key; env fallback STOW_LOCAL_ACCESS_KEY_ID and STOW_LOCAL_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; a generated pair when neither is set (cmd/stow-s3/serve_flags.go:58-67; cmd/stow-s3/main.go:210-217, 358-368).
The server credential pair must be non-empty or every request is refused; there is no way to configure more than one access key (internal/auth/auth.go:49-51).

The body must be replayable (http.Request.GetBody) for a signed-payload request to verify; internal/s3api supplies this at internal/s3api/request.go:238-265, but a caller invoking the verifier directly must arrange it.

implementation: detectSignedRequest branches on the query first: any X-Amz-Algorithm or X-Amz-Signature parameter routes to parsePresignedQuery, which reads six X-Amz-* parameters through authQueryValue (exact case, exactly once, refusing folded variants) and pins the payload hash to UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD (sigv4.go:214-218; sigv4_presigned_query.go:32-160). Otherwise refuseLegacyScheme names SigV2 and the Authorization header is parsed by hand into a signedRequest of credential scope, signed-header list, signature, date and payload hash (sigv4.go:47-242). verifySignedRequest then runs the ordered checks: credential scope (access key, service, region, host-signed, date-signed, date-stamp prefix), x-amz-* headers all signed, request time against MaxSkew (and, for presigned, the future edge plus X-Amz-Expires, bounded to 604800 seconds), payload hash against the body read through GetBody (or UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD / the empty-body hash), and finally the signature (sigv4.go:270-417). The signature is computed by rebuilding the canonical request — canonical URIPath from the decoded path encoded once, canonicalQueryString from encoded names/values sorted by the encoded name, canonicalHeaders from the signed list with each header's full value set normalized — then the string-to-sign, then the AWS4 signing key chain, and compared with hmac.Equal (sigv4_canonical.go, sigv4.go:429-481). Random credential minting lives in credentials.go. The module depends only on the standard library.

callers.scope: SigV4Auth returns an AuthFunc that calls v.Authenticate(r, creds) for every non-admin request
ServeHTTP's auth stage invokes the configured AuthFunc once per request
serve constructs auth.NewVerifier(region) and s3api.SigV4Auth(verifier, creds)
Workspace.Facade starts an authenticated loopback server from auth.GenerateCredentials and auth.NewVerifier
the conformance harness builds its verifier with auth.NewVerifier and drives it with the real AWS SDK as reference signer
the module's own tests exercise Authenticate/AuthenticateAt over hand-built and SDK-built signatures

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Delete internal/auth and the complexity does not vanish; it reconcentrates across every caller. internal/s3api/server.go would have to rebuild canonical request construction, signed-header rules, skew and expiry checks, payload hashing and the HMAC comparison; cmd/stow-s3/main.go:292 and pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go would have to reproduce the local credential-minting the module also owns. The module's small exported surface (Verifier, Credentials, Error, five functions) hides a large body of security-relevant decisions behind it, which is the definition of a deep module.

leverage: Callers get one call — Authenticate or AuthenticateAt — that turns a raw *http.Request into an authenticated-or-refused decision, with SigV4 header auth, presigned URLs, payload hashing, skew/expiry, strict parsing and the SigV2 refusal all handled behind it. The S3 server and the library facade do not encode any signing rule; they only supply a region, a credential pair and (for payload verification) a replayable body.
locality: Maintainers get a single package to change when the signing contract moves. The canonical-query ordering, the required signed-header set and the presigned parameter rules all live in three small files, so a compatibility change (such as the encoded-name ordering in commit bd074095) is reviewable and testable in one place. Knowledge of the failure vocabulary stays in errors.go and the s3api adapter rather than spreading.
risks: The access key ID is compared with a plain string != (internal/auth/sigv4.go:313) while the signature uses hmac.Equal (internal/auth/sigv4.go:293); a reader who assumes the whole path is constant-time would be wrong about the access-key comparison.

The payload hash is compared with strings.EqualFold (internal/auth/sigv4.go:382, 392) while the signature is deliberately not case-folded; both are hex, so the two comparisons are inconsistent and the payload-hash path is not constant-time.

The canonical query ordering by encoded names (internal/auth/sigv4_canonical.go:61-71) is a signing-compatibility boundary with no runtime fallback: an SDK or client that sorts decoded names produces a signature the verifier refuses, and reverting the ordering would silently reject conforming SDKs. It is currently guarded only by query_order_test.go and the pinned Node fixture.

Payload verification depends on the caller having made the body replayable; a caller invoking the verifier directly with a streaming body receives AccessDenied 'cannot verify signed payload without request body' (internal/auth/sigv4.go:404) rather than an authentication decision, so the interface has an ordering requirement on the host that it does not state in its types.
