Presigned validity has no lower bound on the signing time beyond the expiry (internal/auth/sigv4.go:354-376): a URL signed at any past time is accepted until it expires, which is a property callers may not expect from a 'clock skew' check.

priority.rationale: Blast radius is the entire S3 HTTP surface: this is the single gate every non-admin request passes, so a defect admits unauthenticated reads and writes rather than degrading one feature. The demonstrated risks (non-constant-time access-key and payload-hash comparisons, and the encoded-name query ordering that is a silent compatibility boundary guarded only by tests) are interface-level and reachable, which keeps impact at P1 rather than lower; nothing here is demonstrated broken, so it stays below P0.

next_action: Document the exact signing contract and reconcile the two comparison inconsistencies. Add a doc comment on Verifier.AuthenticateAt enumerating the canonical request rules a client must satisfy — encoded-name query ordering, the required host/date signed headers, the every-x-amz-header-must-be-signed rule, the payload-hash default and the presigned parameter uniqueness and expiry ceiling — because callers today must infer them from the test suite. If the inconsistencies are to be fixed, change the internal comparison helpers so the payload hash is compared with the same constant-time primitive as the signature (hmac.Equal), and either make the access-key comparison constant-time or state in the interface that it is not a secret comparison; the only exported interface that would change is the documented behaviour of Verifier.AuthenticateAt.

title: Object-store MCP server (bounded reads, retained saves, read-only browser)
summary: One of the two MCP servers the internal/mcpstorage package builds. NewObjects turns a caller-supplied native object-store directory and one exact bucket into an mcp.Server named "stow-objects" that exposes five scoped object tools and, when enabled, a read-only MCP App bucket browser. Every tool binds the client to the configured bucket: the client cannot name a bucket. Reads return bounded bytes plus an opaque live observation token; saves consume that token (or an explicit replace) together with a persisted request key so an interrupted or re-opened session can resolve the original receipt instead of re-writing. It is the surface the extensions/stow bucket browser and the documented guarded-save workflow (docs/implementation-2026-09-30.md, "Native object MCP wrapper addendum") drive; no ADR describes this MCP object profile.

trace.scope: mcpCommand object mode -> runObjectMCP -> mcpstorage.NewObjects
NewObjects validates config, opens stow.OpenFilesystem, requires the bucket, registers tools
stow_object_save -> saveInput -> runtime.SaveObject with Condition and RequestKey
Instance.SaveObject commits the bytes and, with a RequestKey, the durable save-request receipt through the configured store

evidence.detail: maxObjectPayload is 64 KiB and maxObjectObservations 256; these are the adapter ceilings a caller's MaxObjectBytes/MaxObservations may not exceed

normalizeObjectConfig requires a non-empty Dir and a valid bucket, forbids ReadOnly with CreateBucket, rejects negative bounds, caps MaxObjectBytes/MaxObservations, and defaults them to the adapter maxima
requireBucket refuses when the configured bucket is absent and CreateBucket is false, closing the just-opened runtime
the five object tools are registered: stow_object_read_for_save, stow_object_save, stow_object_resolve_save, stow_object_release_observation, stow_object_capabilities
a read whose body exceeds MaxObjectBytes is refused with payload_too_large before any observation token is retained
saveInput requires a non-empty request_key and exactly one of observation_token or replace:true, otherwise invalid
stow_object_resolve_save calls runtime.ResolveSave with bucket/key/request key, never starting a new save
retainObservation mints a 16-byte hex token capped by MaxObservations; observation() rejects expired, unknown, or wrong-key tokens with distinct codes
limitCalls caps tools/call at 8 concurrent slots and returns code busy when full; oversize arguments return payload_too_large

objectFailureOf maps stow error values to the object code vocabulary (conflict, request_conflict, not_found, not_committed, retention_full, quota_exceeded, invalid, closed, canceled, unsupported, denied, unavailable)
addBrowser registers the read-only stow_browser and stow_object_mentions tools plus the ui://stow/browser-v1 resource and stow://objects/{bucket}/{key} template
readBrowserUI gunzips the embedded bundle and serves it as text/html;profile=mcp-app with an empty CSP domain list

esbuild bundles src/app.ts into JS/CSS, injects it into src/index.html, and tools/mcp-browser-pack compresses the result into the embed target internal/mcpstorage/browser.html.gz; --check asserts the checked-in bundle is byte-identical to a fresh build (line 29)
the caller-visible lifecycle is exercised: read-absence token, committed save, live replay, resolve of the original key, request_conflict on changed bytes, and receipt survival after delete
payload and response limits release the observation and never retain a token on failure; a broken encoding preserves committed/unknown outcome with response_encoding
a real child-process client sees the five object tools, and resolving after a discarded reply and a reopen still returns the committed original object

interface.types: ObjectConfig{Dir, Bucket string; MaxBytes, MaxObjects int64; MaxObjectBytes, MaxObservations int; CreateBucket, ReadOnly, Browser bool}; NewObjects(ObjectConfig) (*ObjectServer, error); ObjectServer{Server *mcp.Server; runtime *stow.Runtime; config ObjectConfig; mu sync.Mutex; observations map[string]objectObservation; now func() time.Time; closed bool} with Close() error. The server announces implementation name "stow-objects" version 1. Tool inputs are objectKeyInput{key}, objectSaveInput{key, data_base64, content_type?, metadata?, observation_token?, replace?, request_key}, objectResolveInput{key, request_key}, objectReleaseInput{observation_token}, objectCapabilitiesInput{}. Every tool returns the objectResult envelope {version:1, outcome, available, object?, observation_token?, absent, replayed, released?, capabilities?, error?} duplicated as StructuredContent and as a text block. stow.Runtime is pkg/stow's alias of internal/embedded.Runtime (pkg/stow/runtime.go:6).
invariants: NewObjects refuses an empty Dir, an invalid bucket name, ReadOnly together with CreateBucket, any negative bound, MaxObjectBytes above 65536, or MaxObservations above 256 (internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:68-93).
The configured bucket must exist unless CreateBucket is set; otherwise the runtime is closed and construction fails (internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:95-108).

The client cannot choose a bucket: every handler reads config.Bucket and the tool input structs declare no bucket or path field, so an unknown input field such as bucket is rejected by the SDK schema validation; the test asserts rejection of bucket, path and if_match (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:14-33, 60, 86, 119, 172, internal/mcpstorage/object_server_test.go:109-120).
Reads are bounded twice: a head of size greater than MaxObjectBytes and a body longer than MaxObjectBytes both produce payload_too_large (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:64-66, 82-104).

A save requires exactly one of observation_token or replace:true and a non-empty request_key; the request key determines idempotent replay, not the bytes alone (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:132-150).

An observation token is bound to one key and expires observer-side after 15 minutes; the number retained is capped by MaxObservations (internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:16-17, internal/mcpstorage/object_observations.go:40-50).
At most 8 tools/call requests are served concurrently; the ninth is refused with code busy (internal/mcpstorage/object_admission.go:10-31).

Every encoded response is bounded to maxResponseBytes = 256 KiB; overflow becomes response_too_large or response_encoding without claiming a state change (internal/mcpstorage/results.go:12, internal/mcpstorage/object_results.go:65-94).
error_modes: Validation, authority, and lifecycle failures surface inside objectResult.error with a stable code and message "object request <code>" or "object operation <code>" (internal/mcpstorage/object_results.go:104-129).

Codes the client must distinguish include invalid, invalid_observation, expired_observation, observation_full, payload_too_large, response_too_large, response_encoding, conflict, request_conflict, not_found, not_committed, retention_full, quota_exceeded, denied, closed, canceled, unsupported, busy, unavailable (internal/mcpstorage/object_results.go:104-129, internal/mcpstorage/object_observations.go:45-48).
A read-only host returns code denied because saveAuthority checks ObjectWrite on the runtime authority (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:123-129).

A failed finishObject still reports the committed/unknown outcome with the error attached, so an effect is never reported as absent (internal/mcpstorage/object_results.go:65-94, internal/mcpstorage/object_bounds_test.go:74-87).
ordering: read_for_save must precede a guarded save: the returned observation token is the live comparison condition (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:44-80).
On a lost or uncertain reply, the caller resolves the original request_key instead of re-reading and blindly retrying; resolve never starts a new save (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:162-174).
release_observation is idempotent: repeating the release succeeds and the durable receipts are unaffected (internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:176-188).

Close marks the host closed, clears volatile observations, and closes the runtime; later calls return code closed (internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:111-117, internal/mcpstorage/object_observations.go:53-60).
configuration: Object mode is selected by visiting --object-dir or --bucket; both are required for a usable host (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:63-64, 77).

The single `mcp` verb serves exactly one profile: validateMCPMode refuses the other profile's flags before any storage is opened, so a client never has both servers in one process (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:74-88).
Optional flags: --max-objects (10000), --max-object-bytes (65536, capped at 65536), --max-observations (256, capped at 256), --create-bucket, --read-only, --browser (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:65-70).
--max-bytes is shared with the workspace profile and is copied into ObjectConfig.MaxBytes before NewObjects runs (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:44, 58).
The object profile reads no environment variables; all scope and bounds come from flags.

implementation: ObjectServer owns the runtime, the config, a mutex serialising every tool, an observation map keyed by random token, an injectable clock, and a closed flag. NewObjects validates the config, applies authority ReadWrite or ReadOnly, opens the filesystem runtime, requires or creates the bucket, registers the tools, and conditionally adds the browser. object_tools.go implements the five verbs: readObject preflights key validity and size, calls runtime.ReadForSave, retains the observation, and deletes the token if the response fails; saveObject validates token-XOR-replace and request key, base64-decodes strictly, and calls runtime.SaveObject; resolveObject calls runtime.ResolveSave; releaseObservation deletes the token; objectCapabilities returns the runtime capability set plus the adapter bounds. object_observations.go mints, reaps, and validates tokens. object_admission.go is a receiving middleware that caps concurrency at 8 and shrinks oversize results. object_results.go builds the envelope and maps stow errors to codes. browser.go adds the two read-only browser tools and the two resources; browser_ui.go decompresses the embedded bundle; the bundle itself is generated by extensions/stow/build.mjs and checked in as browser.html.gz. The durable save-request receipts themselves live in the filesystem store reached through internal/runtime's SaveRequestStore path, not in this module; the module owns only the request-key contract and the token that binds a save to a live observation.

callers.scope: runObjectMCP calls mcpstorage.NewObjects and serves objects.Server over stdio; the only non-test caller in the repository
launches the built binary as `mcp --object-dir ... --bucket objects` and drives it through a real MCP client
constructs ObjectServer directly and asserts the tool schemas, capabilities, and unsafe-field rejection

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting NewObjects would push the whole bounded-read/guarded-save protocol onto every host that wanted it: the 64 KiB read ceiling, the token-XOR-replace rule, strict base64 validation, the request-key replay, the observation TTL and pool, the 8-way admission limit, the 256 KiB response bound, the error-code vocabulary, and the bucket scoping. Those are decisions the client cannot re-derive from stow.Runtime, so the complexity concentrates rather than vanishing: the module is deep.

leverage: A host gets one self-contained, bucket-scoped guarded-save service: five tools that encode idempotent saves, bounded reads, expiring observations, and a read-only browser with no protocol logic of its own.
locality: Change concentrates in four files: object_server.go (config, bucket, lifecycle, browser toggle), object_tools.go (verb semantics), object_observations.go (token lifecycle), and object_results.go (codes and envelope).
risks: The bucket is fixed at construction and never recomputed, so an MCP client that expects multi-bucket access silently has no way to reach a second bucket (internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:19-25, 68-93).

Observation tokens live in process memory only; after a restart the client must fall back to stow_object_resolve_save with the original request key, and a client that re-reads instead can act on a newer version (internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:33-41, internal/mcpstorage/object_workflows_test.go:94-126).

The browser and the save tools share one runtime and one mutex, so a large listing or preview serialises against saves (internal/mcpstorage/browser.go:59-81, internal/mcpstorage/object_tools.go:44-121).

The object server and the workspace server are two profiles of one package: they share the maxResponseBytes constant (internal/mcpstorage/results.go:12, used at results.go:75 and object_results.go:81) and one CLI flag set (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:54-71), so changing the workspace response bound also moves the object bound without a declared relationship. Their implementation names (stow-objects vs stow-storage) and stow:// resource namespaces (stow://objects/{bucket}/{key} vs stow://guides/checkpoints/v1) are disjoint, and only one profile runs per process, so a client cannot confuse the two servers themselves.

priority.rationale: Blast radius is bounded to one caller (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go) and the developer-supplied object directory, but the scoping and replay rules are subtle enough that a scoping mistake or a token/replay confusion would surface as silent data loss to an agent. Unclear seam and hidden coupling inside one package raise it above P3; no repository-wide blast radius keeps it below P1.

next_action: Document the object server as its own module in the MCP-tool-servers overview, separate from the workspace server: state the exact client contract (one fixed bucket, read-then-save with a persisted request_key, resolve instead of retry, 64 KiB read and 256 KiB response bounds, 15-minute observation TTL) and name the shared package as a container rather than a module. The concrete interface to change is ObjectConfig: if the two servers are to remain one package, factor the shared envelope and maxResponseBytes into an internal leaf so the two server contracts stop sharing hidden state by file proximity.

title: Workspace and checkpoint MCP server
summary: The workspace/checkpoint half of internal/mcpstorage. New turns a registry directory and one workspace ID into an mcp.Server named "stow-storage" that exposes five tools (a workspace inspect plus four checkpoint verbs) and, only when transfer roots are configured, two handoff tools, alongside the stow://guides/checkpoints/v1 resource. It is the read/inspect/capture surface for a single named workspace: capture and resolve are request-key idempotent, inspect and diff are paginated with a cursor bound to the checkpoint, and every workspace-bearing request is refused unless the ID is the configured workspace or one adopted through stow_handoff_adopt. The adapter holds no runtime and no workspace handle; it stores only Config plus an in-memory adopted set and re-resolves the workspace through pkg/stow on every call.

trace.scope: mcpCommand workspace branch -> mcpstorage.New(options.workspace); taken only when validateMCPMode finds neither --object-dir nor --bucket visited
New validates config, resolves RegistryDir to an absolute path, looks the workspace up once, registers the five tools and the guide resource
stow_checkpoint_create -> request() -> stow.CaptureCheckpoint under context.WithTimeout(ctx, config.Timeout)
CaptureCheckpoint re-looks-up and locks the workspace, then writes the checkpoint into the configured registry for that workspace

evidence.detail: New requires a non-empty RegistryDir and WorkspaceID and positive MaxBytes/MaxFiles/Timeout; it then absolutizes RegistryDir with filepath.Abs (a relative dir is accepted), confirms the workspace exists via stow.LookupWorkspace, and only then builds the server
five tools are added at lines 62-66: stow_workspace_inspect, stow_checkpoint_create, stow_checkpoint_resolve, stow_checkpoint_inspect, stow_checkpoint_diff
the guide resource stow://guides/checkpoints/v1 returns the Guide text, which is also passed as the server's Instructions
scope() permits only config.WorkspaceID or an ID present in the in-memory adopted set; every workspace-bearing tool calls it
checkpoint() loads a checkpoint with stow.LoadCheckpoint and then applies scope() to the checkpoint's own WorkspaceID, so inspect/diff/export cannot cross into another workspace
request() rejects negative limits or limits wider than the configured bounds and substitutes the configured bound when the request sends zero

capture and resolve run under context.WithTimeout(ctx, config.Timeout); both build the same CheckpointRequest (key plus options) and call stow.CaptureCheckpoint / stow.ResolveCheckpoint with the registry dir and workspace ID, so the workspace is re-resolved per call rather than held as a handle
page() defaults the limit to 100, refuses limits outside 1..1000, and binds the cursor to a sha256 of registry dir + workspace ID + checkpoint identity
stow_handoff_export is added when ExportRoot is set and stow_handoff_adopt only when both ExportRoot and AdoptRoot are set

adopt validates the bundle and destination as visible direct children, refuses symlinks and non-regular files, rejects a bundle team, and only registers the adopted workspace after a successful import
finish builds the version-1 result envelope and maps errors to failure{code,phase,attempts,retryable,message}, preferring CheckpointError and HandoffError details

validateMCPMode selects object mode when --object-dir or --bucket was visited and otherwise leaves the default workspace branch; each mode refuses the other mode's flags, so the CLI cannot start both servers
the caller-visible contract is exercised: capture then resolve replays the same checkpoint ID, an out-of-scope workspace_id is refused, and the guide resource equals Guide
a real child-process client launches `mcp --registry-dir ... --workspace-id ... --timeout 10s`, lists exactly 5 workspace tools, and captures/resolves over stdio

interface.types: Config{RegistryDir, WorkspaceID string; MaxBytes, MaxFiles int64; Timeout time.Duration; ExportRoot, AdoptRoot string}; New(Config) (*mcp.Server, error). The adapter it builds stores only the Config plus an in-memory adopted map; it neither opens nor receives a runtime or workspace handle, re-resolving the workspace through pkg/stow on every call. The server announces implementation name "stow-storage" version 1 with the Guide text as instructions. Tool inputs: workspaceInput{workspace_id}; captureInput{workspace_id, request_key, parent_id?, max_bytes?, max_files?}; inspectInput{checkpoint_id, limit?, cursor?}; diffInput{from_id, to_id, limit?, cursor?}; exportInput{workspace_id, checkpoint_id, bundle}; adoptInput{bundle, destination, expect_sha256?}. Every tool returns result{version:1, outcome, workspace?, capture?, checkpoint_id?, entries?, next_cursor?, handoff?, bundle?, origin_checkpoint_id?, error?}.
invariants: Both RegistryDir and WorkspaceID are mandatory and the workspace must already exist in the registry at construction time; RegistryDir is absolutized, so a relative path is accepted (internal/mcpstorage/server.go:43-56).
Every workspace_id in a request must equal config.WorkspaceID or an ID adopted through stow_handoff_adopt; otherwise the request is refused (internal/mcpstorage/server.go:74-82).

Inspect/diff/export resolve the checkpoint first and then re-check scope against the checkpoint's own WorkspaceID, so a checkpoint ID cannot be used to read another workspace (internal/mcpstorage/server.go:84-90).
Capture/resolve limits must be non-negative and no larger than the configured bounds; zero means use the configured bound (internal/mcpstorage/capture.go:38-46).

Capture and resolve share one CheckpointRequest (key plus parent/max options); resolve never creates a new checkpoint and replays the original (internal/mcpstorage/capture.go:34-48, internal/mcpstorage/server.go:64).
Page limits are 1..1000 with a default of 100, and a cursor from one checkpoint/workspace/registry cannot be replayed on another (internal/mcpstorage/inspect.go:85-107).
An adopt that imports a checkpoint but then fails returns outcome partial_import so the caller does not treat it as a clean failure (internal/mcpstorage/handoff.go:124-131).

The adapter holds no workspace state beyond the config and the adopted set; every call that needs the workspace re-looks it up by ID (internal/mcpstorage/capture.go:27,55,68; internal/mcpstorage/server.go:85).
error_modes: Validation and scope failures become failure{code:"invalid_request", phase:"validation", message:err} with outcome "failed" (internal/mcpstorage/results.go:55-59).
A *stow.CheckpointError supplies its own outcome, code, phase, attempts, and retryable, so a caller can distinguish a retryable capture from a terminal one (internal/mcpstorage/results.go:60-64).

A *stow.HandoffError becomes code "outcome_unknown", phase "commit", attempts 1, retryable false; the bundle receipt is preserved (internal/mcpstorage/results.go:65-69, internal/mcpstorage/handoff_reader_test.go:60-69).
A response larger than 256 KiB is rejected with a message to request a smaller page rather than truncated (internal/mcpstorage/results.go:75-77).
ordering: capture or resolve runs under a per-call timeout derived from config.Timeout; a zero timeout is rejected at construction (internal/mcpstorage/server.go:46-48, internal/mcpstorage/capture.go:55-57).
stow_handoff_adopt registers the new workspace ID in the adopted set only after the import succeeds, so later inspect/diff calls accept it (internal/mcpstorage/handoff.go:133-137).

resolve must reuse the original request key and options; a changed key creates a different request and a changed option payload is rejected as a request_conflict (internal/mcpstorage/server.go:64, pkg/stow/checkpoint_request.go:149-151).
configuration: Workspace mode requires --registry-dir and --workspace-id and a positive --timeout; --max-bytes (default 1GiB) and --max-files (default 100000) set the capture ceilings (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:56-62).

The CLI selects this server when neither --object-dir nor --bucket was visited; object mode (mcpstorage.NewObjects) wins when either was, and each mode rejects the other's flags (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:43-51,74-88).
--export-root enables stow_handoff_export; --adopt-root additionally enables stow_handoff_adopt (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go:60-61, internal/mcpstorage/handoff.go:52-58).

Both roots are absolutized and resolved once at construction and must already exist as directories; adopt re-pins the export root's directory identity per call through internal/rooted rather than trusting the startup value (internal/mcpstorage/handoff.go:27-50,102).
The workspace profile reads no environment variables; all scope and bounds come from flags (no os.Getenv/os.LookupEnv anywhere in internal/mcpstorage).

implementation: adapter holds the config, a read-write mutex, and the in-memory adopted-workspace set; it holds no store, runtime, or workspace handle. New validates config, absolutizes the registry, looks the workspace up, validates the export/adopt roots, registers the five tools plus the conditional handoff tools, and adds the guide resource. capture.go resolves and bounds the request, then calls stow.CaptureCheckpoint / stow.ResolveCheckpoint (registry dir + workspace ID) under the configured timeout, so the workspace is re-resolved and locked inside pkg/stow on each call. inspect.go flattens checkpoint entries (files, objects, buckets, exclusions) and diff changes into a single paged list with a digest-bound cursor. handoff.go validates bundle/destination as visible direct children, refuses symlinks and special files, reads handoff.json through a rooted file, rejects a bundle team, and calls stow.AdoptHandoffArchive. results.go encodes the version-1 envelope and maps stow error types onto failure codes. Everything workspace-bearing passes through scope(), and checkpoints are additionally scoped by their own WorkspaceID. The browser bundle (browser.html.gz, embedded by the object server in browser.go and served only when ObjectConfig.Browser is set) is not part of this module.

callers.scope: mcpCommand workspace mode calls mcpstorage.New and serves the returned server over stdio; the only non-test caller in the repository
launches the built binary as `mcp --registry-dir ... --workspace-id ... --timeout 10s` and drives the five tools through a real MCP client
constructs the server against a freshly opened workspace and asserts capture/resolve replay, scope refusal, pagination, and the guide resource

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting New would push the checkpoint workflow surface onto the CLI: request-key idempotence for capture/resolve, narrowing of caller-supplied capture limits, the digest-bound pagination cursor, the workspace/checkpoint scope checks, the timeout wrapping, the handoff bundle path validation, and the outcome/error mapping. None of that is derivable from stow's exported checkpoint calls, so the complexity concentrates in the one caller rather than vanishing: the module is deep (though the single caller keeps its blast radius small).

leverage: A host gets an idempotent, single-workspace checkpoint service: five tools that encode capture, resolve, paginated inspect and diff, and optional bundle export/adopt, with scope and outcome semantics already decided.
locality: Change concentrates in server.go (scope and registration), capture.go (bounds and timeout), inspect.go (entry flattening and cursors), and handoff.go (roots and bundle validation); results.go holds the shared envelope.
risks: The adopted-workspace set is process-local memory, so a restart drops adopted IDs and makes those workspaces out of scope until they are adopted again (internal/mcpstorage/server.go:36-40, internal/mcpstorage/handoff.go:134-136).

Handoff export/adopt act on the MCP server process's own filesystem; the roots are fixed at startup, and although adopt re-pins the export root's identity per call through internal/rooted, a root swapped before the first adopt is trusted for the bundle name (internal/mcpstorage/handoff.go:52-58, 93-139).

Inspect and diff materialise the whole checkpoint entry list before paging, so a very large checkpoint is bounded only by the 256 KiB response limit, not by the page size (internal/mcpstorage/inspect.go:38-55).

priority.rationale: One caller (cmd/stow-s3/mcp.go) and one registry directory bound the blast radius, but the scope checks and request-key idempotence are the load-bearing safety properties for agent checkpointing; a scope regression would let one workspace read another's checkpoint. That consequence plus the process-local adopted set keeps it at P2, not P3 or P1.

next_action: Document the workspace/checkpoint server as its own module in the MCP-tool-servers overview, listing its five tools plus the two conditional handoff tools, its scope rule (configured workspace plus adopted IDs, and checkpoints re-scoped by their own WorkspaceID), its pagination and outcome/error vocabulary, its per-call workspace re-resolution, and the exact flags a client must supply. The concrete interface to change is Config: the adopted-workspace set is invisible to a caller yet changes what every later call accepts, so either persist it or expose it as part of the server's state rather than hiding it behind scope().

title: Session readiness record (serve -> inherited fd -> TS and Python readers)
summary: One value - the session readiness record - flows from `stow-s3 serve` to the two client packages. The Go package internal/ready defines it (constant ProtocolVersion=1 and a Message with eight value fields plus a Capabilities sub-object) and publishes exactly one newline-terminated JSON object to a caller-supplied inherited file descriptor, or - when no descriptor is supplied, the --ready-fd default of -1 - to the legacy STOW_READY stdout line instead. The TypeScript reader in packages/stow-s3/src/ready-reader.ts frames and packages/stow-s3/src/ready.ts parses it; the Python reader in packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/session.py reads the client-allocated pipe and packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/ready.py parses it. Each side rejects any protocolVersion other than 1 with a named protocol_mismatch error. The load-bearing fact is that the three implementations do not share a schema or definition file: the Go structs, the TypeScript interfaces and the Python dataclasses restate the field set independently, and they already disagree - the writer publishes capabilities.maxMultipartUploads, which neither reader declares, and ADR 0004's canonical example documents neither that field nor maxConcurrentRequests.

trace.scope: serve calls announceStartup(opts.readyFd, readyDetails{...}) only after the listener has bound and srv.Addr() is non-empty; this is the single publication site for the readiness record
WriteToFd rejects fd<0, json.Marshal's Message and writes exactly one append(encoded,'\n') to os.NewFile(fd); the descriptor is not closed, and a marshal or write failure is returned (not swallowed)

the TypeScript onReadyData accumulates child.stdio[READY_FD=3] text (descriptor selected at line 114) and only parses newline-terminated records via takeCompleteRecords, failing an unterminated tail over 256 KiB
parseReadyMessage rejects non-JSON, non-objects, protocolVersion !== 1, a missing capabilities object, and any missing or wrong-typed field with StowProtocolError

parse_ready_message is the Python parser: it rejects invalid JSON, non-objects, protocolVersion != 1, a missing capabilities object, and any missing or wrong-typed field with StowProtocolError; it is called from session.py:362 after _read_ready_line (session.py:208-251) reads one line off the client-allocated pipe on a daemon thread

the parsed StowReady configures the StowInstance (endpoint/accessKeyId/secretAccessKey/mode from ready.line, region from ready.message) and is returned as startStowWithReady().ready; Python lands the same value in a Session (session.py:363-380)

evidence.detail: ProtocolVersion = 1 is the Go definition of the message shape; Message (ready.go:43-53) and Capabilities (ready.go:21-40) fix the wire field names in json tags
WriteToFd is the single publication point: one JSON object plus newline to an inherited fd, never closed, fd<0 rejected, marshal/write errors returned

announceStartup writes to the descriptor when readyFd>=0 and returns, deliberately suppressing the legacy STOW_READY stdout line; with no --ready-fd (default -1) it prints the STOW_READY line with credentials to stdout instead
--ready-fd defaults to -1, so the versioned channel is opt-in and the no-descriptor path is the legacy stdout line
READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1 restated in TypeScript; StowReady (ready.ts:21-31) and StowReadyCapabilities (ready.ts:9-19) are a second, independent definition of the field set

READY_FD = 3 is the TypeScript launcher's descriptor convention (start.ts:174 passes --ready-fd 3, start.ts:293 opens stdio slot 3); Python instead allocates a pipe fd (session.py:313), so no descriptor number is shared
READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1 restated a third time; StowReady (ready.py:64-76) and StowCapabilities (ready.py:38-61) are the third independent definition
capabilities.maxMultipartUploads is published by the writer (and filled at main.go:89) but is absent from both readers' capability types and from ADR 0004's example
the ADR's canonical readiness example (lines 88-109) omits both maxMultipartUploads and maxConcurrentRequests, so the documented schema already trails the Go writer

the cross-language version gate compares SESSION_GOGC (check-version.mjs:169-183) and STOW_OWNER_MARKER (:185-198) between Go and the clients, but no gate compares READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION or the readiness field set - there is no generated schema to compare against
the end-to-end contract test restates a fifth, partial record shape (readyRecord, no capabilities) and hardcodes protocolVersion 1 at line 179, confirming there is no generated type to reuse
the Python parser suite asserts protocolVersion 99 is rejected with code protocol_mismatch and the client's version echoed in the message

interface.types: One newline-terminated JSON object. Top level: protocolVersion (int), binaryVersion, endpoint, region, accessKeyId, secretAccessKey, mode, backend (all strings), and capabilities (object). capabilities: persistent, multipart, upstream, conditionalWrites, presignedUrls (booleans); maxBytes, maxObjects, maxRequestBytes (numbers, 0 = no limit reported); maxMultipartUploads (number, Go writer only); maxConcurrentRequests (number, always emitted by Go, optional in TypeScript, defaulted to 0 in Python only when absent). Go side: ready.Message, ready.Capabilities, ready.Input, ready.New(Input) Message, ready.WriteToFd(fd int, Message) error, ready.ReportedLimit(int64) int64, const ProtocolVersion = 1. TypeScript side: StowReady, StowReadyCapabilities, READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION (=1), StowProtocolError (code: protocol_mismatch|cancelled|internal), parseReadyMessage(line) StowReady. Python side: StowReady, StowCapabilities, READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION (=1), StowProtocolError(code, message), parse_ready_message(line) StowReady.
invariants: Exactly one JSON object, terminated by a newline, is written to the readiness descriptor; a reader must not parse an unterminated fragment (ready.go:114, ready-reader.ts:190-205, ready-framing.ts:30-34).

The record is published to a caller-supplied inherited descriptor and not to stdout when --ready-fd is set; with --ready-fd absent (default -1) the legacy STOW_READY stdout line is printed instead, credentials included (main.go:47-61, serve_flags.go:81).
The writer never closes the descriptor: the client owns the pipe and may read past the first record (ready.go:96-101).
protocolVersion must equal 1; a reader rejects any other value with code protocol_mismatch rather than guessing (ready.ts:95-101, ready.py:118-124).
A capability limit of 0 means 'the server reported no limit' and is carried through unchanged, never treated as missing or as unlimited (ready.go:55-67, ready.py:55-61, test_ready.py:116-125).
Credentials travel only in this record, never on stdout, when the versioned channel is used (probe_contract_test.go:210-221).
error_modes: Go writer: fd<0 returns 'ready: file descriptor must not be negative'; a marshal failure returns 'ready: encode'; a write failure returns 'ready: write to fd <n>'; the serve caller turns any of these into log.Fatalf (ready.go:102-117, main.go:63-67).

TypeScript reader: invalid JSON, a non-object payload, protocolVersion !== 1, a missing capabilities object, or any missing/wrong-typed field throws StowProtocolError with code protocol_mismatch (ready.ts:82-127); an unterminated record over 256 KiB is protocol_mismatch (ready-reader.ts:197-205); a descriptor that closes before a record rejects after a 50 ms grace (ready-reader.ts:237-253); the child exiting first rejects with the exit code and captured stdout/stderr (ready-reader.ts:163-175); an abort rejects with code cancelled (ready-reader.ts:147-155).

TypeScript fallback: a server that ignores --ready-fd and prints only the legacy STOW_READY stdout line is still parsed, and its capabilities are reported as false/0 with backend 'unknown' rather than invented (ready-reader.ts:27-42,79-100,255-276).

Python reader: invalid JSON, a non-object payload, protocolVersion != 1, a missing capabilities object, or any missing/wrong-typed field raises StowProtocolError with code protocol_mismatch (ready.py:103-149); a reader that times out raises TimeoutError (session.py:237-242); an empty/absent line raises StowProtocolError code 'internal' (session.py:243-251).
Python has no legacy STOW_READY fallback: a server that ignores --ready-fd produces no line on the pipe and the session fails rather than being configured from stdout (session.py:208-251,362).
ordering: The record is published only after the HTTP listener has bound and srv.Addr() is non-empty, so the endpoint is the port actually bound rather than the requested one (main.go:406-420).

announceStartup prints the banner first, then the listening line, then the record; a launcher must drain stdout or a large banner could stall the child (main.go:48-51, probe_contract_test.go:137-141).
In Python, the parent closes its copy of the pipe's write end only after Popen, so the reader sees EOF if the child dies before writing (session.py:354-358).
TypeScript resolves only after a newline is seen; the trailing partial fragment is carried to the next read (ready-reader.ts:190-196).
configuration: --ready-fd on serve selects the descriptor and defaults to -1, meaning the legacy stdout line (serve_flags.go:81).
TypeScript pins its launcher descriptor to READY_FD=3 and passes stdio slot 3 to spawn (ready-reader.ts:63, start.ts:174, start.ts:291-295).

Python allocates the descriptor with os.pipe() and passes it in pass_fds, because CPython closes inherited descriptors above 2 unless they are named (session.py:313-314,338; session.py:265-270 comment).
The record's mode/backend/region/capabilities are reconciled from CLI flags, environment and the runtime instance before publication (main.go:69-94,420-431).

implementation: internal/ready is a small, single-purpose writer: constant ProtocolVersion (ready.go:18), Capabilities and Message structs with json tags (ready.go:21-53), ReportedLimit to keep an unlimited int64 out of the JSON number space (ready.go:55-67), New(Input) to copy the fields (ready.go:82-94), and WriteToFd to marshal and write one newline-terminated line without closing the descriptor (ready.go:102-117). The serve verb maps its runtime into that Input in readyMessage, deriving Upstream from the mode and taking MaxMultipartUploads from the runtime capabilities (main.go:69-94), then publishes through announceStartup (main.go:420). cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go is a second consumer of the package, reading ready.ProtocolVersion into its report (doctor.go:115). The TypeScript reader re-implements the whole contract: its own constant and interfaces (ready.ts:7-31), a strict requireString/requireBoolean/requireNumber parser (ready.ts:54-127), newline framing with a size ceiling (ready-reader.ts:190-225, ready-framing.ts:30-34), a fixed launcher descriptor 3 (ready-reader.ts:63,114), and a legacy-stdout fallback that manufactures a message (ready-reader.ts:27-42,79-100,255-276). The Python reader does the same a third time in ready.py:103-149, with its own bool-is-int guard (ready.py:86-100), reading a dynamically allocated pipe fd (session.py:313-338,361-362) and building a Session from the parsed fields (session.py:363-380). The three definitions are maintained by hand and already diverge: the writer publishes capabilities.maxMultipartUploads (ready.go:36, main.go:89) that neither reader declares (ready.ts:9-19, ready.py:38-61), maxConcurrentRequests is unconditional in Go (ready.go:39) but declared optional in TypeScript (ready.ts:18) and defaulted in Python only when absent (ready.py:148), and ADR 0004's example (docs/adr/0004-agent-session-contract.md:88-109) is missing both fields. The only executable cross-check is the Go contract test, which restates yet another partial shape without capabilities (probe_contract_test.go:56-65). No generated fixture exists: internal/ready/testdata/ready-v1.json, named as a MUST in docs/history/architecture/environment-implementation.md:693, is absent from the tree.

callers.scope: the CLI command table dispatches `serve`, the host that publishes the record (announceStartup at main.go:420)
the doctor report copies ready.ProtocolVersion into its own protocolVersion field, a second production consumer of the package's constant
startStowWithReady awaits waitForReady(child, ...) and configures the instance from the result
open_session parses the record and hands back a Session
the writer's own test asserts exactly one JSON line and rejects a negative descriptor
the TypeScript parser suite asserts protocolVersion 99 is rejected with protocol_mismatch
the Python parser suite asserts the same version rejection
the end-to-end test runs the real binary and asserts the record carries the bound endpoint and credentials

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting internal/ready removes the Go half of the protocol: the field names, the version constant, the ReportedLimit normalization and the one-line fd write would have to move into cmd/stow-s3 (its only importing package, main.go and doctor.go), so that complexity concentrates rather than vanishes, and the write path is genuinely load-bearing. But the field set itself is already restated independently in the two readers, in the fallback in ready-reader.ts and in ADR 0004, so deleting the Go package does not remove the duplication that carries the risk; it only moves the writer. The interface's depth is in the wire contract it fixes and the credential-off-stdout decision it encodes, not in the size of the code.

leverage: Callers get a single defined message and a version they can reject on: a launcher in any language reads one descriptor and learns the bound endpoint, the generated credentials, the region, the mode and the limits the server is enforcing, without parsing human-readable logs and without a credential appearing on stdout. The strict readers convert a shape change into an immediate, named protocol_mismatch instead of a half-configured session that fails later.
locality: The writer lives entirely in internal/ready plus the mapping in cmd/stow-s3/main.go (and one constant read in doctor.go). The protocol knowledge, however, is not local: the field set is spread across internal/ready/ready.go, packages/stow-s3/src/ready.ts, packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/ready.py, the fallback in packages/stow-s3/src/ready-reader.ts, the partial struct in cmd/stow-s3/probe_contract_test.go, and the ADR example. A field change requires editing the writer and both parsers by hand, and nothing compares them.
risks: No shared schema: the Go structs (ready.go:21-53), the TypeScript interfaces (ready.ts:9-31) and the Python dataclasses (ready.py:38-76) restate the field set independently, with three separate version constants (ready.go:18, ready.ts:7, ready.py:19); nothing generates one from another, no fixture is shared (internal/ready/testdata/ready-v1.json is named as a MUST at environment-implementation.md:693 but does not exist), and check-version.mjs gates SESSION_GOGC and STOW_OWNER_MARKER but not READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION (check-version.mjs:169-198), so a field added to the writer can silently disappear from the clients.

The writer already publishes capabilities.maxMultipartUploads (ready.go:36, main.go:89) that neither reader declares or reads (ready.ts:9-19, ready.py:38-61), so a client cannot report or enforce the outstanding-multipart limit the server actually applies.

ADR 0004's canonical example (docs/adr/0004-agent-session-contract.md:88-109) omits maxMultipartUploads and maxConcurrentRequests, so the document a new implementer would follow is already behind the writer; a third client built from the ADR would be incomplete.

The two reference clients embed different descriptor conventions: TypeScript pins index 3 (ready-reader.ts:63, start.ts:174) while Python allocates a dynamic pipe fd and passes it in pass_fds (session.py:265-270,313,338). The wire protocol deliberately does not fix a descriptor number - it is a --ready-fd argument - so the fd choice is restated per client rather than shared, and a launcher that copies one client's convention does not transfer to the other.

Python has no legacy STOW_READY fallback while TypeScript does (ready-reader.ts:255-276), so a server that ignores --ready-fd is usable from TypeScript and fails the Python session (session.py:243-251) even though ADR 0004:84 says the legacy line 'remains supported'.

maxConcurrentRequests is unconditional on the wire in Go (ready.go:39, no omitempty) but declared optional in TypeScript (ready.ts:18) and defaulted to 0 in Python only when absent (ready.py:148); the two readers therefore tolerate a record that omits the field while the writer never omits it, and the clients agree on its requiredness by accident rather than by a shared definition.

priority.rationale: The blast radius of a change to this record is both published client packages, and the coupling is hidden: three hand-maintained definitions, three version constants, no generated schema and no drift gate, with one field (maxMultipartUploads) already diverged. It is startup-only and does not touch the S3 request path, so impact stays at P2 rather than P1; the unclear seam is what raises it above a cosmetic concern.

next_action: Write the readiness message down once as a machine-checkable contract generated from internal/ready/ready.go (for example the internal/ready/testdata/ready-v1.json fixture already specified in docs/history/architecture/environment-implementation.md:693, or a small codegen step), add a gate that compares the required capability field names and the protocol version against READY_PROTOCOL_VERSION in packages/stow-s3/src/ready.ts and packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/ready.py, and extend scripts/check-version.mjs (currently gating only SESSION_GOGC and STOW_OWNER_MARKER) to cover it. The concrete interfaces to reconcile are ready.Capabilities (internal/ready/ready.go:21-40), StowReadyCapabilities (packages/stow-s3/src/ready.ts:9-19) and StowCapabilities (packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/ready.py:38-61), and ADR 0004's example (docs/adr/0004-agent-session-contract.md:88-109) should be regenerated from it.

title: Run-through adapter: an authoritative local store with a read-through cache and consent-gated upstream propagation
summary: internal/runthrough is the package that turns a real S3-compatible provider into something an agent can use without holding the provider's credential. Its Adapter implements storage.Store and storage.MultipartStore over three stores: an authoritative local store, an optional separate cache store, and an optional upstream Client. Reads resolve local first, then the cache, then the upstream; a cached copy is revalidated against the upstream's ETag and Last-Modified, and a transient upstream failure serves the cached copy rather than failing the read. Writes land in the local store before anything is propagated, and propagation happens only through a durable outbox and only when the environment's live-write consent is present. The same package owns the environment configuration precedence (STOW_* over S3_* over AWS_*), the mode switch, the effective write-policy naming used by the startup banner and the server status payload, the upstream addressing switch, and the retry classification the outbox uses to decide whether an entry is retried or made terminal. It is called from cmd/stow-s3, which builds the store the S3 server serves, and from internal/s3api, which reads its upstream error vocabulary and its cache and outbox inspection surfaces.

trace.scope: buildStore: the serve path's construction site for the run-through adapter, its upstream client and its durable outbox
NewWithOutbox: resolves the effective authority, validates the resource policy, and fixes the local, cache, upstream and outbox wiring once
resolveObject: the read resolution starts at the authoritative local store
resolveCachedObject: the separate cache, its TTL, the offline refusal, and the choice between revalidating and refreshing
revalidateCachedObject: the upstream HEAD, the ETag and Last-Modified comparison, and the stale serve on a transient failure
S3Client.GetObject: the outbound call that lands at the upstream provider

evidence.detail: resolveObject heads the local store first; a local error other than ErrObjectNotFound is returned unchanged, which is where ADR 0012's refusal of an ungiven bucket is enforced.
A head error that is not ErrObjectNotFound serves the cached copy, so a transient upstream failure during revalidation does not fail the read.
upstreamChanged compares normalized ETags first and falls back to Last-Modified, which is the whole revalidation rule.
cacheOverBudget is the byte and object bound, and both trackCacheObject and touchCache return early when the cache is not a separate store, so the bounds are inert without one.
effectiveAuthority folds AllowLiveWrites into the grant once, at construction, so there is one mechanism rather than two kept in step.
decideUpstreamWrite consults the grant and nothing else for the write consent, and a mirrorWrites policy with the grant withholding UpstreamWrite returns writeError.

EffectiveWritePolicy is the one exported derivation of the reported write policy; the banner (banner.go:36) and the server status payload (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:372, internal/s3api/admin.go:185) read it, and its sibling PropagatesUpstream is what startup validation reads (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:261).
The addressing switch reaches the SDK as UsePathStyle, derived from the configuration rather than from whether an endpoint happens to be set.
An unclassified upstream error is retried rather than dropped, so the durable outbox is the safety boundary for an unknown failure shape.
The serve path constructs the upstream client inside the branch guarded by the mode check at line 26, so local mode holds no object capable of reaching a provider.

The prewarm verb constructs an upstream client from the environment with no mode check; the only guard is the missing-credentials check at lines 111-113, which --offline bypasses (the client is still constructed at line 114).

PutObject records a write-ahead prepared intent in the outbox before the local write (adapter.go:331) and writes the authoritative local store at line 337; the intent is committed and propagated only after the local write succeeds (adapter.go:346-351), so a failed propagation leaves the local write standing.
A read of a bucket the local store never held returns ErrBucketNotFound with zero upstream GETs, which is ADR 0012's refusal asserted on the provider.
ADR 0005 states the rule the code implements: a policy is a routing choice, the live-write flag is the consent, and neither implies the other.
ADR 0012 records the credential-boundary argument for refusing a bucket the local store was not given (the decision is at line 33), and names upstreamEnabled as the read-side chokepoint at line 59.

interface.types: runthrough.Adapter is the exported type; it is built by New(cfg, local, upstream), NewWithCache(cfg, local, cache, upstream) or NewWithOutbox(cfg, local, cache, upstream, outbox), and it satisfies storage.Store and storage.MultipartStore so it can be handed to internal/runtime or to internal/s3api as an ordinary store. The inputs a caller must supply are a Config and the stores. Config carries the policy (readThroughCache or mirrorWrites), the AllowLiveWrites consent, the Revalidate switch, the Offline switch, the CachePolicy bounds (MaxBytes, MaxObjects, TTL), an optional resource policy, the environment's authority, and an UpstreamConfig holding the endpoint, credentials, region, an optional pinned bucket and the addressing style. The upstream is held behind the Client interface (HeadObject, GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject, ListObjectsV2), and the write-ahead log behind the Outbox interface. Several administrative surfaces are exported for the server's admin routes: CacheStats, CacheEvictions, CachedObjects, OutboxStats, OutboxEntries, OutboxPreparedEntries, RetryPending and DiscardOutboxEntry. EffectiveWritePolicy(cfg), PropagatesUpstream(cfg), StartupBanner(cfg, mode), ConfigFromEnv, ConfigFromEnvChecked and DetectMode are the package-level functions other packages call; ParsePolicy and ParseAddressing are package-level but are used only inside the package.
invariants: The local store is the namespace, not merely a cache: a bucket it was never given does not exist as far as the adapter is concerned, and the read is refused with the local store's own error without the upstream being consulted (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:386, docs/adr/0012-run-through-serves-only-its-own-buckets.md:33).

The effective authority is resolved once, at construction, by folding AllowLiveWrites into the caller's grant; every upstream decision consults that one value and nothing else (internal/runthrough/config.go:114, internal/runthrough/adapter.go:91).

Live-write consent is STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES or --allow-live-writes and nothing else; a mirrorWrites policy alone is not consent (internal/runthrough/config.go:217, docs/adr/0005-live-write-requires-explicit-consent.md:71).
Upstream propagation requires a durable and coordinated outbox; without one the local mutation is refused before it happens (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:249).
With separate stores the local store is authoritative for reads and is never replaced by an upstream revalidation; in the legacy single-store mode it is (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:374).
Offline makes no upstream call of any kind, and an uncached read is refused immediately rather than by a timeout (internal/runthrough/config.go:88, internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:44).
A pinned Upstream.Bucket restricts every reach to that one bucket, including the retry worker (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:226).

The cache's byte and object bounds are enforced only when the cache is a store of its own, and an object larger than MaxBytes is streamed rather than cached (internal/runthrough/cache_policy.go:65, internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:111).
A cached entry past its TTL is deleted rather than served stale (internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:21).
A refused propagation leaves the outbox entry pending rather than terminal, so a write the operator may yet authorise is not discarded (internal/runthrough/outbox_adapter.go:239).

The outbox records the upstream ETag a write was based on and propagates with If-Match, so a concurrent upstream writer is caught rather than overwritten (internal/runthrough/provenance.go:60, internal/runthrough/outbox_adapter.go:160).
error_modes: storage.ErrObjectNotFound: the object is in neither the local store nor the cache, the bucket is outside the pinned scope, the policy denies the key, or the adapter is offline (internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:47, internal/runthrough/adapter.go:390).
storage.ErrBucketNotFound: the bucket is not in the local namespace; this is ADR 0012's refusal and it never reaches the upstream (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:386).

runthrough.ErrLiveWritesDisabled: the policy is mirrorWrites and the grant withholds UpstreamWrite, so the mutation is refused rather than propagated (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:273, internal/runthrough/errors.go:7).

runthrough.ErrDurableOutboxRequired: propagation was requested through an outbox that is not durable and coordinated, and the local mutation is refused before it happens (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:250, internal/runthrough/errors.go:11).

storage.ErrMutationCommitted: the local mutation committed and a later propagation step failed; the caller must verify the outcome before retrying (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:347, internal/s3api/errors.go:181).

runthrough.UpstreamError: a provider error carrying a status, a code and a retry class; internal/s3api maps a 5xx or a missing response to 503 ServiceUnavailable and passes a 4xx through (internal/runthrough/upstream.go:231, internal/s3api/errors.go:217).
runthrough.ErrUpstreamConflict: the upstream object changed after stow decided to write it; the entry goes terminal and somebody decides which object wins (internal/runthrough/outbox_adapter.go:176).
runthrough.ErrOutboxPreparedUnresolved: a prepared intent for the same key could not be reconciled (internal/runthrough/outbox_adapter.go:359).
runthrough.ErrOutboxClaimHeld: another process holds the claim on the entry (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:202).
ordering: A read consults the local store before the cache, and the cache before the upstream; the separate cache is only reached after the local store answers ErrObjectNotFound (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:373, internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:20).

Revalidation is a HEAD against the upstream and happens before a cached copy is served; an entry past its TTL is dropped before the revalidation question is asked (internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:21, internal/runthrough/cache_read.go:53).

A write records its outbox intent before the local mutation and commits and propagates it only after the local write has succeeded: PutObject prepares the intent at adapter.go:331, writes the local store at adapter.go:337, then commits at adapter.go:346 and propagates at adapter.go:349; a failed local write instead reconciles the prepared intent (adapter.go:340).
Cache invalidation follows the local write and precedes propagation, so a propagated object is not served from a stale cache entry (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:344).

The propagation funnel re-checks reachability, the grant and the resource policy at propagation time, not only at enqueue time, because the retry worker and the admin retry route run outside anything that asked (internal/runthrough/outbox_adapter.go:236).
The outbox propagates one entry per key at a time, oldest first (internal/runthrough/outbox_adapter.go:342).
configuration: STOW_POLICY: readThroughCache or mirrorWrites; an unrecognised value is refused at startup (internal/runthrough/config.go:189, internal/runthrough/config.go:252).
STOW_ALLOW_LIVE_WRITES: the live-write consent, and the whole of it (internal/runthrough/config.go:217).
STOW_REVALIDATE and STOW_CACHE=revalidate-never: whether cached copies are revalidated against the upstream (internal/runthrough/config.go:222, internal/runthrough/config.go:219).
STOW_CACHE_MAX_BYTES, STOW_CACHE_MAX_OBJECTS, STOW_CACHE_TTL: the cache bounds (internal/runthrough/config.go:266).
STOW_OFFLINE: refuse every upstream call; an unrecognised value is refused at startup (internal/runthrough/config.go:204, internal/runthrough/config.go:247).
STOW_UPSTREAM_ADDRESSING: path or virtual-hosted; an unrecognised value is refused at startup (internal/runthrough/config.go:171, internal/runthrough/config.go:257).
STOW_BUCKET or S3_BUCKET: pins the upstream to one bucket (internal/runthrough/config.go:165).
STOW_MODE: run-through or local; local is the default and an unrecognised value is local rather than an error (internal/runthrough/config.go:324).
STOW_ENDPOINT, STOW_ACCESS_KEY_ID, STOW_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, STOW_SESSION_TOKEN, STOW_REGION with the precedence STOW_* over S3_* over AWS_* (internal/runthrough/config.go:128).
STOW_CACHE_DIR: the directory the separate cache and the durable outbox live in (internal/runthrough/config.go:183).

Command line: --mode, --backend, --allow-live-writes, --offline, --cache-dir, --cache-max-bytes, --cache-max-objects and --cache-ttl, reconciled over the environment by serveRunThroughConfig (cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:41, with the cache-limit merge at cmd/stow-s3/main.go:220).

implementation: The package is split by concern rather than by layer. adapter.go holds the Adapter type, its constructors and the decision functions every path goes through: upstreamReachable, which asks whether the upstream is usable at all, upstreamPermitted, which asks about the grant and the pinned bucket, upstreamEnabled, which adds the per-object policy, and allows, the single place a policy is consulted. decideUpstreamWrite collapses the policy, the grant and the per-object policy into one of three actions, and it is the whole of the write-consent mechanism. cache_read.go holds the cache half of the read: a hit, a hit needing revalidation, and the miss that reaches upstream, kept together because the choice between them is one decision. cache_policy.go holds the eviction index, the byte, object and TTL bounds and the startup reconciliation that rebuilds the index from the cache store. upstream.go holds the Client interface, the S3 client that implements it, the SDK-error to storage-error mapping, and the ETag and Last-Modified comparison. retry.go holds the classification the outbox uses. config.go holds the environment precedence and the mode switch; writepolicy.go holds the one effective-write-policy derivation; addressing.go holds the addressing style; transport_policy.go holds the endpoint validation and redirect confinement. The outbox files hold the write-ahead log and its durable file implementation. The implementation decisions that matter to a caller are these. Reads: the local store is authoritative and the namespace; the separate cache is consulted only after the local store misses; a cached copy is revalidated with a HEAD and compared by ETag first and Last-Modified second; a transient failure during that HEAD serves the cached copy; an upstream that has lost the object evicts the cached copy when EvictOnUpstreamMissing is set; an object larger than the cache's byte bound is streamed to the caller instead of cached; a read that would go upstream while offline is refused immediately. Writes: the grant is asked first and on its own, so a policy can never widen it; a mirrorWrites policy with the grant withholding the write is an error rather than a local-only write, because a mirror that does not mirror has not satisfied the policy; under the read-through policy the same state is a local write with no propagation; propagation requires a durable outbox, and the local mutation is refused before it happens when there is none; the outbox intent is prepared before the local write and committed and propagated only after it succeeds, so a propagation failure returns a committed error and the local object stands; the outbox records the upstream ETag the write was based on and propagates with If-Match, turning a concurrent upstream writer into a conflict rather than a silent overwrite; and the propagation funnel re-checks the grant and the policy, so the retry worker and the admin retry route cannot become a way around a withdrawn permission. Listings merge the local list with the upstream list, or with the cache list when the upstream is not enabled. Multipart uploads are served entirely from the local store. The admin surfaces expose cache counters, the cached-object listing with a readability flag, and the outbox's pending, prepared and terminal entries.

callers.scope: buildStore: builds the local store, the separate cache store, the upstream client and the durable outbox, and returns the adapter the S3 server will serve
serve: resolves the mode, builds the store, starts the outbox retry worker, and reports the effective write policy and the startup banner
runPrewarm: the prewarm verb builds an adapter with a separate cache and warms named keys into it
serveRunThroughConfig: reconciles the command line over the environment into the one runthrough.Config the server runs on
bindNativeRuntimeStore: wraps the adapter in the runtime instance and forwards its cache and outbox inspection surfaces to the admin routes
checkS3Configuration: the doctor probe reads runthrough.ConfigFromEnvChecked and RedactEndpoint to report whether an upstream is configured, without constructing a client
upstreamFailure: the S3 server renders the adapter's upstream errors as 503 for a 5xx or an unreachable provider and passes a 4xx through
the admin routes discover the cache listing, the cache counters and the outbox state through interfaces the adapter satisfies
the adapter's own tests: the write guard, the durable-outbox refusal, the read-through miss, the revalidation switch and the bucket filter
the grant tests: no upstream reach without the grant, no propagation without the write grant, and the retry worker unable to bypass the grant
the composition test with the runtime over a separate empty cache, including ADR 0012's refusal of an ungiven bucket
the conformance pair: an adapter in front of a second real stow server, built the way the CLI builds it

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting the package would not remove complexity; it would distribute it. cmd/stow-s3/store.go would have to own the read-resolution order, the revalidation rule, the cache bounds, the consent gate, the outbox protocol and the retry schedule; internal/s3api/errors.go would have to know the upstream error shapes directly; internal/s3api/admin.go would have to learn the cache and outbox internals; and the CLI's mode switch and the prewarm verb's credential handling would have to be re-derived at each site. The interface the callers see does not grow: storage.Store, the Outbox interface and a handful of administrative methods stay the same, and the callers' own code does not change at all. That is the deep-module signature, and it is why the package can sit between an agent and a shared bucket without either of them knowing it is there. One seam inside the package is not real, though: the Client interface at internal/runthrough/upstream.go:19 has a single production adapter, S3Client, so it is a hypothetical seam and the package's substitutability stops at the upstream boundary unless a second client is written.

leverage: Callers get one store type that is simultaneously the authoritative local namespace, a read-through cache and a consent-gated upstream mirror, behind an interface as simple as storage.Store. The S3 server and the runtime composition need no knowledge of an upstream: the same request path serves local bytes, cached bytes and upstream bytes, and the upstream's answers become the server's answers without a second vocabulary. Operators get one place where the consent, the bucket scope, the offline switch, the cache bounds and the addressing style are read, and one function that states what the server will actually do with a write, so the banner, the status payload and startup validation cannot disagree with the adapter. The retry classification gives the outbox a single answer to whether a failure is worth another attempt, so a provider's own error shape decides nothing.
locality: Change, bugs and knowledge concentrate in four places. The read decision lives in adapter.go's resolveObject and cache_read.go's resolveCachedObject and revalidateCachedObject. The write decision lives in adapter.go's decideUpstreamWrite and requireDurableOutbox, and the durable half in outbox_adapter.go's propagation funnel. The cache budget lives in cache_policy.go, indexed in memory and rebuilt from the store at startup. The upstream itself is constructed in cmd/stow-s3/store.go and cmd/stow-s3/prewarm.go, and only the first is behind the mode switch, so a change to the upstream's configuration has two places to land and one of them is outside the switch. The configuration that produces all of this is read in one package, config.go, with the precedence rules spelled out there.
risks: The upstream client is constructed in two production places and only one of them consults the mode switch. cmd/stow-s3/store.go:31 is inside the branch guarded by the mode check at line 26, but cmd/stow-s3/prewarm.go:114 builds one from the environment with no mode check: runPrewarm reads the environment, refuses only when the credentials are absent and --offline was not given (prewarm.go:111-113), and then constructs the client unconditionally. The reach is read-only, since prewarm only resolves objects, but it contradicts the invariant in docs/adr/0011-local-is-the-default-mode.md:14-19 that no explicit request means no upstream, and STOW_MODE=local does not stop it.

Under mirrorWrites without live-write consent and a reachable upstream, the mutation is refused outright with ErrLiveWritesDisabled rather than kept local (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:273), while the reported policy says writes stay local (internal/runthrough/writepolicy.go:17, internal/runthrough/banner.go:41) and ADR 0005 says writes still succeed locally (docs/adr/0005-live-write-requires-explicit-consent.md:123). internal/s3api/errors.go has no mapping for that error, so the client receives a 500 InternalError rather than a 403. The same reported policy name describes the opposite outcome when the grant withholds UpstreamRead as well, because then the upstream is not enabled and the write stays local (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:257).

The cache's byte, object and TTL bounds apply only when the cache is a separate store: trackCacheObject and touchCache return early otherwise (internal/runthrough/cache_policy.go:42, internal/runthrough/cache_policy.go:65), and the separate-cache mode is decided by comparing two interface values (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:115). A caller that passes the same store twice, or uses runthrough.New, gets the legacy behaviour with the bounds inert and no error, while the local store is no longer authoritative for reads (internal/runthrough/adapter.go:374).

The upstream Client interface has one production adapter (internal/runthrough/upstream.go:28), so the package's substitutability at the upstream boundary is hypothetical: a second provider means a new implementation inside this package, not a caller-supplied one, and the interface leaks the storage package's own object shapes.

The Client interface carries no timeout or cancellation contract of its own, so the cost of an unreachable upstream falls on the caller's context: a hung provider turns every read into a request that runs until the caller gives up, which is the case the Offline switch exists to bound (internal/runthrough/config.go:92).

priority.rationale: The adapter is the boundary between an agent's own store and a provider shared with other people, so a mistake on either side of it lands on someone else's data: every run-through read and every propagated write passes through it, and the same package also owns the single boolean that decides whether a mutation leaves the machine. The blast radius is every request a run-through server serves, plus the outbox retry worker and the admin retry route, which run outside anything that asked. The demonstrated risk is not hypothetical: the prewarm verb constructs an upstream client without consulting the mode switch, so the ADR 0011 invariant does not hold for that verb, and the mirrorWrites-without-consent state is reported as writes staying local while the code refuses the write and the S3 server turns that refusal into a 500. Neither is data loss, and both are bounded by one configuration, so the impact is P1 rather than P0.

next_action: Write the adapter's two load-bearing rules down in one place the code cannot contradict, and align the two names that already disagree. First, the reporting side: the write policy reported as mirrorWrites-disabled says writes stay local, while decideUpstreamWrite refuses them with ErrLiveWritesDisabled whenever the upstream is enabled, so either the branch at internal/runthrough/adapter.go:273 should keep the write local and the policy name should change, or the name, the banner at internal/runthrough/banner.go:41 and the consequence at docs/adr/0005-live-write-requires-explicit-consent.md:123 should say that the write is refused. The concrete interface to change is the meaning of runthrough.WritePolicyMirrorWritesDisabled, and internal/s3api/errors.go needs a mapping for runthrough.ErrLiveWritesDisabled so the refusal is a 403 AccessDenied rather than a 500 InternalError. Second, the construction side: cmd/stow-s3/prewarm.go:114 should take the mode into account the way cmd/stow-s3/store.go:26 does, so that no verb constructs an upstream client unless the mode asked for one. The documentation action is a run-through section in docs/storage-admission-contract.md stating the read-resolution order, the fact that the local store is authoritative for reads only when a separate cache is configured, and the fact that the cache bounds are inert without one.

title: Runtime instance: authority, quota and usage accounting over a storage.Store
summary: internal/runtime.Instance is the in-process governance layer every stow surface passes through before it touches bytes. It owns the authority-and-policy decision on every verb (object, bucket, multipart, save, recovery hold), the quota admission against MaxBytes/MaxObjects/MaxMultipartUploads, the incremental usage counters and the reservation accounting for in-flight multipart uploads and staged writes, the guarded-save condition binding and durable save-request replay, and the reset/close lifecycle. It delegates the bytes themselves - storage, pagination, conditional-copy evaluation, guarded comparison, save-request replay, recovery holds, multipart parts - to a storage.Store and its optional interfaces, and it discovers what the bound store can do by type assertion. It publishes itself back to callers as a storage.Store through runtime.StoreAdapter, so the native S3 server, the in-process embedded library, the workspace facade and the MCP tool server all reach the same decisions.

trace.scope: the native CLI binds its backing store to a runtime instance with runtime.OpenWithStore, so every S3 request the server handles passes through this instance
runtime.NewStoreAdapter publishes the instance back as a storage.Store, and that adapter is the value the S3 server holds
StoreAdapter.PutObject routes a request body into instance.PutObjectStream, choosing the owned, the sized and the buffered path by type assertion
the authority-and-policy admission for object.write on the named resource, taken before the lock is held and before any bytes move
the bytes are staged through the store's optional storage.StagedWriteStore, outside the instance lock and under a reserved quota
pending.Commit publishes the object in the store and finishPut moves the usage counters
the object record is written into the filesystem store's buckets tree - the point at which the runtime's admitted bytes land

evidence.detail: Instance embeds usageState and holds the bound storage.Store, a storeEpoch, the discovered multipart capability, the resolved authority, the policy source, and the close state; the whole module's mutable state is these fields.

The multipart capability is captured once by type assertion at construction: multipart, _ := store.(storage.MultipartStore). The runtime's optional capabilities are discovered on the bound store, never declared to it.

checkUpload resolves the resource behind an upload ID from the instance's own i.multipart map rather than from the store, with the reason written out: the store's answer would have to be read before authorisation to know what to authorise.

currentPolicy re-reads the policy.Source and re-validates it against the authority on every decision, because a later revision can be wider than the one before it; a policy that fails validation refuses rather than being skipped.
Reset is the only operation that replaces the store: it closes the old one, swaps in a new one, bumps storeEpoch, re-derives the multipart capability and replaces the usage state wholesale.
Close closes the bound store exactly once under a sync.Once and returns the same error on every later call; the instance marks itself closed before releasing the lock.

The module states its own reason for existing: every object verb consults the environment's Authority before touching anything, which is what makes the answer the same whether a caller arrived over S3 or in process.
DeleteObjects authorises each key on its own and does all of them before touching any, so a refusal leaves the batch unapplied rather than partly applied.

A copy is accounted with finishStoredPut, which takes the size the store reported (meta.Size); a put is accounted with finishPut, which takes the size the caller declared. Two sources feed the same counter.

quotaStore resolves the store whose bytes are counted for the quota, through storage.QuotaStoreProvider; without it the wrapper itself is counted, so a wrapper must name its authoritative store to be counted correctly.

objectQuotaFits and bytesQuotaFits are the two quota formulas: the object count plus the reserved objects against MaxObjects, and the bytes plus the reserved bytes minus the replaced size against MaxBytes.

scanStoredUsage rebuilds the counters from the store at open and refuses with ErrQuotaExceeded when the store already holds more than the limits allow, so opening an over-full store fails rather than starting at zero.
A multipart target that already holds a reservation has spent its object slot, so only a first upload for a missing object needs room for one; the reservation is per target, not per upload.

The staged path drops the instance lock while the bytes are staged and carries a storeEpoch captured at admission; a Reset between the reservation and the commit fails the write with 'runtime store changed while object was staged' rather than writing into the replaced store.

bindSaveCondition refuses a condition whose owner is not this instance or whose bucket/key differ, and refuses IfMatch/IfNoneMatch alongside a condition; the guard is then handed to the store, which performs the actual comparison.

StoreAdapter exposes an Instance through the storage.Store compatibility contract so that runtime lifecycle, quotas and usage accounting stay authoritative, while the S3 server and the workspace facade keep speaking storage.Store.

The module's error vocabulary: ErrClosed, ErrQuotaExceeded, ErrUnsupportedBackend, ErrInvalidListLimit, ErrExternalResetUnsupported, ErrResourceUnresolved, and ErrMultipartUnsupported aliased to storage.ErrMultipartUnsupported so the absence has one vocabulary wherever it is discovered.

The S3 layer's error table maps runtime.ErrQuotaExceeded to 507 InsufficientStorage, runtime.ErrClosed to 503 ServiceUnavailable and runtime.ErrMultipartUnsupported to 501 NotImplemented; runtime.ErrResourceUnresolved is absent from the table.
