The package's dependency boundary is enforced by test: os, path/filepath, syscall and log must not be direct imports of internal/runtime or internal/storage, and the filesystem backend plus path/filepath and log must not appear in the dependency closure of internal/runtime, so the runtime reads no environment variable and touches no platform package.

The package's own tests fix the accounting contract: in-flight uploads count as reservations and not as usage, a second upload for the same key reuses the object slot, and a closed instance refuses every verb with ErrClosed.

interface.types: Two exported types carry the surface. *runtime.Instance is the runtime itself: the constructors Open(Options) and OpenWithStore(Options, storage.Store, func() (storage.Store, error)); the namespace verbs CreateBucket, DeleteBucket, HeadBucket, ListBuckets, PutObject, PutObjectStream, OpenObject, OpenObjectRange, GetObject, HeadObject, ListObjects, DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, CopyObject and CopyObjectCond; the multipart verbs CreateMultipartUpload, GetMultipartUpload, UploadPart, ListParts, ListPartsPage, CompleteMultipartUpload, AbortMultipartUpload, ValidateMultipartUpload and ListMultipartUploads; the save verbs ReadForSave, SaveObject and ResolveSave; the recovery verbs BeginObjectRecoveryHold and ReleaseObjectRecoveryHold; the lifecycle verbs Reset, Close and RefreshUsage; and the introspection verbs Usage, Capabilities, Authority and Authorize. *runtime.StoreAdapter re-presents an instance as storage.Store (var _ storage.Store = (*StoreAdapter)(nil) at internal/runtime/adapter.go:19) and additionally offers CopyObjectCond and ComputesPutChecksums. The value types are Options (backend, three quotas, an *authority.Authority pointer and a policy.Source), Capabilities, Usage, Bucket, Object, ObjectPage, ListOptions, PutOptions, StreamPutOptions, SaveCondition, SaveOptions, SaveResult, SaveOutcome, ObjectRecoveryReference and ObjectRecoveryHoldOptions.
invariants: The authority is the floor and the policy only narrows it: a nil Options.Authority permits everything, &authority.None() permits nothing, and a policy wider than the authority is refused rather than clipped; policy.New validates every entry with env.IsSupersetOf and returns policy.ErrWidening otherwise (internal/runtime/types.go:112-132, internal/runtime/instance.go:95-108, internal/policy/policy.go:140-151).
The policy is resolved per decision and never cached at open, so a revocation takes effect without a reopen (internal/runtime/instance.go:92-94).
Usage() counts committed objects only. An in-flight multipart upload or a staged write is a reservation, not usage (internal/runtime/instance_test.go:39-41, internal/runtime/usage_state.go:90-102).

One object slot is spent per target, not per upload: a second upload for the same key reuses the slot and a different key needs its own (internal/runtime/state.go:52-59, internal/runtime/instance_test.go:30-34).

A copy checks the source's read permission before the destination's write permission, because the copy reads the source and discloses its bytes at a destination the caller chose (internal/runtime/objects.go:262-272).
DeleteObjects authorises every key before touching any of them, so a refusal leaves the batch unapplied rather than partly applied (internal/runtime/objects.go:181-185).

A SaveCondition is bound to the instance and the exact bucket and key that issued it; a save naming a different instance or resource is refused with ErrInvalidSaveCondition (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:149-162).

The instance's own map of upload IDs is the authority for which resource an upload ID addresses. A policy-bearing instance refuses an upload it cannot resolve rather than asking the store (internal/runtime/instance.go:74-90).

A mutation that landed but whose follow-up step failed is still accounted: storage.ErrMutationCommitted counts as a committed mutation for usage while the error is still returned to the caller (internal/runtime/usage_state.go:32-38, internal/runtime/adapter.go:112-115).
Close closes the bound store exactly once and is idempotent; a second Close returns the first result (internal/runtime/instance.go:245-254, internal/runtime/instance_test.go:214-219).

Reset replaces the bound store, increments the store epoch, re-derives the multipart capability and zeroes the usage counters, and refuses with ErrExternalResetUnsupported when no resetStore was supplied (internal/runtime/instance.go:214-243).
error_modes: ErrClosed - the instance has been closed; every verb returns it (internal/runtime/instance.go:184-189).

ErrQuotaExceeded - the byte, object or outstanding-multipart-upload limit would be passed. The multipart form wraps a message naming the limit and the remedy (internal/runtime/types.go:41, internal/runtime/state.go:207-211).
ErrUnsupportedBackend - Open refuses every backend but memory, and OpenWithStore refuses a backend name the runtime does not know (internal/runtime/types.go:80-90).

ErrResourceUnresolved - a multipart verb addressed an upload ID this instance cannot resolve. It appears only when a policy is configured, because without one there is nothing to evaluate (internal/runtime/instance.go:87, internal/runtime/types.go:45-48).
ErrInvalidListLimit - a negative list limit (internal/runtime/objects.go:117-119).
ErrExternalResetUnsupported - Reset on an instance opened without a resetStore (internal/runtime/instance.go:226-228).
ErrMultipartUnsupported, an alias of storage.ErrMultipartUnsupported - the bound store is not a storage.MultipartStore (internal/runtime/multipart.go:296-301, internal/runtime/types.go:52).

ErrGuardedSavesUnsupported and ErrInvalidSaveCondition - the store cannot guard writes, or the condition came from another instance or resource or conflicts with IfMatch/IfNoneMatch (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:13-14, :143-157).

*authority.ErrNotAuthorized - the environment or the policy refused the operation (internal/authority/authority.go:189); the S3 layer turns it into 403 AccessDenied rather than a 500 (internal/s3api/errors.go:155-169).

Store errors pass through unchanged - storage.ErrObjectNotFound, storage.ErrBucketNotFound, storage.ErrPreconditionFailed, storage.ErrSaveConflict, storage.ErrSaveRequestUnknown - and storage.ErrMutationCommitted is surfaced alongside the accounting it triggered (internal/runtime/objects.go:206-210, internal/runtime/adapter.go:112-115).
SaveOutcome separates the three save results: committed, not committed and unknown, where unknown covers a request whose receipt could not be established (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:164-181).
ordering: Every object, bucket and listing verb consults the authority and the policy before taking the instance lock and before touching the store, and the policy is resolved and validated first so that a widening policy refuses with its own reason rather than the environment's (internal/runtime/instance.go:133-146, internal/runtime/objects.go:231-236, internal/runtime/buckets.go:33-41). The upload-ID-addressed multipart verbs are the exception and cannot be otherwise: they take the lock first and only then call checkUpload, because the resource behind an upload ID is read from the instance's own map, which the same mutex guards (internal/runtime/multipart.go:55-60, :79-84, :140-145).
Under the lock the order is: the open check, then quota admission, then the store call, then the usage accounting (internal/runtime/stream-writes.go:55-66, internal/runtime/multipart.go:21-48).

A multipart upload is admitted against the outstanding-upload count before the store creates it, a part is admitted against the byte quota before the store stores it, and a completion is re-admitted against the completed size before the store publishes it (internal/runtime/multipart.go:29-31, :94-97, :159-161).

A streaming write reserves its quota delta before the bytes leave the process, stages them outside the lock, and re-checks the store epoch and the open state before committing; a Reset between the two fails the write with 'runtime store changed while object was staged' (internal/runtime/staged-writes.go:26-63, :88-107).

ReadForSave must precede SaveObject: the condition it returns is the observation the save compares against and it is valid only for the instance and resource that produced it (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:60-89, :149-162).

SaveObject replays a request-keyed save from the store's receipt before applying it, so a retried save returns the original receipt instead of writing twice (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:104-109).
An object read re-checks the authority on every Read and Seek, and a revoked permission closes the stream mid-read (internal/runtime/streams.go:111-114, :154-163, :178-181).
configuration: Options.Backend - memory, filesystem, workspace or host. An unrecognised name is refused rather than treated as memory, so a caller who asked for durable bytes is not handed volatile ones (internal/runtime/types.go:13-25, :55-65).

Options.MaxBytes, Options.MaxObjects and Options.MaxMultipartUploads - zero takes the default (64 MiB, 10 000 objects, 1 024 outstanding uploads) and a negative value is refused (internal/runtime/types.go:27-29, :91-102).

runtime.UnlimitedBytes and runtime.UnlimitedObjects, both math.MaxInt64, disable byte and object enforcement; the native CLI maps a non-positive limit to unlimited (internal/runtime/types.go:35-36, cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:23-35).
Options.Authority - a pointer, because unset and explicitly empty must be distinguishable; nil permits everything (internal/runtime/types.go:112-121).
Options.Policy - a policy.Source consulted per decision; nil means no policy is consulted (internal/runtime/types.go:123-132).
The resetStore argument of OpenWithStore - nil disables Reset, which then returns ErrExternalResetUnsupported instead of mutating a store it does not own (internal/runtime/adapter.go:29-35).

The package reads no environment variable and imports no platform package; its dependency-boundary test forbids os, path/filepath, syscall and log as direct imports of internal/runtime and internal/storage, and forbids the filesystem backend, path/filepath and log in the dependency closure (internal/runtime/dependencies_test.go:11-41).

The store's own capabilities are configuration in the sense that they are discovered by type assertion on the bound store: multipart (internal/runtime/instance.go:61), guarded writes (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:49), durable save requests (internal/runtime/save_requests.go:12), recovery holds (internal/runtime/object_recovery.go:21), ranged reads (internal/runtime/streams.go:59), staged writes (internal/runtime/stream-writes.go:60), conditional copy (internal/runtime/objects.go:320), object-usage scanning (internal/runtime/state.go:109), put checksums (internal/runtime/adapter.go:252) and the authoritative quota store (internal/runtime/objects.go:372).

implementation: The instance holds the decisions a caller would otherwise have to make. Instance embeds a usageState (internal/runtime/usage_state.go:9) carrying the limits, the byte and object counters, the usage revision, the per-upload part sizes, the per-target multipart counts, the reserved targets and the staged reservation, and it holds the bound store, the store epoch, the multipart capability, the authority and the policy source (internal/runtime/instance.go:13-27). The authority is resolved once at construction into an authority.Authority value defaulting to authority.All() (internal/runtime/instance.go:53-57); the policy is deliberately not resolved, because a policy read at open could only change by restarting the process (internal/runtime/instance.go:58-60). Admission is four shared steps: checkContext (a nil context is accepted, a cancelled one is not), checkResource/check/checkCollection (authority, then policy), checkOpen (closed?) and checkMutationLocked (closed? plus a usage refresh) (internal/runtime/instance.go:116-189, internal/runtime/workspace_usage.go:55-60). The policy path resolves the source, validates it against the authority - a widening policy is refused rather than clipped - and then asks Set.Allows for a named resource or Set.Deny for a collection or the environment (internal/runtime/instance.go:92-161). Quota is two formulas over four numbers: the counters and the reservations (internal/runtime/state.go:10-20). objectQuotaFits charges the object count plus the reserved objects and discounts a reservation the target already holds; bytesQuotaFits charges the bytes plus the reserved bytes minus the size being replaced. A multipart upload reserves one object slot for a target with no committed object yet, released when the object appears or the upload goes away (internal/runtime/state.go:35-67). A staged write reserves the size delta for the duration of the staging (internal/runtime/usage_state.go:90-102). Usage is maintained incrementally rather than recounted: applyPut and applyDelete move the counters and recordMutation decides whether the mutation counts (internal/runtime/usage_state.go:32-78); a mutation that returned storage.ErrMutationCommitted counts, because the bytes did land. The counters are rebuilt from the store at open by scanStoredUsage (internal/runtime/state.go:76-92) and, for a workspace or a filesystem store with durable save requests, re-derived before each mutation by refreshPersistentUsageLocked, which asks the store for a usage revision first and refuses when the usage changed while it was being read (internal/runtime/usage_recovery.go:28-51, internal/runtime/workspace_usage.go:21-46). Multipart is the fullest accounting: initiation admits the upload against the outstanding count and reserves the target slot, each part reserves its bytes against the store's reported part size, and completion re-admits the completed size against the bytes already reserved before it publishes (internal/runtime/multipart.go:14-171, internal/runtime/usage_multipart.go:9-69). When a completion fails, the runtime asks the store whether the upload still exists, drops its own record if it does not, and joins the two errors rather than reporting a clean failure (internal/runtime/multipart.go:173-180). Listing is filtered twice under a policy: the runtime resolves a scope once, then either pages the store directly or re-pages it in 1000-key windows until enough visible keys have been collected, and the count it reports is of what it returned rather than of what the store holds (internal/runtime/objects.go:78-171, internal/runtime/list_scoped.go:9-41). Writes have two paths. A store that implements storage.StagedWriteStore gets the staged path - reserve, stage outside the lock, re-check the epoch, commit (internal/runtime/stream-writes.go:60-63, internal/runtime/staged-writes.go:24-68). Any other store gets the buffered path - the quota is checked and the bytes are handed to store.PutObject under the lock (internal/runtime/stream-writes.go:12-30). In both the body is wrapped in a sizedObjectReader that refuses a stream longer or shorter than the declared size (internal/runtime/stream-writes.go:69-97). Guarded saves bind an observation to a write: ReadForSave reads the object or observes its absence and computes the fingerprint the store will compare against, and SaveObject refuses a foreign condition, refuses IfMatch/IfNoneMatch alongside a condition, replays a request-keyed save from the store's receipt, and then applies the write with the guard attached (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:60-162, internal/runtime/save_requests.go:23-49). What the runtime delegates is everything about the bytes: the store stores them, lists them, paginates them, evaluates the copy's source conditions when it can, performs the guarded comparison, replays save requests, holds recovery holds and keeps the multipart parts (internal/runtime/objects.go:309-331, internal/runtime/streams.go:58-81, internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:143-146). What it reserves for itself is the decision to admit, the accounting, and the lifecycle.

callers.scope: the native CLI binds its chosen store to a runtime instance and publishes the instance's Capabilities into the server's readiness payload
the embedded library facade opens either a memory instance or one over a caller-supplied store, and maps the runtime's sentinels onto the public stow vocabulary
the public workspace constructor opens a workspace-backend instance and delegates the workspace Destroy decision to Instance.Authorize
the workspace's loopback S3 server wraps the instance's adapter in a borrowed store whose Close is a no-op, so the facade cannot close the workspace's runtime
OpenFilesystem opens a filesystem-backend instance over an exclusively locked directory
the S3 layer's error table consumes the runtime's sentinels to shape the XML error a client receives

the MCP object server reports the runtime's Capabilities to an agent; it holds a *stow.Runtime and reaches the instance through the public embedded facade rather than through the internal type directly

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Delete internal/runtime.Instance and the complexity concentrates in its callers rather than vanishing. cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:37, internal/embedded/runtime.go:19, pkg/stow/workspace.go:140 and pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:28 would each have to re-implement the authority-and-policy consultation, the byte and object quota arithmetic, the usage counters, the multipart reservation bookkeeping, the staged-write epoch guard, the store-epoch reset and the same store-capability discovery by type assertion - and each would have to rediscover the same ordering rules, including that the source of a copy is checked before the destination and that a batch delete authorises every key before touching any. The knowledge would be duplicated across four surfaces, and the guarantee the layer states as its own reason for existing (internal/runtime/objects.go:14) - the same answer whether a caller arrived over S3 or in process - would be lost. The module earns its keep.

leverage: Every surface gets one place where a decision is made. A caller of internal/runtime.Instance gets authorisation, quota admission, usage accounting, guarded-save semantics and multipart reservation without implementing any of them. The native S3 server binds one instance and inherits all of it (cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:37). The embedded library maps the runtime's sentinels onto a public vocabulary once (internal/embedded/runtime.go:177) instead of once per surface. The workspace gets a byte budget over real files without becoming a second PutObject implementation (pkg/stow/workspace.go:140). StoreAdapter is what makes this pay: it lets the runtime keep the decisions while the S3 server, the workspace facade and the MCP tools keep speaking storage.Store, so a change to the admission rules lands in one file rather than in every protocol (internal/runtime/adapter.go:12-14).
locality: Change, bugs and knowledge concentrate in internal/runtime. The admission order and the lifecycle are in instance.go; the quota formulas and the open-time scan are in state.go; the counters are in usage_state.go; the multipart reservation bookkeeping is in usage_multipart.go; the persistent-usage reconciliation is in usage_recovery.go and workspace_usage.go; the verb-by-verb decisions are in objects.go, buckets.go, multipart.go, streams.go, stream-writes.go, staged-writes.go, guarded_save.go, save_requests.go, object_recovery.go and list_scoped.go; the translation back to storage.Store is in adapter.go. The callers are thin - a bind, a map and a forward - so a maintainer looking for why a write was refused lands in internal/runtime rather than in the protocol layer.
risks: Three independent byte budgets bound the same bytes and refuse in three vocabularies. The runtime enforces MaxBytes and MaxObjects against its own counters (internal/runtime/state.go:18); the filesystem store can be bound to a capacity.Namespace with an independent MaxBytes (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:20, internal/capacity/types.go:35); and the run-through adapter carries its own cache budget (internal/runthrough/cache_policy.go:362). Only the runtime's refusal is mapped at the S3 layer: runtime.ErrQuotaExceeded becomes 507 InsufficientStorage (internal/s3api/errors.go:141), while capacity.ErrFull has no entry in that table (internal/s3api/errors.go:127) and reaches the client as 500 InternalError. A caller that hits the store's budget is told the server failed, and a 500 invites a retry that cannot succeed.

The runtime accounts bytes from two different sources. A put is accounted from the size the caller declared (internal/runtime/stream-writes.go:26, internal/runtime/staged-writes.go:64), while a copy is accounted from the size the store reported (internal/runtime/objects.go:299). Usage().Bytes is therefore a mixture, and the runtime never checks that the store's size matches the declared one - the store owns the byte count while the runtime owns the budget, and neither says so.

ErrResourceUnresolved is the only runtime sentinel with no mapping anywhere outside the package. It is raised when a multipart verb addresses an upload ID the instance's own map cannot resolve (internal/runtime/instance.go:87), and it appears only when a policy is configured - without a policy the same request reaches the store and gets storage.ErrUploadNotFound (internal/runtime/multipart.go:92). Neither the S3 error table (internal/s3api/errors.go:127) nor the embedded facade's mapping (internal/embedded/runtime.go:177) names it, so over S3 the refusal arrives as 500 InternalError rather than 404 NoSuchUpload, and the client is invited to retry an upload that can never succeed.

The resource behind an upload ID is resolved from the instance's own in-memory map, not from the store (internal/runtime/instance.go:76-90), and that map is repopulated only at open (internal/runtime/state.go:144) or for a workspace, or a filesystem store with durable save requests (internal/runtime/workspace_usage.go:22). An upload created by another process after this instance opened is unaddressable, and the runtime refuses it before the store is asked - the comment states the reason, and the cost is that the store can no longer answer.

Capability discovery is by type assertion on the bound store, and the multipart capability is captured once at construction (internal/runtime/instance.go:61) while guarded writes, durable save requests and recovery holds are re-asserted on every call (internal/runtime/guarded_save.go:49, internal/runtime/save_requests.go:12, internal/runtime/object_recovery.go:21). The advertised capability therefore depends on the concrete type the caller happened to supply, and it passes through a two-level chain: embedded.adaptStore only wraps a caller's store in storage.MultipartStore when the caller's public store implements embedded.MultipartStore (internal/embedded/store.go:126), so a caller who implements the public interface but not the internal one silently loses multipart.

Close closes the bound store exactly once and the ownership is stated only in a comment (internal/runtime/adapter.go:29). pkg/stow works around it by wrapping the adapter in a borrowed store whose Close is a no-op (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:32), so a caller who closes the adapter closes the workspace's runtime and its directory handle. The Instance type does not say this, so the rule is invisible to anyone reading it.

priority.rationale: The blast radius is every mutation on every surface: the native S3 server, the embedded library, the workspace facade and the MCP tools all pass through this module, so a defect here reaches all of them at once. The hidden coupling is demonstrated rather than inferred - three independent byte budgets bound the same bytes, one of which has no S3 error mapping; the byte counter is fed from two different sources; and a policy-bearing refusal (ErrResourceUnresolved) has no mapping on either the S3 or the embedded path, so an authorisation refusal is reported as a server fault. The consequence is a misreported refusal and an uncounted byte, not data loss, which keeps this below P0.

next_action: State the runtime's ownership in the interface and remove the duplicate decisions. Concretely: (a) document internal/runtime.Instance as the single admission point - its limits, its ordering rules and its capability discovery - in docs/CODE_STANDARDS.md, and give it one accounting source, so finishPut and finishStoredPut both derive the accounted size from the store's meta.Size and the declared size is checked against it; (b) close the sentinel vocabulary by adding ErrResourceUnresolved to the mapping at internal/embedded/runtime.go:177 and to the table at internal/s3api/errors.go:127, mapping it to a refusal rather than letting it fall through to 500; (c) make the closing rule part of the type - either state on Instance.Close that it closes the bound store, or expose a borrowing accessor - so pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:32 stops needing a no-op Close wrapper to keep a workspace's runtime alive; (d) state that the runtime owns the byte and object budget while the store owns the byte count, and require a store that carries its own budget (the capacity.Namespace, the run-through cache) to publish its refusal in the runtime's vocabulary.

title: S3-compatible HTTP server
summary: internal/s3api is the translation layer between an S3 client and a storage.Store. It owns the SigV4 gate, request admission and the request-body size limit, the route table and dispatch, the S3 XML wire vocabulary (request and response bodies, the error envelope), the conditional-request, checksum, Content-Length, metadata and range rules that it evaluates itself, the CORS policy, and the /_stow admin and metrics routes. It holds no storage state: every object operation is a translation of an HTTP request into a storage.Store (and optionally storage.MultipartStore) call and back. The one decision it owns that nothing below it owns is the error vocabulary: mapStorageError in internal/s3api/errors.go:147 maps storage sentinels, runtime refusals, authority refusals and upstream refusals onto one S3 code-and-status set, which is why this package is the only internal package whose production files import both internal/runtime and internal/runthrough (internal/s3api/errors.go:14-15). What an S3 client must know is therefore fixed here: the supported operation set, the XML shapes, the error codes and their statuses, the conditional and checksum rules, and the fact that an unsupported S3 feature is a deliberate 501 rather than a silent no-op. The S3 layer's own decisions are the wire ones and the request-admission ones; the runtime's decisions are the quota, authority and policy ones; the store's decisions are the persistence and multipart part-size ones.

trace.scope: (*Server).ServeHTTP is the single request entry: it admits the request into the concurrency slot channel, mints a request id, installs the per-request body cache and the CORS allowlist, validates the query string, answers a CORS preflight, caps the body, and branches between the /_stow admin surface and the S3 surface.

The SigV4 gate: s.auth(r) refuses with 403 and the verifier's own code (AccessDenied, SignatureDoesNotMatch, RequestTimeTooSkewed) before any route is parsed. prepareRequestForAuth has already materialised the body once so the payload hash and the handler read the same bytes.

parseRoute turns Host plus path into a bucket and a key, choosing virtual-hosted addressing when the Host carries a .baseHost suffix and path-style otherwise; an undecodable name is an InvalidBucketName or InvalidArgument refusal.

dispatch refuses eighteen unsupported semantic markers and a versionId before it chooses root, bucket or object, so an unsupported feature cannot fall through to a supported operation; the object branch recognises multipart requests before the plain object switch.

handlePutObject reads the body once and then enforces Content-Length presence and agreement, Content-MD5, the checksum algorithm and value, and the 2 KiB user-metadata ceiling before it touches the store.
s.store.PutObject receives the bytes as a storage.OwnedBody; the store owns quota, authority and persistence, and its refusal comes back as an error rather than as a wire shape.

writeError renders the refusal as the one S3 error shape (Error/Code/Message/Resource/RequestId) with the matching x-amz-request-id header; the success path renders through writeXML at internal/s3api/errors.go:249, and both apply the same CORS allowlist.

evidence.detail: New is the only constructor: it refuses a nil Store and a nil Auth, applies the Host, Region, BaseHost and request-limit defaults, and type-asserts the store to storage.MultipartStore once (server.go:102), which is what later decides whether multipart routes exist.
The /_stow branch is taken before the SigV4 call at server.go:253, so the admin and metrics routes are outside S3 authentication entirely and are governed by authorizeAdmin (server.go:355) instead.
http.MaxBytesReader wraps the request body at the HTTP boundary, so SigV4 payload verification, checksum validation, PutObject and every multipart part read the same bounded bytes.

admitRequest is a non-blocking send on a buffered channel of MaxConcurrentRequests slots; on overflow it sets Retry-After: 1 and writes SlowDown with 503, so admission precedes body buffering and authentication.
requireMultipart reads the capability from the store, so a store without storage.MultipartStore is refused with NotImplemented before a byte is read rather than partway through an upload.
unsupportedSemanticMarker is the explicit refusal list: eighteen query markers and KMS server-side encryption are refused, and versionId is refused as InvalidArgument rather than silently ignored.

storageErrorCases is a 17-row table mapping storage sentinels, runtime.ErrQuotaExceeded, runtime.ErrClosed, runtime.ErrInvalidListLimit and runtime.ErrMultipartUnsupported onto S3 codes and statuses; the comment at errors.go:113-119 states that the order matters because the first match wins.
An authority refusal becomes 403 AccessDenied and not InternalError, and the message names only the refused operation, so a caller learns what it may not do without learning what it may.

storage.ErrMutationCommitted is checked ahead of the upstream branch and the table because its cause would otherwise be matched as a missing key, which would tell a caller the object does not exist after the server had just written it.

upstreamFailure splits by who is at fault and whether waiting helps: no response or a 5xx is 503 ServiceUnavailable, a 4xx is passed through with the upstream's own code, and the message says the fault is not in the server being talked to.

Nine optional provider interfaces are declared here (admin.go:17-63) and discovered by type assertion on s.store (admin.go:203-213, 270, 349-354, 366-382, 402, 421, 440-458), so the concrete type of Config.Store is part of the HTTP contract rather than an implementation detail.

runThroughRuntimeStore is the type the native CLI actually hands to the server: it embeds the runtime adapter and forwards all eleven provider methods to the runthrough.Adapter, which is what makes the admin routes answer with real cache and outbox state instead of zeros.

originAllowed refuses to reflect an arbitrary Origin: with no configured allowlist only loopback origins are permitted, a configured allowlist replaces that default, and the wildcard is an explicit opt-in. setCORS always sets Vary: Origin.
checkPreconditions is one function for both reads and copy sources, with notModifiedIsSuccess as the only difference: a matching If-None-Match on a read is 304 and on a copy source is 412.

copyVerbatim hands the source conditions to storage.ConditionalCopyStore so the version copied is the version the conditions were checked against, and falls back to a head-then-check path only for a store that cannot evaluate conditions.

serveRange emits representation headers but deliberately not the whole-object checksum header, because a 206 carries a fragment and an SDK that hashes what it received would report a mismatch on a truthful answer.
takeRequestBody hands the materialised bytes to the store as a storage.OwnedBody and clears the per-request cache, so the body is read once per request and ownership is explicit at the handoff.
A caller-visible fact the source fixes: from one address with no credential, an S3 path answers 403 while /_stow/health answers 200, and the two mean opposite things.
wireStores runs the same wire assertions over the memory, filesystem and workspace stores, which is what shows the handlers inherit the store's return value rather than reinterpreting it.

interface.types: A Server built by New(Config) (*Server, error) (internal/s3api/server.go:81). Config (internal/s3api/server.go:19) carries the injected storage.Store, the AuthFunc, the listen Host and Port, BaseHost for virtual-hosted routing, DataDir, Region, CORSOrigins, the reporting strings Mode, CachePolicy, WritePolicy and UpstreamHost, the AdminToken and the deprecated no-op AllowPublicAdmin, MaxRequestBytes and MaxConcurrentRequests. The package's exported surface is exactly: Config, Server, New, (*Server).ListenAndServe, .Ready, .Addr, .Shutdown, .ServeHTTP, .Handler, AuthFunc, DevBypass, SigV4Auth, AdminTokenHeader, DefaultMaxRequestBytes, DefaultMaxConcurrentRequests, ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout. AuthFunc is func(*http.Request) error, returning nil to allow (internal/s3api/auth.go:11); SigV4Auth(*auth.Verifier, auth.Credentials) AuthFunc (internal/s3api/auth.go:19) is the production adapter and DevBypass (internal/s3api/auth.go:14) the test adapter. (*Server).Handler() http.Handler (internal/s3api/server.go:380) returns the server itself so a caller can mount it in httptest without binding a port. AdminTokenHeader is "X-Stow-Admin" (internal/s3api/cors.go:13), deliberately not Authorization so it can never be confused with or interfere with a SigV4 signature. The store's own type is part of the interface: New type-asserts it to storage.MultipartStore once (internal/s3api/server.go:102), and four more capabilities are discovered by type assertion at request time, so a caller that wants multipart, store-side checksum computation, conditional copy, paged part listing or the admin routes must pass a store whose concrete type carries them.
invariants: New rejects a nil Store and a nil Auth (internal/s3api/server.go:82-87): authentication is explicit and there is no implicit-open default.

New applies defaults: Host to 127.0.0.1, Region to us-east-1, MaxRequestBytes to DefaultMaxRequestBytes (8 MiB), MaxConcurrentRequests to DefaultMaxConcurrentRequests (16); a negative limit is an error, not a silent clamp (internal/s3api/server.go:88-100, internal/s3api/request_admission.go:11-22).

One body read per request: the body cache is installed on every request (internal/s3api/server.go:217, internal/s3api/request.go:44-46) so the auth stage and the handler share one materialisation, and takeRequestBody (internal/s3api/request.go:58-65) transfers ownership of those bytes to the store as a storage.OwnedBody and clears the cache.

The body is bounded at the HTTP boundary before authentication and before any handler reads it (internal/s3api/server.go:238-240), so SigV4 payload verification, checksum validation, PutObject and every multipart part are under one cap.

Admission precedes body buffering and authentication (internal/s3api/server.go:208, internal/s3api/request_admission.go:24-33): an over-limit request gets SlowDown with 503 and Retry-After: 1 without its body being read.

The /_stow surface is outside SigV4: the admin branch (internal/s3api/server.go:242-251) precedes the auth call (internal/s3api/server.go:253), so admin routes are authorized by the admin-token and loopback rule instead.

The store's type shape is part of the contract: storage.MultipartStore (internal/s3api/server.go:102), storage.PutChecksumStore (internal/s3api/request.go:280), storage.ConditionalCopyStore (internal/s3api/copy.go:85), multipartPartsPager (internal/s3api/multipart_paging.go:33-45) and the nine admin provider interfaces (internal/s3api/admin.go:17-63) are all found by type assertion. A missing one degrades the answer silently rather than failing loudly.
Every response on an S3 path carries at most one body and one x-amz-request-id, and the id in the XML body matches the header (internal/s3api/errors.go:38-53, internal/s3api/errors.go:249-261).

A GET carrying a Range header answers 206 with a Content-Range and no whole-object checksum header (internal/s3api/handlers_multipart.go:265-301, internal/s3api/validators.go:38-48); a 304 carries validators only, with no body, no Content-Length and no checksum header (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:228-236, internal/s3api/validators.go:67-80).

Shutdown closes the store exactly once through sync.Once (internal/s3api/server.go:199), and ListenAndServe refuses a second start (internal/s3api/server.go:123-126); Ready closes after the listener has bound or startup has failed (internal/s3api/server.go:162, :167).
An unauthorized admin request is answered 404, not 403, so the route's existence is not advertised to a caller that could not use it (internal/s3api/server.go:244, :353-354).
error_modes: Every refusal on an S3 path is an S3 XML Error body with Code, Message, Resource and RequestId (internal/s3api/errors.go:55-61) plus the matching x-amz-request-id header (internal/s3api/errors.go:44).

mapStorageError (internal/s3api/errors.go:147) is the single mapping point and its order is the contract: request-too-large becomes EntityTooLarge 400; authority.ErrNotAuthorized becomes AccessDenied 403; storage.ErrMutationCommitted becomes InternalError 500 asking the caller to verify the outcome before retrying; an upstream failure takes the upstream branch; then the storageErrorCases table matches first-wins; anything unrecognised becomes InternalError 500 'internal storage error'.
An auth failure is 403 carrying the verifier's own code, via authError (internal/s3api/auth.go:25-42).

An unsupported S3 operation is 501 NotImplemented and a versionId or KMS server-side-encryption request is 400 InvalidArgument, decided before routing by unsupportedSemanticMarker (internal/s3api/dispatch.go:158-176).
Concurrency overflow is 503 SlowDown with Retry-After: 1 (internal/s3api/request_admission.go:29-30).

An unauthorized admin request is 404 (internal/s3api/server.go:244); an unknown /_stow path is 404 with the JSON body {"error":"not found"} rather than the S3 XML shape (internal/s3api/admin.go:104-107); a failed admin operation answers plain text through http.Error (internal/s3api/admin.go:111-113).
A malformed query string is 400 InvalidArgument before anything else happens (internal/s3api/server.go:223-227).
A CORS preflight from a disallowed origin is 403 with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all (internal/s3api/cors.go:86-91).

A metadata size over 2 KiB is 400 InvalidArgument (internal/s3api/errors.go:66, internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:198-201); a checksum mismatch is 400 BadDigest and a malformed Content-MD5 is 400 InvalidArgument (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:166-182).
ordering: ServeHTTP's order is fixed: admission, request id, body cache, CORS allowlist, query-string parse, CORS preflight, body size cap, admin branch, SigV4, route parse, dispatch (internal/s3api/server.go:207-286).

Inside dispatch, the unsupported-semantic-marker check runs before the root/bucket/object split (internal/s3api/dispatch.go:14-30), so a request carrying ?versioning cannot fall through to a supported operation.

Inside a PUT, the body is read once and the checks run in order: Content-Length present and agreeing, Content-MD5, checksum algorithm and value, metadata extraction and the size ceiling, then the store call (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:153-215).
On a read, the preconditions are evaluated before the range is parsed (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:228-245).

On a copy, the metadata directive is read before the source is opened, and the source conditions are evaluated against the same opened version whose bytes are handed to the store (internal/s3api/copy.go:112-145).
On an admin request the authorization decision is made before the route is dispatched: token match, then destructive-path check, then loopback check (internal/s3api/server.go:355-363).
configuration: Config.AdminToken is the credential for the admin and metrics routes, sent as X-Stow-Admin; with it empty, the read-only admin routes are reachable from loopback only and the outbox routes are unreachable at all (internal/s3api/server.go:38-44).

Config.AllowPublicAdmin is retained for source compatibility and grants nothing by itself (internal/s3api/server.go:45-50); the deprecation warning is printed by the CLI at cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:54-56, not by this package.
Config.CORSOrigins replaces the loopback default rather than adding to it; the literal * is the explicit opt-in to any origin (internal/s3api/cors.go:20, :27-45).

Config.MaxRequestBytes bounds the bytes read from one request body and Config.MaxConcurrentRequests bounds active handlers; both take their defaults from the package constants (internal/s3api/server.go:51-56, internal/s3api/request_admission.go:9, :19).

Config.Mode, CachePolicy, WritePolicy, UpstreamHost and Region are reporting strings, not behaviour switches: /_stow/status substitutes 'local', 'none' and 'local-only' when they are empty (internal/s3api/admin.go:177-188).
Config.BaseHost selects virtual-hosted-style bucket routing; when it is unset the suffix is derived from the bound address after the listener binds (internal/s3api/server.go:94-97, :141-147).
The underlying http.Server carries ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout of five minutes each and MaxHeaderBytes of 1 MiB (internal/s3api/errors.go:76-79, internal/s3api/server.go:148-155).

implementation: Eighteen non-test files, about 3,340 lines, and one entry function. ServeHTTP (internal/s3api/server.go:207) takes a slot from a bounded channel, mints a request id, installs a per-request body cache and the CORS allowlist on the request context, validates the query string, answers a CORS preflight, wraps the body in http.MaxBytesReader, then branches: /_stow/* goes to authorizeAdmin and handleAdmin and never reaches SigV4; everything else goes through prepareRequestForAuth (which materialises the body once so the SigV4 payload hash and the handler read the same bytes) and s.auth. parseRoute (internal/s3api/router.go:16) turns host and path into a bucket and a key, choosing virtual-hosted addressing when the Host carries a .baseHost suffix and path-style otherwise, and refusing an undecodable name. dispatch (internal/s3api/dispatch.go:12) refuses eighteen unsupported semantic markers and a versionId before it chooses root, bucket or object, and the object branch recognises multipart requests (uploadId, POST ?uploads, PUT ?partNumber) before the plain object switch, so a store without multipart is refused before a byte is read. The handlers are thin translators: handlePutObject (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:153) reads the body once, then enforces Content-Length, Content-MD5, the checksum headers and the 2 KiB metadata ceiling before calling s.store.PutObject; handleGetObject (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:221) applies the read preconditions and then either a 206 range response or the whole object; handleDeleteObjects (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:295) copies the store's returned key list into the response, which is why a key that was never there appears in Deleted; handleCopyObject (internal/s3api/handlers_bucket.go:332) reads x-amz-metadata-directive and routes to copyVerbatim or replaceMetadata in internal/s3api/copy.go, where source conditions are handed to storage.ConditionalCopyStore so the version copied is the version the conditions were checked against. The XML vocabulary (internal/s3api/xml.go) is declarations plus two small projections; the wire shapes are fixed there and the decisions are in the handlers and in the error mapper. The error vocabulary (internal/s3api/errors.go:127-247) is the one place where three refusal vocabularies become one: storage sentinels, the runtime's quota/closed/list-limit/multipart sentinels, authority.ErrNotAuthorized and runthrough.UpstreamError are all rendered as S3 codes and statuses, and the mapping is deliberately order-sensitive because the first match wins. The admin surface (internal/s3api/admin.go) is a second, JSON-shaped surface on the same port with its own authorization rule: read-only routes answer unsigned from loopback, everything else needs the constant-time-compared X-Stow-Admin token, and the two outbox routes need it on every address, with a 404 rather than a 403 so the route is not advertised. The nine optional provider interfaces there are discovered by type assertion on the concrete store, so the cache counters, the cache listing, the outbox statistics, the outbox entries and the outbox retry and discard actions exist only when the store type carries them.

callers.scope: The native serve command builds the one production server: s3api.New with s3api.SigV4Auth(verifier, creds) (main.go:383), then srv.ListenAndServe() on a goroutine (main.go:403) and srv.Addr() (main.go:410) to publish the readiness record.

startWorkspaceFacade builds a second production server over a runtime.StoreAdapter, with AdminToken set to the generated secret, and waits on server.Ready() (workspace_facade.go:100) before returning the loopback endpoint and credentials.

The doctor check builds a throwaway server over a memory store with doctorAuth (doctor.go:250) and probes /_stow/health (doctor.go:310), which is the only way the check knows this machine can actually serve.

The type the native CLI actually hands to the server. It embeds the runtime adapter and forwards the eleven provider methods the admin routes find by type assertion, which is what makes the admin surface answer with real cache and outbox state.
The shared conformance harness drives the server with the AWS SDK for Go v2 against a real SigV4 verifier, over memory, filesystem and runtime-backed stores.
A test caller with a real SigV4 verifier that pins the unsigned-S3-path-versus-unsigned-diagnostic-route split and the off-loopback admin token rule.
A test caller that runs the same wire assertions over the memory, filesystem and workspace stores, showing the handlers inherit the store's return value rather than reinterpreting it.
An in-package test caller that constructs &Server{store: store} directly and calls writeInspect, showing the admin handlers are exercisable without a listener or a bound port.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Delete internal/s3api and the complexity does not vanish with it; it reappears in every caller. cmd/stow-s3/main.go:379 would have to re-implement the SigV4 gate, the request-id and CORS middleware, the body-size cap, the route table, the XML error envelope, the conditional-request and checksum rules and the multipart refusal; pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:88 would have to re-implement them a second time for the same wire; and the conformance harness would lose the thing it exists to check. The part that would genuinely have to be re-derived rather than relocated is the error vocabulary: with the package gone, the runtime refusals, the authority refusals and the upstream refusals would each need a mapping in each caller, which is three copies of mapStorageError instead of one, and the copies would drift. What does not survive the deletion is any state: the package holds no storage state of its own, holds no long-lived data, and owns no resource beyond the listener and the request slots.

leverage: Callers get the whole S3 wire contract from one call: a store plus a credential yields a server an unmodified AWS SDK can drive, which is why cmd/stow-s3/main.go:379, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:88, cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:270 and conformance/harness_test.go:119 all share one route table, one error vocabulary and one set of conditional and checksum rules, so a change to the wire is made once rather than per client. The error vocabulary is the highest-leverage part of it: mapStorageError is the only place where a runtime refusal, an upstream refusal and a storage refusal become one S3 code, which is what internal/s3api/errors.go:14-15 importing both internal/runtime and internal/runthrough buys, and what makes 'the upstream went away' read as 503 ServiceUnavailable instead of a corrupt workspace. The second leverage is the request-admission and body-limit envelope, which the CLI, the workspace facade and the readiness record all quote, so a client learns the limits from one place and the server enforces them at one place.
locality: Everything a client can observe is in this one directory: the route table in internal/s3api/dispatch.go, the wire shapes in internal/s3api/xml.go, the error codes and statuses in internal/s3api/errors.go, the conditional, checksum, metadata and validator rules in internal/s3api/validators.go and internal/s3api/request.go, the range rules in internal/s3api/range.go, the CORS policy in internal/s3api/cors.go, the admission and body limit in internal/s3api/request_admission.go, and the admin surface in internal/s3api/admin.go. A change to an S3 error code, a status, a header or a route is a change in one package, and the tests that pin it are next to it. What is deliberately not here is the storage decision: quotas, authority and policy live in internal/runtime and internal/authority, propagation and the outbox live in internal/runthrough, and persistence and the multipart part-size minimum live in internal/storage. The S3 layer translates what those return; it does not decide them. The one place the boundary is soft is the store's optional type shape, which the S3 layer reads by assertion and therefore depends on without declaring.
risks: The store's concrete type is an undeclared part of the HTTP contract. Nine optional provider interfaces in internal/s3api/admin.go:17-63 are discovered by type assertion on s.store, so a store that implements none answers /_stow/status with zeros and /_stow/inspect with an empty cache list, which reads as 'the cache is empty' rather than 'nobody wired this up'. That is the exact failure cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go:74-85 exists to prevent, and nothing in the type system prevents it from recurring. The same is true of storage.MultipartStore (internal/s3api/server.go:102), storage.PutChecksumStore (internal/s3api/request.go:280) and storage.ConditionalCopyStore (internal/s3api/copy.go:85): a missing optional interface silently degrades the answer instead of failing loudly.

The error vocabulary is order-sensitive and the order is not visible in the rows. mapStorageError puts the request-too-large, authority-refusal and committed-mutation cases ahead of the table, and the upstream branch ahead of the table again (internal/s3api/errors.go:147-203). A new row placed before the upstream branch would make an upstream 404 look like a missing local key. Only internal/s3api/errors_upstream_test.go:136 currently guards that the upstream branch does not shadow the table.

The admin surface deliberately bypasses SigV4 (internal/s3api/server.go:242 precedes :253) and its loopback allowance is a property of RemoteAddr. The only defence against a local reverse proxy is the presence of a forwarding header (internal/s3api/server.go:334-341); a proxy that strips those headers restores the allowance for the read-only routes. The two destructive outbox routes are unaffected, because they always require the token.

Two authorization vocabularies and two error shapes coexist on one port: S3 XML on S3 paths and plain text or JSON on /_stow/* (internal/s3api/admin.go:111-113 against internal/s3api/errors.go:38). A client that assumes one error shape for the whole port misreads the other, and the 404-not-403 refusal on admin routes makes the two surfaces harder to tell apart from the outside.

Request bodies are buffered whole. requestBody materialises the entire body in memory (internal/s3api/request.go:68) and the defaults are 8 MiB per request with 16 concurrent requests (internal/s3api/errors.go:70, internal/s3api/request_admission.go:9), so roughly 128 MiB of request bodies can be resident at once before the store's own quota says anything. The limit bounds the body, not process memory.

Config.AllowPublicAdmin's doc comment promises that the server logs a deprecation warning (internal/s3api/server.go:45-49), but the package never reads the field; the warning is printed by cmd/stow-s3/offline.go:54-56. A caller reading the package documentation will expect a warning this package does not produce.

The declared list of unsupported S3 features (internal/s3api/dispatch.go:159-167) is a flat string list with no link to docs/compat-contract.md section 5, so the two lists can drift independently and a client that trusts one of them will meet the other.

priority.rationale: Blast radius is the whole S3 surface: three production callers (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:379, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:88, cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:270) and the AWS-SDK conformance harness all drive the same wire, so an error-code, status or header change reaches every client at once. The coupling is hidden in two places that no type signature shows: the store's optional capabilities, which the package reads by type assertion rather than declares, and the order-sensitive error table, where the position of a row rather than its content decides the client's answer. The admin surface adds a second authorization scheme and a second error shape on the same port, and it depends on a forwarding-header heuristic for its loopback trust. That justifies P2 for impact. Overall stays at P2 rather than rising, because the package holds no state, its behaviour is fully observable at the wire and is pinned by package-level tests, and every decision it makes has exactly one implementation site.

next_action: Document and then narrow the store-type contract the S3 layer silently depends on. The exported surface says nothing about it: Config.Store's documentation does not say that a store may need to implement storage.MultipartStore, storage.PutChecksumStore, storage.ConditionalCopyStore or the nine admin provider interfaces, and internal/s3api/admin.go declares those nine privately, so no store package can compile against them and cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go has to forward all eleven methods by hand. The interface that should change is Config.Store: export one named aggregate (for example s3api.AdminProvider, covering the cache and outbox providers) so a store implementation can be checked at compile time and the forwarding wrapper in cmd/stow-s3/runtime_store.go can be asserted once rather than re-derived, or else have Config carry the admin capabilities explicitly instead of discovering them by assertion. In the same pass, correct the Config.AllowPublicAdmin doc comment (internal/s3api/server.go:45-49), which promises a deprecation warning this package does not emit, and record the ordering rule of mapStorageError's special cases inside the storageErrorCases comment (internal/s3api/errors.go:113-119) so the first-match-wins contract is visible where the rows are rather than only in the function body.

title: Durable filesystem object store
summary: internal/storage/fs is the durable, on-disk implementation of storage.Store and nine of its optional extensions. It owns the whole data-directory contract: the directory layout (buckets/<bucket>/bucket.json, buckets/<bucket>/objects/..., .multipart/, .save-requests/, .save-pending.json, .save-identity.json, .recovery-holds.json, .capacity-binding.json, .stow.lock, .stow-owner), the version-2 object-record codec (an 8-byte STOWOBJ2 magic, a four-byte little-endian header length, a protobuf header, then the raw payload), the exclusive advisory lock that makes one process the owner of a directory, atomic publication, staged writes, the durable save-request journal, the multipart manifest, capacity accounting and recovery holds. It is constructed only by fs.NewFilesystemStore or fs.NewFilesystemStoreWithNamespace and is used by the CLI (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:120), the Go library (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:44) and the doctor probe (cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:202); the runtime finds its optional capabilities by type assertion and is forbidden from importing the package (internal/runtime/dependencies_test.go:25).

trace.scope: serve --backend filesystem: openLocalStore constructs fs.NewFilesystemStore(dataDir) and hands it to the runtime as a storage.Store
newFilesystemStore: takes the exclusive .stow.lock, removes stale .tmp- files, initialises the save journal and writes the .stow-owner marker last
PutObject: StageObject then Commit, so the body is staged outside the publication and the conditions are re-checked at commit time
commitStreamLocked: re-checks write preconditions and recovery holds, then builds the version-2 objectRecord with a fresh record version
encodeRecordPrefix: the STOWOBJ2 magic, the little-endian header length and a deterministic protobuf header carrying the metadata and the exact payload length
writeRecordBody: the header prefix and the payload are written together as one file through atomicfile.WriteStream
os.Rename over the object path, followed by the parent-directory fsync that makes the publication durable

evidence.detail: newFilesystemStore is the single construction path: it creates buckets/ and .multipart/, acquires the store lock, cleans stale temps, warns about the legacy layout, initialises the save journal and writes the ownership marker last.
binaryRecordMagic = 'STOWOBJ2', binaryRecordVersion = 2 and binaryRecordPrefixSize = magic+4 define the on-disk record framing; the payload follows the header verbatim.
decodeRecordHeader refuses any header whose Version is not 2 or whose PayloadSize is negative, so a future codec that changes the framing bricks every existing directory rather than misreading it.
readRecordHeader verifies that the file length equals the header's declared payload size, refusing a truncated or over-long record.
readLegacyRecord is the version-1 JSON fallback; it requires record.Version == 1 and returns a -1 offset so the reader materialises the payload in memory.
TestLegacyJSONRecordReadableAndRewritten shows a version-1 record is readable and listed and is rewritten as version 2 only on overwrite.
The store lock is flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) on .stow.lock: one process at a time owns a directory, and the kernel releases the lock when the owner dies.
On aix, js, plan9, solaris and wasip1 the lock is unsupported and store construction fails rather than proceeding unguarded.
writeOwnerMarker writes .stow-owner; its failure is logged rather than fatal, because the marker's absence only makes a later reset refuse.
resetOwnedData is the reader of the marker and the layer that refuses a directory stow did not create, plus the home, cwd and ancestor backstop.
The quality gate compares the Go marker name with the TypeScript marker name and fails the build when they drift.
Publication of a streamed object is a single atomicfile.WriteStream of the header prefix followed by the body, so header and payload can never disagree.
The durable sink: rename over the target followed by a parent-directory fsync, with the temporary file removed on every failure path.
Commit takes the store lock, re-checks the stage options, the write preconditions and the recovery holds before publishing; a consumed stage cannot commit twice.
publishSaveLocked moves the receipt through prepared/publishing and only settles it after the object is written, so an interrupted publication is recoverable rather than silently lost.
verifyPublishedSaveLocked re-derives the truth from the published object (request key, meaning, fingerprint and metadata) before a 'publishing' entry becomes 'committed'.
The multipart manifest carries the upload's content type, metadata and checksum on disk, which is what lets a completion in another process publish the same object.
checkRecoveryHoldsLocked refuses a mutation of a pinned object with storage.ErrRecoveryHeld; reads are unaffected.
scanCapacityLocked walks the whole data directory, refuses symlinks and classifies each file, so every byte in the tree is charged to the namespace.
The bounded digest layout is chosen for keys whose reversible path would overflow a filesystem limit; the key is then carried in the record header because the path cannot be reversed.

internal/runtime is forbidden from linking internal/storage/fs, so the runtime's dependence on this package's guarded-save, save-request and recovery-hold behaviour travels through type assertions it cannot name.
SupportsGuardedWrites is true only on darwin and linux, which is why the durable journal, the holds and the ancestor fence are absent elsewhere.

interface.types: fs.FilesystemStore is a struct with no exported fields. It is created only by fs.NewFilesystemStore(dataDir string) (*FilesystemStore, error) (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:42) or fs.NewFilesystemStoreWithNamespace(dataDir string, namespace *capacity.Namespace) (*FilesystemStore, error) (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:46); there is no other constructor and no way to open an existing store without taking its lock. The type satisfies storage.Store (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:39), storage.MultipartStore, storage.ConditionalCopyStore, storage.StagedWriteStore (internal/storage/fs/staged_put.go:16), storage.PutChecksumStore (internal/storage/fs/fs_put.go:128), storage.UsageRevisionStore (internal/storage/fs/usage_revision.go:5), storage.ObjectUsageStore (internal/storage/fs/fs_list.go:134), storage.GuardedWriteStore (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:46), storage.SaveRequestStore (internal/storage/fs/save_requests.go:26) and storage.RecoveryHoldStore (internal/storage/fs/recovery_holds.go:65) - ten interfaces in all, no more. The package also exports fs.OwnerMarkerName, fs.OwnerMarkerVersion, fs.OwnerMarker, fs.IsOwnedDataDir and fs.OwnedDataDirError (internal/storage/fs/owner.go:18-67), which describe the data-directory ownership marker rather than the store.
invariants: One directory has one owner: a second store on the same dataDir fails while the first holds .stow.lock (internal/storage/fs/fs_lock_test.go:20, internal/storage/fs/fs_test.go:20).

One object is one file: an 8-byte 'STOWOBJ2' magic, a four-byte little-endian uint32 header length, a deterministic protobuf ObjectHeader, then the raw payload (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:15-40).
The header's declared payload size equals the file's payload length; a mismatch is refused (internal/storage/fs/record_io.go:39).
A record whose header version is not 2 is refused, never partially interpreted (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:62).

A version-1 JSON record is readable in a mixed directory and is rewritten as version 2 only when the object is overwritten; opening a directory never rewrites its objects (internal/storage/fs/record_format_test.go:90, docs/adr/0020-binary-object-records.md:53-55).
Publication is atomic: a reader sees the old record or the new one, and a write that returns success survives a crash (internal/atomicfile/atomicfile.go:48-92).
A staged object is invisible until Commit; a stage is consumed exactly once, so a second Commit or a Commit after Abort is refused (internal/storage/fs/staged_put.go:138).
The write conditions and the recovery holds are re-evaluated at Commit, not at Stage (internal/storage/fs/staged_put.go:176-183).

A save request is idempotent by request key: a replayed request returns the retained receipt and never writes twice; a request key reused with a different meaning is a conflict (internal/storage/fs/save_requests.go:57-77).

An interrupted save publication is reported as unknown and blocks every subsequent mutation until it settles; the outcome is always one of committed, not_committed or unknown (internal/storage/fs/runtime_recovery_test.go:37-87).
A pending hold refuses any mutation of the pinned objects with storage.ErrRecoveryHeld and leaves reads unaffected (internal/storage/fs/recovery_holds.go:166-184).

A multipart completion publishes exactly the content type and metadata recorded in the manifest, and a failed cleanup returns the committed metadata with storage.CommittedError rather than reporting a failure (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:219-225).
A delete of a missing key is confirmed rather than reported as an error (internal/storage/fs/contract_test.go:80-86).
A reader opened on an object keeps that version across a later overwrite and a later delete (internal/storage/fs/record_format_test.go:35).

A directory that is not stow's is never deleted on a caller's behalf: the .stow-owner marker must be present, and the protected-path backstop is enforced by the TypeScript reader (internal/storage/fs/owner.go:44, packages/stow-s3/src/ownership.ts:83).

In a namespace-bound store every file in the data directory is charged to the namespace, and a file the store does not recognise is refused as capacity.ErrUnknown rather than skipped (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:114-119).
error_modes: storage.ErrBucketNotFound, storage.ErrBucketExists and storage.ErrBucketNotEmpty for bucket operations (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:208, internal/storage/fs/fs.go:226, internal/storage/fs/fs.go:249).
storage.ErrObjectNotFound for a missing object, in both the read and the delete paths (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:321, internal/storage/fs/fs.go:379).

storage.ErrUploadNotFound, storage.ErrNoSuchUpload and storage.ErrInvalidPart for multipart (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:125, internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:234, internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:171).

storage.ErrSaveRequestUnknown when a publication's effect cannot be established; it reaches the runtime as SaveUnknown and blocks every later mutation until settled (internal/storage/fs/save_requests.go:189, internal/storage/fs/runtime_recovery_test.go:84).
storage.ErrSaveRequestConflict, ErrSaveRequestNotFound, ErrSaveRequestNotCommitted, ErrSaveRequestFull, ErrInvalidSaveRequest and ErrSaveRequestsUnsupported (internal/storage/save_requests.go:9-15).
storage.ErrRecoveryHeld, ErrInvalidRecoveryHold, ErrRecoveryHoldNotFound and ErrRecoveryHoldFull (internal/storage/recovery.go:9-12).

storage.ErrMutationCommitted (wrapped) when a write committed but a later step failed: multipart cleanup (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:224) and a capacity admission failure (internal/storage/fs/capacity_save.go:37).

capacity.ErrConflict when the directory is bound to another namespace or host (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:63) or when a hold's meaning conflicts (internal/storage/fs/recovery_holds.go:89); capacity.ErrUnknown when a file in the tree cannot be classified (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:114).
storage.ErrSaveConflict from a failed content guard (internal/storage/fs/fs_put.go:50) and storage.ErrPreconditionFailed from a failed IfMatch/IfNoneMatch check (internal/storage/fs/fs_put.go:47).
storage.ErrChecksumMismatch when a supplied checksum does not match (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:387).
A bare 'object path digest collision' error when a digest-addressed record holds a different key (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:327, internal/storage/fs/fs_records.go:114).
A raw OS error, wrapped as 'acquire store lock', when the directory is already owned or the host cannot lock at all (internal/storage/fs/fs_lock.go:18, internal/storage/fs/fs_lock_other.go:8).
storage.ErrInvalidRecoveryHold for an unreadable, oversized or checksum-mismatched hold journal (internal/storage/fs/recovery_hold_journal.go:33-50).
ordering: Construct before use: a store owns its directory from construction and releases the lock only on Close (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:441).
Mutations are serialised by an internal write mutex and reads take the read lock, so a caller never sees a half-written record (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:217, internal/storage/fs/fs.go:312).

Every mutating call settles the pending save publication before it does anything else, so a mutation is never applied on top of an unresolved publication (internal/storage/fs/fs_put.go:22, internal/storage/fs/fs.go:220).
A staged object must be committed or aborted exactly once (internal/storage/fs/staged_put.go:138).
The receipt is written before the object it describes, so the object is never newer than its receipt (internal/storage/fs/save_requests.go:137-156).

The multipart manifest is written before any part, and the object is published before the upload directory is removed (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:93, internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:219).
A capacity namespace may be bound only while no stage is active (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:27).
The recovery-hold identity marker is written together with the journal, so the pair is consistent from the first write (internal/storage/fs/recovery_hold_journal.go:151-166).
configuration: dataDir: the directory the store takes ownership of. It must be creatable and writable (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:59) and must not already be bound to a different capacity namespace (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:53).

An optional capacity.Namespace binds the store to a byte budget; binding is refused while a stage is active (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:27) and is recorded in .capacity-binding.json (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:32).

Platform: the store lock is unavailable on aix, js, plan9, solaris and wasip1, where construction fails (internal/storage/fs/fs_lock_other.go:8); the durable save-request journal, the recovery holds and the per-publication ancestor fence are enabled only on darwin and linux (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:46).

Fixed on-disk limits that are not configurable: 1024 save receipts, 8 MiB of save journal and 64 KiB per receipt (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:20-23); 256 recovery holds with 32 references each and 2 MiB of journal (internal/storage/fs/recovery_holds.go:21-25); 10,000 parts per upload (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:113).

No environment variable and no configuration file is read by this package. The only name that crosses the language boundary is the .stow-owner marker, duplicated in packages/stow-s3/src/ownership.ts:12 and compared by scripts/check-version.mjs:188.

implementation: Twenty-seven Go files hold the store. The data directory is a tree with a fixed shape: buckets/<bucket>/bucket.json holding the creation time, buckets/<bucket>/objects/... holding one file per object, .multipart/<uploadID>/manifest.json plus part-%05d, .save-requests/<sha256(requestKey)>.json plus .save-pending.json and .save-identity.json, .recovery-holds.json plus .recovery-holds.identity, .capacity-binding.json, .stow.lock, .stow-owner, and transient .tmp-* files. The path of an object is chosen per key: a reversible hex path, sharded into '_'-prefixed directories when the key is too long for one component, or the bounded digest layout _long/<2 hex>/<64 hex> when the reversible path would overflow a filesystem limit - and only the digest layout records the key in its record header, because its path cannot be reversed back to the key (internal/storage/fs/paths.go:79-87, internal/storage/fs/fs.go:129-155, internal/storage/fs/fs_records.go:50-61). The record itself is one file: an 8-byte STOWOBJ2 magic, a little-endian uint32 header length, a deterministic protobuf header holding the logical metadata and the exact payload length, then the raw payload (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:15-55). A version-1 JSON record is still read, in memory rather than as a section, and is rewritten as version 2 only when the object is overwritten (internal/storage/fs/record_io.go:45-64). Publication always runs through a temporary file, an fsync, a rename and a parent-directory fsync, so a reader sees the old record or the new one (internal/atomicfile/atomicfile.go:48-92). Beyond the object model the package owns four journals. The save-request journal turns an ambiguous write into a three-valued outcome: a receipt moves through prepared, publishing and committed, and after a crash the truth is re-derived from the published object by comparing the request key, the meaning digest, the object fingerprint and the metadata (internal/storage/fs/save_requests.go:137-274). The multipart manifest carries the upload's content type, metadata and checksum on disk, so a completion issued by a different process publishes the same object (internal/storage/fs/fs_multipart.go:19-35). The recovery-hold journal pins bytes across a process death, is validated by identity and checksum on every read, and refuses any mutation of the pinned objects while leaving reads free (internal/storage/fs/recovery_hold_journal.go:57-78, internal/storage/fs/recovery_holds.go:166-184). The capacity binding charges every file in the tree to a namespace and refuses to classify a file it does not recognise, because a scan that skips one under-reports the budget it feeds (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:68-153). A single RWMutex serialises the mutations, and every mutating path settles any pending save publication before it proceeds (internal/storage/fs/usage_revision.go:12).

callers.scope: the CLI's local-backend selection: serve --backend filesystem opens the store and hands it to the runtime as a storage.Store
the public Go library's OpenFilesystem opens the store (with or without a capacity namespace) and passes it to runtime.OpenWithStore
the doctor probe opens a throwaway store in a temporary directory and round-trips one object through it, so a broken backend is reported without touching a real data directory
the shared backend contract suite runs this store against the memory and workspace backends, which is where the object model's cross-backend guarantees are pinned
the runtime discovers the staged-write capability by asserting the store to storage.StagedWriteStore and then publishes through the staged path
the runtime discovers the guarded-write capability by asserting the store to storage.GuardedWriteStore, which is what decides whether a save can be conditional at all
the runtime discovers the recovery-hold capability by asserting the store to storage.RecoveryHoldStore
the package's own test asserts that a second store on the same directory fails while the first holds the lock

depth_assessment.deletion_test: The complexity concentrates rather than vanishing. Deleting internal/storage/fs removes the only durable backend: cmd/stow-s3/main.go:120 loses --backend filesystem entirely, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:44 loses OpenFilesystem, and the memory and workspace stores cannot be substituted because they have no directory to own, no record format, no lock, no journal and no reset rule. Everything the package hides would have to reappear inside whichever caller wanted durability: the STOWOBJ2 record framing and its version-1 read path, the sharded and digest path layouts, the atomic publish sequence, the save-request journal with its three-valued outcome, the multipart manifest, the recovery-hold journal, the capacity scan and the .stow-owner marker. The three callers that construct the store today write four lines each (cmd/stow-s3/main.go:120, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:44, cmd/stow-s3/doctor.go:202); none of them holds any of that knowledge. The test went deep, not shallow. The package is deep at the boundary but is itself wide: 3,733 non-test lines across 27 files own five separable concerns (record format, path layout, atomic publication, journals, capacity accounting) behind one concrete type with no internal seam, which is why the map names the codec separately from the store.

leverage: A caller gets crash-consistent objects, exclusive ownership of a directory, an idempotent save protocol with a three-valued outcome, cross-process multipart manifests, a byte budget charged for every file in the tree, and a reset rule that refuses to delete a directory stow did not create - from one constructor call. The callers know none of it: cmd/stow-s3/main.go:120 passes a path and receives a store satisfying ten storage interfaces (storage.Store plus nine optional extensions); internal/runtime never imports the package at all and still gets guarded saves, recovery holds and staged writes, because those capabilities are discovered by type assertion and this store is the only implementation of two of them.
locality: Everything about the durable format lives in one directory: the record codec in record_codec.go, the path layout in paths.go, the atomic publish in fs_records.go plus internal/atomicfile, the save journal in save_journal.go and save_requests.go, the multipart manifest in fs_multipart.go, the recovery-hold journal in recovery_hold_journal.go, the capacity accounting in capacity.go and capacity_*.go, the lock in fs_lock*.go, the marker in owner.go. A bug in a record, a receipt, a manifest or a hold is found in internal/storage/fs and nowhere else. Exactly one artefact leaves the package: the .stow-owner marker name, duplicated in packages/stow-s3/src/ownership.ts:12 and held in step by scripts/check-version.mjs:188. The package's own doc.go carries a single-line package comment (internal/storage/fs/doc.go:1) and no written statement of what it promises on disk.
risks: The codec is shared by every object ever written. decodeRecordHeader (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:62) refuses any header whose version is not 2, so a codec change without a migration path turns every existing data directory into an unreadable directory rather than a partially readable one. The blast radius is the whole store, because the same header is read by GET (internal/storage/fs/record_io.go:14), HEAD, listing (internal/storage/fs/fs_list.go:91), the capacity scan (internal/storage/fs/capacity.go:137) and the save-journal verification (internal/storage/fs/save_requests.go:255) - and the generated schema is pinned, so a field-number change is caught only by the regeneration check (docs/adr/0020-binary-object-records.md:59-61), not by anything that would keep old data readable.

The durability features are gated on the host OS without saying so in the constructor's signature. SupportsGuardedWrites is true only on darwin and linux (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:46), so on Windows the durable save-request journal, the recovery holds and the per-publication ancestor fence are absent; a caller learns this only by asking the runtime's capabilities (internal/embedded/runtime.go:172), never from fs.NewFilesystemStore itself.

storage.SaveRequestStore and storage.RecoveryHoldStore have exactly one adapter - this package - while internal/runtime is forbidden from importing it (internal/runtime/dependencies_test.go:25). The runtime therefore depends on this concrete package's behaviour through a type assertion it cannot name, so the seam is hypothetical in the storage package and load-bearing in the runtime.

Two directory-lock mechanisms exist with different failure policies: atomicfile.Acquire (internal/atomicfile/lock.go:24), used by internal/policystore, and this package's own storeLock (internal/storage/fs/fs_lock.go:15), which returns errors.ErrUnsupported on aix/js/plan9/solaris/wasip1 so that construction fails rather than proceeding unguarded.

The legacy .stowmeta sidecar layout is detected on open and only warned about (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:107-119); the sidecar files are excluded from the bucket-emptiness check (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:464) and from listing (internal/storage/fs/fs_list.go:67), so that layout is left exactly as it is and is neither migrated nor reported per object.
