The save-journal store identity is minted only when the directory has neither receipts nor a pending entry (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:144-158); a directory with receipts but no identity file is refused with storage.ErrSaveRequestUnknown, so a half-copied data directory cannot be opened rather than being silently re-keyed.

priority.rationale: The blast radius of the record codec is every object ever written by every stow version that used this store, and the failure mode is total: an incompatible codec makes each existing data directory unreadable rather than partially unreadable, because the version check refuses the record (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:62). The package also holds hidden coupling that no caller can see - the runtime depends on guarded saves, durable save requests and recovery holds that only this concrete store provides, across a boundary the runtime is forbidden to import (internal/runtime/dependencies_test.go:25) - and a platform gate that silently removes those capabilities on Windows (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:46). It is not P0 because nothing in the source is currently broken: the codec, the migration rule and the platform gate are all implemented and tested, and the risk is in what a future change would cost, not in a live defect.

next_action: Write down the on-disk contract where the format is defined, and make the codec's blast radius explicit at the interface. Two concrete changes: (1) replace the single-line package comment in internal/storage/fs/doc.go with a package document stating the directory layout, the version-2 record framing, the version-1 read-and-rewrite rule, the journal and hold invariants and limits, the platform gate on SupportsGuardedWrites (internal/storage/fs/save_journal.go:46), and the fact that the .stow-owner marker is read by another language - so that a maintainer changing any of it sees the obligations it carries. (2) Change the codec interface so a future format change is a declared version rather than a silent edit: binaryRecordMagic and binaryRecordVersion are unexported package constants (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:15-17) and the version negotiation in decodeRecordHeader (internal/storage/fs/record_codec.go:62) is invisible to any caller deciding whether an existing directory can be opened; exposing the accepted record version, and refusing a directory whose records are all of an unreadable version with an error that names the version, turns an unreadable-directory failure into a diagnosable one and gives the migration a place to live.

title: The logical snapshot reader: a workspace's object state, read without opening the store or claiming the session
summary: ReadLogicalSnapshot (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:47) reads a workspace's object state the way a capture needs it: without opening a writable store, without taking the session lock, and without writing anything. It pins the root with internal/rooted, reads the manifest and the index through the pinned root with a bounded read, walks the tree refusing a symbolic link outright, adds the escaped keys the index records, and returns a LogicalSnapshot of bucket, key, source path, size, SHA-256, mode, content type, metadata and checksum. It is the only reader in the package that refuses a link rather than treating it as an absence (absence.go:28 makes rooted.ErrSymlink absence everywhere else), and the only one that applies a byte cap and an object cap while it reads. Its one production consumer is the portable checkpoint's inventory step (pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:45).

trace.scope: scanPortableObjects asks for a logical snapshot of the target directory with a byte cap, an object cap and a Select filter. This is the portable checkpoint's inventory step, and the only production call of the function; it is reached from pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture_core.go:51 (captureCheckpoint) and, for a live workspace, from the public CheckpointOf (pkg/stow/checkpoint_external.go:57).

ReadLogicalSnapshot pins the root with rooted.Open, reads the two documents, and builds a logicalSnapshotReader over the pinned root. It never calls workspace.New, so it never writes an index entry, never adopts a file and never takes the session lock.

snapshotKeys walks the pinned filesystem, skips the internal subtree and .git, and refuses a symbolic link with an error rather than skipping it — the opposite of the store's own listing, which skips only the internal subtree.
snapshotObject opens each source through the pinned root, requires a regular file, and derives size, mode, content type, metadata, SHA-256 and any declared checksum.

the snapshot's objects and payloads become the capture manifest's Objects and Payloads (pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable_capture.go:72-73) and are written as the checkpoint's manifest.json and renamed into the registry (pkg/stow/checkpoint_publish.go:35, :48) — the point a capture's state lands. ExportCheckpoint later re-encodes the same manifest into the portable gzip archive's manifest.json and payload members (pkg/stow/checkpoint_archive.go:225, :228).

evidence.detail: The doc comment on LogicalSnapshot states the two properties that distinguish it from the store: it reads object state without opening a writable store and without claiming its session.

ReadLogicalSnapshot opens a rooted.Root, reads the documents through it, walks every bucket, and returns pinned.Check() as its last act (:91) — so the root's identity is re-proved after the read as well as before it.

snapshotDocuments reads .stow/manifest.json and .stow/index.json through the pinned root with a 16 MiB bound (:112-116), refuses a version mismatch as ErrManifestCorrupt (:120-122), and validates that the manifest's bucket and workspace ID are well formed (:124-126). A missing index.json is tolerated and treated as empty.
snapshotKeys skips the internal subtree and any directory named .git, case-insensitively, and skips the whole subtree below it — so a repository's .git internals are not captured as objects.

A symbolic link found by the walk is an error, not a skip: 'workspace: snapshot refuses symbolic link %q'. This is stricter than the store's own listing, which omits non-regular files silently (internal/storage/workspace/list_rooted.go:49-51), and stricter than escapedObjects, which skips a linked escaped key (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:386).

snapshotIndexedKeys adds the escaped keys the index records, using the exact directory-entry spelling observed by the walk for natural paths so that case-sensitive object identities are preserved without re-reading each directory.

The object cap is enforced during the walk (:160-162, :203-205) and again before each object is appended (:73-75), and the byte cap is enforced against the running total (:76-87); exceeding either is an error rather than a truncated result.
snapshotChecksum recomputes a declared checksum and drops it if it no longer matches the recorded value, so a checkpoint does not carry a checksum claim the bytes contradict.
snapshotBuckets reads <root>/.stow/buckets through the pinned root and refuses a linked bucket directory with 'workspace: snapshot refuses linked bucket' (:294-296) rather than counting it.

The consumer checks that snapshot.WorkspaceID equals the workspace ID it asked about and refuses the capture if the identity changed during the read — the snapshot is trusted only because it is tied to a workspace identity.

The consumer cross-checks the snapshot against the file inventory taken by a separate walk of the same directory (pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture.go:97-135, produced by scanCheckpointRoot): if the object and the file disagree on digest or size it refuses with 'file and object changed during capture'. The snapshot is one of two witnesses, not the only one.

The capture's manifest — which carries the snapshot's objects and payloads (pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable_capture.go:72-73) — is written as manifest.json and renamed into the registry (:48), which is the sink the capture's entry point reaches.

ExportCheckpoint (pkg/stow/checkpoint_archive.go:65, called only from the export/handoff paths, e.g. pkg/stow/handoff.go:308) re-encodes the published manifest into the portable archive's manifest.json (:225) and payload members (:228). It is a downstream sink of the same state, not a step on the capture path.

interface.types: ReadLogicalSnapshot(ctx context.Context, root string, options SnapshotOptions) (LogicalSnapshot, error) is the whole entry point (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:47). SnapshotOptions carries MaxBytes int64, MaxObjects int64 and Select func(bucket, key string) bool (:41-45); a zero MaxBytes or MaxObjects means unlimited, and a nil Select accepts every key. LogicalSnapshot carries WorkspaceID, PrimaryBucket, Buckets []string and Objects []SnapshotObject (:21-26). SnapshotObject carries Bucket, Key, Source (the path the bytes are at: the root the caller passed joined with the key's natural or escaped path — absolute only when the caller passed an absolute root), Size, SHA256, Mode, ContentType, Metadata, ChecksumAlgorithm and ChecksumValue (:28-39). The reader is a separate type, logicalSnapshotReader, which composes a Store value for the layout helpers with the pinned root (:94-98).
invariants: The read is read-only in the strongest sense: it never opens a writable Store, never writes an index entry, never adopts a file and never takes the session lock, so a capture can run beside a writer (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:20, :47-57); the package's own test pins that a snapshot leaves .stow/index.json byte-identical (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot_reconcile_test.go:26-29).
The root is pinned with rooted.Open for the whole read, and the pin's identity is re-proved at the end by pinned.Check() (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:48-52, :91).
Every file is opened through the pinned root and must be a regular file; a path that cannot be opened is an error, not an absence (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:219-227).
A symbolic link anywhere in the tree, and a linked bucket directory, are errors rather than skipped entries (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:154-156, :294-296).
The internal subtree and any .git directory are excluded from the object set (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:148).

The manifest and the index are read with a 16 MiB bound each and a version check; a manifest whose bucket or workspace ID is malformed is ErrManifestCorrupt (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:104-126).
The byte and object caps are enforced while reading, not after; exceeding either is an error, never a truncated snapshot (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:73-87).
A declared checksum that no longer matches the bytes is dropped from the snapshot rather than carried (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:250-265).

The returned object carries no modification time: the mtime is read into an internal ManifestEntry (internal/storage/workspace/rooted_reads.go:104) and used only for a staleness flag that the snapshot discards, so a caller cannot detect a between-walk-and-read change from the snapshot alone.
error_modes: workspace.ErrManifestCorrupt — a document that cannot be parsed, carries an unimplemented version, or names a malformed bucket or workspace ID (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:121, :125).
'workspace: snapshot refuses symbolic link %q' — a link inside the captured tree (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:155).
'workspace: snapshot refuses linked bucket' — a symlinked bucket directory (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:295).
'workspace: snapshot object count exceeds limit' and 'workspace: snapshot bytes exceed limit' — the caps (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:74, :86, :161, :204, :229).
'workspace: snapshot requires a regular object' — a source that is not a regular file (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:226).
'workspace: cannot read bounded snapshot %s' — a document larger than 16 MiB or unreadable (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:115).

rooted.ErrUnsupported, rooted.ErrSymlink or rooted.ErrNotRegular — propagated from the pinned root's no-follow open (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:219-222; internal/rooted/root.go:12-20, :71-88).
ordering: The documents are read before the tree, so the bucket list and the primary bucket are known before any object is visited (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:53-62).
The tree walk for a bucket completes before that bucket's objects are read, so the index's escaped keys can be added to the same key set (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:169).
Objects are returned sorted by key within a bucket, because the walk's key set is sorted before it is read (:172-177).
The root identity is checked after the whole read, so a root replaced mid-capture fails the snapshot rather than producing a mixed result (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:91).
configuration: SnapshotOptions.MaxBytes caps the total bytes read across all buckets; zero means unlimited (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:76, :304-308).
SnapshotOptions.MaxObjects caps the number of objects; zero means unlimited (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:73).
SnapshotOptions.Select filters by bucket and key; a nil Select accepts everything (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:70).
The context is honoured between reads, so a cancelled snapshot stops promptly (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:267-277).

implementation: The reader is built from three layers. The first pins the workspace: rooted.Open refuses a root that is not a real directory and re-proves its identity, giving an os.Root whose FS and OpenRegularFile never follow a link. The second reads the two documents through that pin with an explicit size bound, a version check and a malformed-identity check, so a corrupt workspace is refused rather than inventoried. The third walks the pinned filesystem per bucket, skipping the internal subtree and .git, refusing a link, collecting the natural keys with the exact spelling the directory reported, and then adding the escaped keys the index records — the escaped ones are located by their digest path and opened through the same pin. Each object is then opened through the pin, required to be regular, hashed with SHA-256 while its metadata is derived, and any declared checksum recomputed and dropped if it no longer matches. The whole thing is bounded by the two caps, which are checked during the walk rather than after it, so an over-budget workspace fails fast instead of being read to completion and then rejected.

callers.scope: scanPortableObjects is the one production caller: it asks for the snapshot with the archive's byte and file caps and a Select that drops sensitive-looking keys, then cross-checks the snapshot's workspace identity against the one it asked about.

the package's own external test calls the function directly and asserts that a snapshot reproduces exact natural and escaped key identity, including host-written files and indexed files the host deleted (the refusal assertion is TestLogicalSnapshotRefusesLinkedInternalDirectory, which calls the function at :66).

a second internal test calls the function before and after a live HeadObject and asserts the snapshot is byte-stable, leaves the index untouched, and agrees with the live read's content type and metadata.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting the snapshot reader moves the complexity into its one caller rather than removing it: pkg/stow would have to supply the bounded read and identity check of the two workspace documents, the escaped-key location by digest, the object inventory with bucket/key/content-type/metadata, the byte and object caps applied during the read, and the rule that a link is a refusal rather than a skip. A symlink-free, capped, hashing walk already exists in the caller (pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture.go:97-135), but it produces only paths and digests, not objects, and it would have to be reconciled with the module's different exclusions and output shape. The complexity concentrates in this module, which is what makes it deep rather than shallow. The reader is a single exported function, but it is a function with a real interface and a real set of refusals, not a helper.

leverage: The caller gets a trustworthy inventory of a workspace it does not own and cannot lock: no session claim, no index write, no adoption side effect, no link followed, and hard caps applied during the read. That is what makes a capture of somebody else's live workspace possible at all.
locality: The rules that decide what a capture contains live here — what is skipped (.stow, .git), what is refused (a link, a non-regular file, an over-budget workspace), how the escaped keys are located, and how the identity documents are bounded. The one place the shape leaks is pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:87-95, which re-implements the .git and .stow exclusion in the caller rather than asking this module for it, so the two lists can drift apart.
risks: The snapshot's exclusion list and the store's listing exclusion list are different: the snapshot skips .git (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:148) and the store's ListObjectsV2 does not (internal/storage/workspace/list_rooted.go:32, internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:264). A caller that lists and then captures sees two different object sets for the same workspace, and the difference is not documented anywhere.

The .git and .stow exclusion is implemented in three places rather than one — internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:148, pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture.go:86-88 and pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:87-95 — so a change to the snapshot's exclusions does not change what the file scan or the portable capture excludes.

The snapshot refuses a symbolic link outright rather than skipping it. In a workspace where an agent has left a link, every capture of that workspace fails, and the failure names the link but not the workspace's other contents — the capture is all-or-nothing (internal/storage/workspace/snapshot.go:154-156).

The snapshot's returned objects carry no modification time (the mtime is read at internal/storage/workspace/rooted_reads.go:104 but never reaches SnapshotObject), so the snapshot alone cannot detect a file that changed between the tree walk and the object's read; the consumer compensates by taking a second independent scan and comparing (pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:68-71, and the second full snapshot at pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable_capture.go:55-61), which means the correctness of a capture depends on a caller outside this package.

priority.rationale: This reader is the input to the portable checkpoint's inventory, so a wrong answer corrupts a checkpoint archive rather than a live workspace, and the failure mode is a refusal rather than silent loss. Its blast radius is narrow — one production caller — but the hidden coupling is real: the snapshot's exclusions and the store's listing exclusions have already diverged, the same exclusion is re-implemented in two callers, and the archive's correctness depends on a second scan taken by the caller. P2 rather than P3 because the divergences are live today and the reader is the only thing standing between a moving tree and a checkpoint that claims a state it never saw.

next_action: Give the snapshot reader an exported statement of what it excludes and what it refuses, so pkg/stow stops re-implementing the .git and .stow list in pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:87-95 and pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture.go:86-88, and so the difference between the snapshot's exclusions and the store's ListObjectsV2 exclusions is a single documented decision rather than three code paths that can drift. The interface that should change is SnapshotOptions: it should carry the exclusion policy rather than the caller guessing it, and the exclusion list should be shared with the listing surface so a caller cannot see two different object sets for one workspace.

title: The workspace object store: real files in a real directory, where the workspace bucket IS the root directory
summary: internal/storage/workspace is the storage backend whose objects are real files in a real directory. Store (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:14) satisfies storage.Store (internal/storage/store.go:13) and additionally storage.MultipartStore, storage.ConditionalCopyStore and storage.PutChecksumStore. The package owns four things a caller must know and cannot learn elsewhere: where a key's bytes live (internal/storage/workspace/layout.go — a natural key is <bucket dir>/<key>, an escaped key is <root>/.stow/keys/<sha256(bucket)>/<sha256(key)>); the two on-disk documents that carry identity and metadata (<root>/.stow/manifest.json and <root>/.stow/index.json, internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:87-94, layout version 3); the case-collision index that keeps two keys differing only in case from becoming one file (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:45-78, :114-130); and the symlink-free confinement every object read and write is routed through (internal/rooted). Its production callers are pkg/stow.OpenWorkspace (pkg/stow/workspace.go:128) and pkg/stow/destroyRegisteredEntry (pkg/stow/workspace_admin.go:43); OpenWorkspace wraps the store in internal/runtime so quota and authority are enforced above the store. The store diverges from an ordinary bucket in three named ways: the workspace bucket IS the root directory, a second bucket is namespaced under <root>/.stow/buckets/<name>, and the workspace bucket cannot be deleted.

trace.scope: OpenWorkspace is the constructor callers normally use: it passes Options.Root, Bucket, TTLSeconds, Now, InitiallyOwned and Adopted to workspace.New, then wraps the store in runtime.OpenWithStore so quota, accounting and authority sit above the store. (pkg/stow/workspace_admin.go:43 is the other production constructor; see callers.)

New creates the root, creates <root>/.stow/keys, loads the manifest and the index, establishes identity, builds the case-folded index over the filesystem, writes the identity document and writes the index. Every later operation depends on this having happened.

pathFor decides the form: a recorded escaped form is preserved; otherwise a key that IsNatural and whose case-folded path is unowned takes the natural path, and everything else takes the escaped path.
putLocked evaluates the write preconditions against the existing entry, prepares the body, writes the bytes and records the index entry — all under the store's single write lock.
writeAtomic re-opens the root as a pinned os.Root and asks it to publish the file, so the write cannot escape the workspace through a link in the path.

the bytes land: the temp file is created inside the pinned root, fsynced, renamed inside the root, and the parent directory is synced. The object is a real file at <root>/<key> that a person can open.

evidence.detail: var _ storage.Store = (*Store)(nil) — the compile-time assertion that the workspace backend satisfies the object-model seam.
internalDir = ".stow" is reserved as a first path segment, so a user key can never be spelled that way and a directory or file with that name at the root is unambiguously stow's.

NewLayout's doc states that the rules are the union of every supported host filesystem's rules, not the intersection: a key Windows cannot spell is escaped on Linux too, so a manifest written on one host means the same thing on another. The cost is that a few pathological keys lose their pretty path on Linux.

EscapedPath is <root>/.stow/keys/<Digest(bucket)>/<Digest(key)>. The bucket is a directory of its own and it has to be: a digest of the key alone gives the same key in two buckets one physical file, so a write in either bucket overwrites the other's object and a read returns the other bucket's bytes.

manifestVersion = 3 — the only on-disk layout this build implements, at layout version 3. Identity and the object index are separate files because identity changes once per workspace and the index per object.

manifestPath = InternalPath(root, "manifest.json") resolves to <root>/.stow/manifest.json; indexPath at :92 resolves to <root>/.stow/index.json. There is no stow-workspace.json anywhere in the Go, TypeScript or Python source; the name appears only in docs (docs/adr/0008-workspace-backend-real-files.md:71, CONTEXT.md:104).

loadDocument refuses a document whose version this build does not implement, with a message that says the files are still on disk and the workspace must be removed and recreated. A version-1 workspace, which was one file, therefore does not open.

The manifest and index are not the source of truth for existence: an entry pointing at a missing file serves as absent, and a file with no entry exists. Losing either document degrades metadata, never data.

bucketDir returns s.root for the workspace bucket and InternalPath(s.root, "buckets", bucket) for every other one. This is the first of the three divergences: the workspace bucket IS the root directory, and a second bucket is namespaced under the reserved internal directory so the workspace bucket does not cease to be the working directory.

DeleteBucket returns storage.ErrBucketNotFound for the workspace bucket: it is the directory the caller is working in. The second divergence — the workspace bucket cannot be deleted — is reported with the same sentinel as 'no such bucket', so a caller cannot tell protected from absent.
CreateBucket for the workspace bucket is a silent no-op success, where S3 would report that the caller already owns the bucket.

index builds the case-folded path index by walking every bucket's tree on disk rather than reading the index, because an adopted file with no index entry still occupies a path that a later key must not collide with. This is the collision defence of docs/workspace-contract.md section 3.4.

pathFor takes the natural path only when the layout permits it, the case-folded path is unowned or already owned by this same key, and no differently-cased segment occupies the candidate path; otherwise the key is escaped.

resolve finds a key's file, adopts it when there is no index entry, and takes the write lock because adopting means writing an index entry. Adoption is not an import step: a workspace whose files need registering before they can be read is not a working directory.

exactNaturalPath resolves a natural key without letting a case-insensitive filesystem turn a different spelling into the requested object; os.Stat on macOS and Windows can succeed for report.pdf when only Report.pdf exists, which is a path collision and not an exact match for the S3 key.

absence reports only a confirmed absence — a missing path (fs.ErrNotExist), a non-directory component (syscall.ENOTDIR), or a path naming a link or another non-regular file (rooted.ErrSymlink, rooted.ErrNotRegular). Anything else is uncertain and is returned as storage.ErrObjectUncertain, because absence is the guess that loses data.

openRead goes through rooted.Root.OpenRegularFile; rooted.ErrUnsupported is propagated rather than translated, a confirmed absence becomes storage.ErrObjectNotFound, and anything else becomes uncertain.

statWithoutLinks walks the path component by component inside the pinned root and refuses a symlink in any of them (ErrSymlink at :17). This is the symlink-free confinement the workspace depends on, and it is what makes a linked file an absence rather than a read of somebody else's bytes.

The final open goes through os.Root.OpenFile, whose openat adds O_NOFOLLOW on the component it opens, so the refusal and the open are one operation; on a host without that guarantee internal/rooted/regular_other.go:12 returns ErrUnsupported rather than opening a path it cannot prove is not a link.
checkRootIdentity re-proves that the root is still the same directory on every operation; a replaced root makes every subsequent call fail with 'workspace: root identity changed'.

Ownership is set once, by whoever made the directory, and preserved: manifest.Owned = !Adopted && (InitiallyOwned || !rootExisted || manifest.Owned). It has to survive the reopen, or a workspace stow created would quietly become undeletable the second time it was opened.

assertDestructible applies both defences and explains the refusal in terms the caller can act on: an adopted root is not stow's to delete, and a root that is the home directory, the process working directory, or an ancestor of either is refused.

pruneEmptyParents removes the directories a delete leaves behind, stopping at the bucket directory and never crossing into the internal one. For the workspace bucket that means deleting output/report.pdf removes an empty output/ directory from the caller's project.
ComputesPutChecksums reports true, so this backend computes requested checksums on the bytes it owns before publication.

CompleteMultipartUpload assembles the staged parts and publishes them through the same putLocked path a single PutObject uses, so a completed object is a real file at the key's natural path and carries a composite ETag with the parts' content ETag recorded separately.

escapedObjects returns the objects the tree walk cannot see; an index entry whose file is gone serves as absent, and a symlinked one is absent for the same reason, because the read behind the sniff is one this package refuses everywhere else.

interface.types: Store is a concrete struct (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:14) with exactly one exported field, Now func() time.Time (workspace.go:32), opened by New(Options) (*Store, error). It presents storage.Store — CreateBucket, DeleteBucket, HeadBucket, ListBuckets, PutObject, GetObject, HeadObject, DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, CopyObject, ListObjectsV2, Close — plus storage.MultipartStore (CreateMultipartUpload, GetMultipartUpload, UploadPart, CompleteMultipartUpload, AbortMultipartUpload, ListParts, ValidateMultipartUpload, ListMultipartUploads, internal/storage/store.go:48-57), storage.ConditionalCopyStore (CopyObjectCond) and storage.PutChecksumStore (ComputesPutChecksums), and one extra exported method beyond those interfaces, ListPartsPage (internal/storage/workspace/multipart.go:305). The workspace-specific surface is Root() string, WorkspaceBucket() string, ID() string, IsOwned() bool, Path(bucket, key string) (string, bool), Close() error and Destroy() error. Options carries Root (required), Bucket, TTLSeconds, Now func() time.Time, InitiallyOwned bool and Adopted bool. A key is a string; an object is storage.ObjectMeta; the store returns storage.ErrBucketNotFound, storage.ErrObjectNotFound, storage.ErrObjectUncertain, storage.ErrBucketNotEmpty, storage.ErrInvalidKey, storage.ErrInvalidBucketName and storage.ErrMutationCommitted alongside its own ErrClosed, ErrManifestCorrupt and ErrNotDestructible.
invariants: The workspace bucket IS the root directory: bucketDir returns s.root for the manifest's bucket and <root>/.stow/buckets/<name> for every other bucket (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:18-23). A second bucket is therefore invisible in the directory a person browses, and Destroy removes it with the root.

The workspace bucket cannot be deleted: DeleteBucket returns storage.ErrBucketNotFound for it (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:159-161) — the same sentinel as 'no such bucket', so the caller cannot distinguish 'protected' from 'absent'. CreateBucket for it is a silent no-op success (:142-144).

The manifest lives at <root>/.stow/manifest.json and the object index at <root>/.stow/index.json (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:87-94). ADR 0008 section 3 (docs/adr/0008-workspace-backend-real-files.md:71) and CONTEXT.md:104 still name a single stow-workspace.json at the workspace root; the source has neither that name nor that location, and the manifest no longer carries the object entries at all. docs/workspace-contract.md section 4 correctly names <dir>/.stow/manifest.json but still shows one document with an entries map at version 1 (docs/workspace-contract.md:334-374).

Layout version 3 is the only version implemented. A document of any other version is refused with ErrManifestCorrupt and a message saying the files are still on disk (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:21, :146-150); a version-1 workspace, which was one file, does not open.

The filesystem, not the index, is the source of truth for existence: an index entry whose file is gone serves as absent, and a file with no entry exists (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:35-37; internal/storage/workspace/resolve.go:103-148).

Ownership is set at open and preserved across reopens: the root is owned iff stow created it, unless Options.Adopted says otherwise (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:149-150). An adopted workspace can be read, written and closed but never destroyed (internal/storage/workspace/destroy.go:43-46).
Destroy also refuses the user's home directory, the process working directory, and any ancestor of either, independently of ownership (internal/storage/workspace/destroy.go:47-52, :61-74).

The case-collision index is built by walking the filesystem at open, not from the index, so an adopted file whose name differs only in case from a key stow wrote is detected before either is served (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:45-78). A key whose folded path is already owned by another key takes the escaped form (:114-130).

Windows path rules are applied on every host deliberately: reserved device names, the characters <>:\"|?*, a trailing dot or space, and any segment containing the escape marker ~ all force the escaped form on Linux too, as does a relative path longer than 240 bytes (internal/storage/workspace/layout.go:36, :57-86, :117-134, :139-150).

Every object read and write goes through internal/rooted: os.Root confines the path, os.Root.Lstat refuses a symlink in any component, and the final open does not follow a link (internal/rooted/root.go:75-125; internal/rooted/regular_unix.go:13-23; internal/rooted/mutations.go:48-60). The multipart staging area is the one exception (see risks); the identity and index documents are still written through rooted (internal/storage/workspace/rooted_mutations.go:37-51). A symbolic link is an absence, not an unreadable object.

Only a confirmed absence is absence: a path that could not be examined returns storage.ErrObjectUncertain (internal/storage/workspace/absence.go:19-41), and rooted.ErrUnsupported is propagated rather than translated.

The root's identity is pinned at open and re-checked on every operation; a replaced root makes every subsequent call fail with 'workspace: root identity changed' (internal/storage/workspace/rooted_reads.go:107-119).

One non-reentrant RWMutex guards the whole store, and the write lock is held across read-modify-write sequences; the internal helpers therefore exist in paired *Locked variants (internal/storage/workspace/resolve.go:103-120, :181-196).

Close writes the identity document and the object index and deletes nothing; removal is the explicit Destroy (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:201-218; internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:330-331).

Multipart staging lives under <root>/.stow/multipart/<uploadID>/ with upload.json and part-N records; completion assembles the parts and publishes them through the same putLocked path a single PutObject uses (internal/storage/workspace/multipart.go:22-25, :54-61, :198-245).

ObjectMeta.VersionID falls back to the ETag for an object with no index entry (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:355-357), so an adopted file's version identifier is a content hash rather than an opaque version.
error_modes: storage.ErrBucketNotFound — the bucket does not exist, or it is the workspace bucket and the caller asked to delete it (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:159-161, :202-204).
storage.ErrObjectNotFound — the key is absent, or its path names a link or another non-regular file (internal/storage/workspace/resolve.go:123-125; internal/storage/workspace/rooted_reads.go:57-60).
storage.ErrObjectUncertain — the path could not be examined; the object's state is unknown and must not be treated as absent (internal/storage/workspace/absence.go:36-41).
workspace.ErrClosed — every operation after Close (internal/storage/workspace/resolve.go:15; checked at internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:220-225).

workspace.ErrManifestCorrupt — a manifest or index document exists and cannot be parsed, or carries a version this build does not implement; the open is refused and nothing is overwritten (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:29, :144-150).
workspace.ErrNotDestructible — Destroy of an adopted workspace or of a protected path (internal/storage/workspace/destroy.go:16, :39-52).

rooted.ErrUnsupported — the host has no atomic no-follow open; the read and listing surfaces surface it rather than reporting absence (internal/storage/workspace/list_rooted.go:56-58; internal/rooted/regular_other.go:12-13).
storage.ErrBucketNotEmpty — DeleteBucket on a second bucket that still holds objects or an in-flight upload (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:178-194).

storage.ErrMutationCommitted — the bytes landed but the object index could not be persisted; the caller must not retry the write as though nothing happened (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:98-100, :184).

storage.ErrInvalidKey and storage.ErrInvalidBucketName — from storage.ValidateKey and storage.ValidateBucketName (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:24-26; internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:76-80).
ordering: New must complete before any other call: it creates the root, creates <root>/.stow/keys, loads the manifest and the index, establishes identity, builds the case-folded index, writes the identity document and writes the index (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:72-124).
Close is idempotent and terminal: it writes LastUsed and the index, and every later operation returns ErrClosed (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:201-225).
Destroy closes the store first, so it must not race another goroutine's use of the store (internal/storage/workspace/destroy.go:24-35).

CopyObjectCond captures the source and publishes the destination under one write lock, so a source overwritten in between cannot be copied as one version (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:220-260).
PutObject takes the write lock before reading the existing entry, so a conditional write evaluates against the entry it also replaces (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:34-51).
configuration: Options.Root is required and is the workspace directory; it is created if absent and adopted if present (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:73-75, :88-95).
Options.Bucket names the workspace bucket; when empty the store keeps whatever the manifest already records (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:76-80, :143-145).
Options.TTLSeconds records the intended collection window in the manifest; no collector runs automatically (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:51-54, :146-148).
Options.Now replaces the clock, for tests; it is the Store's one exported field (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:31-32, :55-56).
Options.InitiallyOwned reserves a root stow has just created exclusively (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:57-60).

Options.Adopted marks a root as the caller's; it forces ownership false, which is what makes Destroy refuse on ownership grounds (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:61-67, :149-150). Protected paths refuse independently of it.

The store reads no environment variable and no configuration file; its entire configuration is Options. (The package's Registry resolves the user config directory through os.UserConfigDir at internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:62-68, but that is the registry's location, not the store's configuration.)

implementation: The package is organised around four decisions. First, the layout (internal/storage/workspace/layout.go): a key is natural when every segment is non-empty and not '.' or '..', no segment contains the escape marker '~' or a character no filesystem holds, no segment is a Windows device name or ends in a dot or space, the whole relative path is within 240 bytes, and the first segment is not '.stow'; otherwise it is escaped to <root>/.stow/keys/<sha256(bucket)>/<sha256(key)>. The Windows rules are applied on every host so that the rules are testable on Linux CI and a manifest written on one host means the same thing on another. Second, the documents (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go): manifest.json holds the workspace's identity — id, bucket, created, last_used, ttl_seconds, owned — and is written on creation and on Close; index.json holds the per-object entries and is rewritten on every adoption, update and forget; both are versioned, refused rather than migrated when the version is unknown, and written atomically through internal/atomicfile. Third, the collision defence (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go): the store keeps a map from a bucket-qualified case-folded relative path to the key that owns it, built at open by walking the filesystem so that adopted files count, and a key that would collide is escaped rather than allowed to overwrite. Fourth, the confinement (internal/rooted): every object read opens the file through a pinned os.Root that refuses a link in any path component, every object write and delete goes through the same root, and the root's identity is re-proved on every operation. The multipart staging area is the part of the package that does not use internal/rooted (see risks). Around those sit the object verbs, which adopt a host-written file on first read and reconcile the recorded entry against the bytes on disk (internal/storage/workspace/resolve.go:151-160), and the multipart verbs, which stage parts under <root>/.stow/multipart/<uploadID>/ and assemble them into the key's own path on completion.

callers.scope: pkg/stow.OpenWorkspace is the constructor callers normally use. It passes Options.Root, Bucket, TTLSeconds, Now, InitiallyOwned and Adopted, then wraps the store in runtime.OpenWithStore so quota, accounting and authority enforcement sit above the store rather than in it.

destroyRegisteredEntry re-opens the store directly from a registry entry to destroy it as host administration; it checks that the store's ID matches the registered one before deleting. This is the second production constructor of workspace.New.

workspace.AcquireSession(store.Root()) takes the advisory liveness lock that makes the workspace safe to sweep; this is a package-level sibling of the store, and the store itself never takes it, so a caller can read a workspace without claiming it.
restorePortableObjects calls w.store.PutObject directly to republish the objects of a portable checkpoint into a reopened workspace.

the shared backend contract suite constructs the workspace store alongside the memory and filesystem backends; this test file is the only back-edge in the Go packages, because it imports the concrete backends it asserts on.

the package's own tests construct the store directly and assert the WS-03 to WS-14 conformance cases of docs/workspace-contract.md section 8 (stated at internal/storage/workspace/workspace_test.go:17-18).
the namespace test creates two buckets in one store and asserts that an escaped key is one physical file per bucket, and that a delete in one bucket leaves the other readable.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting the object store does not make the complexity vanish; it reappears in every caller. pkg/stow would have to re-derive a manifest format, a key-to-path encoding, a case-folding rule and an adoption rule; pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go would have to re-derive the key-to-file mapping it uses to name a payload (pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:67) and would lose the escape rules its payload naming depends on; and internal/rooted's confinement would have to be re-implemented by each reader that touches a workspace. The complexity concentrates in this module rather than spreading, which is what makes it deep. The shallow part is the exported pure helper set (Layout, NaturalPath, EscapedPath, InternalPath, IsInternal, KeyFromNaturalPath, FoldPath, Digest, Form), which is a namespace of functions with no decisions of their own; it is folded into this record rather than proposed separately.

leverage: A caller gets the whole S3 object model over a directory it can open in a text editor, without writing the encoding, the collision defence, the adoption rule, the two-document on-disk format or the confinement rules. pkg/stow.OpenWorkspace is 30 lines of construction because this module carries the rest. The property that a key the S3 contract accepts is always storable — because a key that cannot be a path is escaped rather than refused — is entirely this module's, and it is what makes the backend a drop-in for the store it replaces.
locality: Everything about the workspace's on-disk shape lives here: the .stow subtree layout, the manifest and index documents and their version, the case-folded index, the multipart staging format and the destructive rules. A change to the workspace's on-disk shape is a change to this directory; the callers in pkg/stow learn the shape only through what this module chooses to expose (Root, ID, WorkspaceBucket, IsOwned, Path). The one place the shape leaks across the boundary is pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:67, which recomputes the escaped payload name as workspace.Digest(bucket + "\x00" + key) and so must be changed with it.
risks: Listing the workspace bucket is listing the caller's directory tree. internal/storage/workspace/list_rooted.go:32 skips only the internal subtree, so .git internals, node_modules and editor swap files are returned as objects. The portable checkpoint path filters .git and .stow separately (pkg/stow/checkpoint_portable.go:87-95) because it had to; the object-listing surface does not.

Deleting an object prunes the directories it empties, up to but not including the bucket directory (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:427-437). For the workspace bucket that removes an empty output/ directory from the caller's project.

HeadBucket reports the root directory's modification time as the workspace bucket's CreationDate (internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:198-210). A directory's mtime changes whenever an entry is added or removed, so the reported creation date drifts with ordinary use.

The multipart staging path is the one part of the store that does not use internal/rooted: writePartRecord publishes through atomicfile.WriteParts (internal/storage/workspace/part_record.go:45), openPartRecord opens with os.Open (:48-51), loadUpload reads upload.json with os.ReadFile (internal/storage/workspace/multipart.go:64) and saveUpload writes it through atomicfile.Write (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:184). The object path's symlink-free confinement does not cover the staging area.

The store does not validate the upload ID: uploadDir joins it into a path (internal/storage/workspace/multipart.go:54-56; internal/storage/workspace/layout.go:210-212) and filepath.Join cleans the result, so an ID containing '..' can resolve outside <root>/.stow/multipart. The runtime gates the write verbs through its own in-memory map and returns storage.ErrUploadNotFound for an ID it did not mint (internal/runtime/multipart.go:90-93, :151-154, :197-199), so the S3 uploadPart/complete/abort paths and the library write path are covered. The read verbs are not gated the same way — GetMultipartUpload, ListParts/ListPartsPage and ValidateMultipartUpload reach the store with the caller's ID, because checkUpload consults the map only when a policy is configured (internal/runtime/instance.go:81-88) — and they rely on loadUpload's own content check. A store used directly as a storage.Store has neither guard.

The index is rewritten in full on every object write, adoption and forget (internal/storage/workspace/manifest.go:159-168), so a workspace with many objects pays the whole index's serialisation on every mutation. Splitting the index from the identity document fixed the identity rewrite, not this.

The store does not implement storage.ObjectUsageStore, so the runtime's initial quota accounting falls back to a paginated ListObjectsV2 scan (internal/runtime/state.go:108-134). Because the workspace bucket is the root directory, that scan walks the caller's entire project tree and opens every file to confirm it is regular.

ADR 0008 section 3 (docs/adr/0008-workspace-backend-real-files.md:71) and CONTEXT.md:104 describe the manifest as a single stow-workspace.json at the workspace root. The source keeps two versioned documents under <root>/.stow/. A reader following the ADR looks in the wrong place for a file that does not exist.

priority.rationale: This is the default agent-facing surface (docs/adr/0007-workspace-is-the-default.md:7) and the only production backing store for pkg/stow.OpenWorkspace, so every workspace verb in the library, the S3 facade, the checkpoint and delta machinery and the MCP surface depends on it. The blast radius is not just a store's: because the workspace bucket IS a directory the caller is working in, a defect here lands in a person's project rather than in a store, and the divergences are only discoverable from the source — the manifest location is documented wrongly in two places. It is not P0 because the confinement is real and tested, the destructive rules are guarded three ways (liveness, ownership, protected paths), and the package carries the WS-03 to WS-14 conformance cases.

next_action: State the workspace's on-disk format once, in a place that names the files the source actually writes — <root>/.stow/manifest.json and <root>/.stow/index.json at layout version 3 — and correct docs/adr/0008-workspace-backend-real-files.md:71 and CONTEXT.md:104, which still name stow-workspace.json at the workspace root; docs/workspace-contract.md section 4 must also stop showing a single document with an entries map and a version of 1. The interface that should change is the layout contract itself: it is stated in three places that disagree, so the fix is one normative statement of the .stow subtree that both the ADR and the contract cite. Separately, the exported pure layout helpers should be unexported or moved, since pkg/stow is the only external consumer and it uses one of them (Digest) to recompute a payload name that belongs to this module.

title: The machine-wide workspace registry: durable entries, advisory locks and recovery holds
summary: internal/storage/workspace/registry.go owns the registry that makes a workspace outlive the process that created it: a directory of one JSON file per workspace ID, under the user's configuration directory by default (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:57-68) and partitioned per team by directory rather than by label (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:70-92). The same package owns the three advisory locks that keep that registry and its workspaces coherent — the session lock, which proves liveness by taking the same flock the holder took (internal/storage/workspace/session.go:90-115); the capture lock, which excludes capture, reconciliation and deletion for one workspace (internal/storage/workspace/capture_lock.go); and the registry mutation lock, which is always taken before the workspace capture lock (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:16-32) — and the recovery-hold journal that records which workspaces and checkpoints a published capture depends on (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_holds.go, internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_journal.go, internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_mutation.go). It is called by every workspace verb in pkg/stow: open, resume, list, collect, prune, destroy, checkpoint, request replay and the recovery-hold surface.

trace.scope: stow.Collect is the public entry point for a sweep: it opens the registry and calls Collect(now). Before this it refuses outright on a host with no advisory locks (:217-219).
Registry.Collect refuses on a host without advisory locks, reads every entry and classifies each one, reporting what it declined as well as what it removed.

classify establishes liveness first, then ownership, then TTL, then age. The order is the design: a workspace that is merely old is never removed while somebody is in it, and a sweep can never remove a directory a caller pointed stow at.

ProbeLiveness answers by attempting the same flock the holder took: acquiring it proves every prior holder is gone, failing to acquire it proves somebody is here now. There is no third answer, which is the point.
RemoveWorkspace holds the registry mutation lock and the workspace capture lock, checks the recovery holds, removes the bytes, removes the checkpoints and only then forgets the entry.

the workspace directory itself is removed by os.RemoveAll — but only after assertDestructible has proved that stow owns the root and that the path is not the home directory, the working directory or an ancestor of either.

evidence.detail: DefaultRegistryDir resolves os.UserConfigDir() + stow-s3/workspaces. The registry holds small metadata only, never object data, and it is not inside any workspace — a registry stored in a workspace would be collectable by its own sweep.

TeamRegistryDir partitions the machine's registry by directory. The comment states the choice explicitly: a label on an entry is a label — `All` would still return every team's workspaces and a sweep would still consider them — whereas a partition is enforced by the filesystem.

ValidTeamName refuses a team name that is empty, longer than 64 characters, '.', '..', contains anything but [A-Za-z0-9._-], or begins with '.', because a team becomes a directory that entries are filed under.
OpenRegistryReadOnly opens without creating the directory, so a read-only verb never brings a registry into existence on a machine that has never had one.
entryPath is <registry>/<id>.json, one file per workspace, which is what lets a workspace outlive the process that made it.

classify: live → 'in-use' (no action); not owned → 'adopted' (no action); TTL <= 0 → 'no-ttl'; not yet expired → 'not-expired'; otherwise 'expired' and act. Ownership is checked before age so a sweep that could remove a developer's project is unreachable by waiting.

Prune is deliberately not Collect with a different threshold: it asks whether anything is there at all, which is a fact, and removes stow's own records. It shares the capture exclusion so retained receipts cannot disappear under a reconcile, and it does not touch bytes.

reclaimWorkspace opens the workspace and destroys it, which routes the removal through the same ownership and protected-path checks a caller gets. The comment says it plainly: the collector has no privilege of its own.

AcquireSession takes the liveness lock at <root>/.stow/session.lock. It is an advisory file lock, which the kernel releases when the holding process dies — including on SIGKILL and on an OOM kill — so there is no stale-lock cleanup to get wrong and no heartbeat to expire wrongly.
ProbeLiveness opens the lock file without O_CREATE, so a probe leaves nothing behind, and if it acquires the lock it takes it back off so a later real session is not blocked by the probe.

On a host with no advisory lock, tryLock never claims one and returns ErrLockUnsupported, and lockSupported is false — so a workspace on that host is never collectable rather than collectable by guesswork.
AcquireCapture fails closed when exclusion is unavailable, and returns ErrCaptureInProgress when another capture of the same workspace holds it.
Release leaves the lock file in place on purpose: removing a file another process may be waiting to open is how a lock ends up held by nobody.
AcquireMutationCapture fixes mutation ordering — registry first, then workspace — and releases in the reverse order. Every mutation path that touches both goes through it.

RegisterWithLimit takes the registry mutation lock, reads the policy, and counts the existing entries under the same lock, so the workspace cap is checked against a consistent set and a concurrent registration cannot exceed it.
ValidWorkspaceID accepts 1-128 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_-] only. The same rule makes the ID safe as a registry file name and safe as a capture-lock file name.
The recovery-hold bounds: 256 holds, 32 references per hold, 2 MiB of journal and 4 MiB of peak reserved bytes.
readRecoveryHolds treats a missing journal as empty only when the identity sidecar is also missing; a journal without its identity file is ErrRecoveryHoldCorrupt, not an empty journal.

validateRecoveryJournal checks the version, the hold count, that each hold's normalised request equals the recorded one, that hold IDs are strictly increasing, that the state is one of pending/released/discarded and that the checksum matches. Any failure is a refusal, never a reset.

AdmitRecoveryHold re-admits an existing hold only when its meaning matches, so a request replayed with the same ID and the same meaning is idempotent and a different meaning is a conflict rather than a silent overwrite.

interface.types: Registry is a concrete struct (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:51) holding one directory, opened by OpenRegistry(dir) (which creates it) or OpenRegistryReadOnly(dir) (which does not). Its surface is Register(Entry) and RegisterWithLimit(Entry, maxWorkspaces), Lookup(id) (Entry, bool, error), All() and AllStrict() ([]Entry, error), Forget(id), Collect(now) ([]Reclaim, error), Prune(includeAdopted) ([]Reclaim, error), RemoveWorkspace(id, remove func() error), ForgetCheckpoints(workspaceID), Policy() and WritePolicy(RegistryPolicy), AdmitRecoveryHold / FinishRecoveryHold / ListRecoveryHolds / LookupRecoveryHold, CheckWorkspaceRecoveryHolds(id) and CheckCheckpointRecoveryHolds(id), and Dir(). Entry (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:26) is the durable record: id, dir, working_directory, bucket, created, last_used, ttl_seconds, policy_version, authority_mask, max_bytes, max_objects, max_checkpoint_bytes, max_checkpoints, owned. Reclaim (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:265) is one workspace a sweep considered, with a Reason of 'expired', 'adopted', 'in-use', 'no-ttl', 'not-expired', 'present', 'gone-adopted', 'pruned' or 'unreadable: …'. The lock surface is the free functions AcquireSession(root) (*Session, error), ProbeLiveness(root) (bool, error), AcquireCapture(registryDir, workspaceID) (*CaptureLock, error), AcquireMutation(registryDir) and AcquireMutationCapture(registryDir, id) (*MutationLock, error), plus LockSupported(), SessionLockSupported() and ValidWorkspaceID(id). The recovery-hold types are RecoveryHoldRequest, RecoveryReference, RecoveryHold, RecoveryHoldQuery and RecoveryHoldPage, with the bounds MaxRecoveryHolds, MaxRecoveryReferences, MaxRecoveryHoldBytes and MaxRecoveryHoldPeakBytes.
invariants: The registry holds metadata only, never object data, and lives outside every workspace — a registry stored in a workspace would be collectable by its own sweep (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:57-68).

One entry per workspace ID at <registry>/<id>.json (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:141-143). The ID must satisfy ValidWorkspaceID — 1 to 128 characters of [A-Za-z0-9_-] (internal/storage/workspace/checkpoints.go:83-92) — which is also what makes it safe as a file name.

A team is a directory partition at <registry>/teams/<team>, not a label on an entry, so the root sweep cannot see a team's entries at all (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:70-92). ValidTeamName refuses a name that could climb out of its namespace or that is not portable (:101-114).
OpenRegistry creates the directory; OpenRegistryReadOnly does not, so a read-only verb never brings a registry into existence (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:116-139).

Liveness is established with an advisory flock on <root>/.stow/session.lock, which the kernel releases when the holder dies, so there is no stale-lock cleanup and no heartbeat to expire wrongly (internal/storage/workspace/session.go:10-11, :42-53, :83-115; internal/storage/workspace/lock_unix.go:15-25).

On a host with no advisory lock — Windows today — lockSupported is false and Collect refuses with ErrLockUnsupported rather than guessing (internal/storage/workspace/lock_other.go:14-18; internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:285-287).

Collect's order is liveness, then ownership, then TTL, then age. A workspace that is merely old is never removed while somebody is in it, and a sweep can never remove a directory a caller pointed stow at (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:273-283, :366-386).
Prune removes registry entries whose directory is gone and touches no bytes; an adopted entry is not pruned unless includeAdopted says so (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:308-363).

The registry mutation lock is always taken before the workspace capture lock, and released in the reverse order (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:20-41). No call site takes the capture lock first: every place that holds both goes through AcquireMutationCapture (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:21-32; internal/storage/workspace/checkpoints.go:18, :65; pkg/stow/checkpoint.go:100; pkg/stow/checkpoint_external.go:98; pkg/stow/checkpoint_import.go:217; pkg/stow/delta_apply.go:47; pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:124).

The capture lock file is <registry>/capture-locks/<workspaceID>.lock and is deliberately left in place on release (internal/storage/workspace/capture_lock.go:50-52, :67-71). The registry mutation lock is the same primitive on <registry>/.stow/capture-locks/registry_mutation.lock (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:16-18).

A pending, unexpired recovery hold that references a workspace or a checkpoint blocks forgetting either (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_holds.go:106-133; internal/storage/workspace/checkpoints.go:70-72; internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:205-207).

The recovery journal is <registry>/.stow/recovery-holds.json with a 32-byte identity sidecar at <registry>/.stow/recovery-holds.identity. A journal whose identity file is missing while the journal exists is corrupt, not empty (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_journal.go:25-27, :32-38, :145-159).

The journal carries a checksum over its holds and is decoded with DisallowUnknownFields; a mismatch is ErrRecoveryHoldCorrupt, never a reset (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_journal.go:54-88, :106-110).
The registry's own policy document is <registry>/.stow/policy.json, version 1, carrying MaxWorkspaces, MaxCheckpoints and MaxCheckpointBytes (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:43-85).
error_modes: workspace.ErrLockUnsupported — the host has no advisory lock, so liveness cannot be established and collection refuses (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:285-287).
workspace.ErrWorkspaceInUse — a live session holds the workspace (internal/storage/workspace/session.go:33-40, :76-79).
workspace.ErrCaptureInProgress — another capture holds the exclusion for this workspace (internal/storage/workspace/capture_lock.go:19, :43-46).
workspace.ErrRecoveryHeld — a pending hold references this workspace or checkpoint (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_holds.go:21, :128).
workspace.ErrRecoveryHoldConflict — the same hold ID with a different meaning, a different owner, or an already-terminal state (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_mutation.go:27, :88-102).
workspace.ErrRecoveryHoldNotFound — no hold with that ID (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_holds.go:23).
workspace.ErrRecoveryHoldFull — the journal is at 256 holds or 2 MiB (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_holds.go:24; internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_journal.go:85, :136-138).
workspace.ErrRecoveryHoldCorrupt — the journal cannot be read, its identity does not match, or its checksum does not (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_journal.go:40, :62-65, :151-158).
A workspace count limit is a plain error rather than a sentinel: 'workspace: workspace count limit reached (%d of %d)' (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:139).
A registry entry whose ID is not ValidWorkspaceID is refused on both write and read (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:151-153, :171-174; internal/storage/workspace/checkpoints.go:83-92).
ordering: Registering a workspace takes the registry mutation lock, reads the policy, then counts the existing entries under the same lock, so the cap is checked against a consistent set (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:113-143).

RemoveWorkspace takes the registry mutation lock and then the workspace capture lock, checks the recovery holds, removes the bytes, removes the checkpoints, and only then forgets the entry (internal/storage/workspace/checkpoints.go:63-80).
The hold journal is read, validated and written as one unit under the mutation gate (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_mutation.go:13-46; pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:68-76).

A team must be resolved to a path before use; pkg/stow resolves it once at every entry point and records the resolved path, because a disagreement about a namespace is not recoverable by retrying (pkg/stow/resume.go:41-51; pkg/stow/workspace.go:189-193).

Collect re-checks the classification immediately before destroying, so a workspace that became live or adopted between the sweep's decision and its action is not destroyed (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:405-416).
configuration: DefaultRegistryDir reads os.UserConfigDir and appends stow-s3/workspaces; the location itself is chosen by the caller, and this package reads no environment variable (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:62-68).
TeamRegistryDir(base, team) partitions a base directory by team name (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:81-92).

RegistryPolicy is read from <registry>/.stow/policy.json and its version must be 1; writing it requires the registry mutation gate and that existing usage fits (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:50-85; pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:24-52).
TTLSeconds on an entry is the collection window; a zero TTL means the workspace is never collectable (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:379-381).

implementation: The registry is a directory of small JSON documents, one per workspace ID, each written atomically through internal/atomicfile and each carrying the identity of the workspace (dir, bucket, working directory, TTL), the policy the workspace was opened with (policy version, authority mask, the four limits) and whether stow owns the directory. Reading is deliberately forgiving — All skips a directory and a non-.json name, and skips an entry it cannot decode, so one bad file does not make every workspace permanent — while writing is strict, because a registry that silently drops entries forgets workspaces and one that forgets a workspace leaks it forever. Three advisory locks sit on top. The session lock lives inside the workspace's own .stow subtree and is the only proof of liveness; the capture lock and the registry mutation lock live inside the registry and exclude capture, reconciliation, deletion and registration for a workspace or for the registry as a whole. The ordering between them is fixed (registry then workspace) so two callers cannot deadlock by taking them in opposite orders. The recovery-hold journal is a single file with a checksum and a separate identity file beside it, holding at most 256 pending or terminal holds of at most 32 references each; admitting a hold validates that every referenced workspace is registered and every referenced checkpoint manifest names that workspace and that checkpoint, so a hold cannot name a dependency that does not exist. The sweep is a classify-then-act loop whose order is the safety property, and the collector reaches destruction only by opening the workspace and calling its own Destroy, so it inherits the ownership and protected-path refusals rather than having privileges of its own.

callers.scope: OpenWorkspace registers the workspace it just opened, with the ID, directory, bucket, TTL, the persisted authority mask and the quota limits, so a later Resume can reopen it with the same policy. A failure to register is reported rather than swallowed.
Resume looks the entry up by ID and reopens the workspace from the directory the entry names; the registry is the only thing that maps an ID to a directory.
Collect is the public sweep; it refuses on a host without advisory locks before it touches anything, and reports every decision rather than only the removals.

List opens the registry read-only and reads every entry through All, summarising a missing directory as Readable=false without ever opening the workspace — so a list never touches a workspace's files.

DestroyRegisteredWorkspace is host administration over a trusted registry; it removes the workspace under the registry's exclusion and hold checks and does not use or widen a restricted Workspace handle.
AddRecoveryHold, ReleaseRecoveryHold and DiscardRecoveryHold are the public surface for the recovery-hold journal; they take the registry mutation lock before touching it.
CaptureCheckpoint takes the registry mutation lock and the workspace capture lock, so a retained request is replayed under exclusion and a capture cannot race another.
Workspace.CreateCheckpoint takes the mutation-capture lock before a capture, so a capture cannot race a reconcile or a sweep on the same workspace.
SetRegistryPolicy takes the registry mutation lock and counts existing workspaces with AllStrict, so a standing cap cannot be written below current usage.
the capacity host takes the same capture-lock primitive with a fixed 'capacity-host' name, so the workspace package's lock file is the exclusion mechanism for an unrelated subsystem too.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: Deleting the registry does not remove complexity from the callers; it moves it into them. pkg/stow would have to re-implement the durable ID-to-directory map, the liveness proof, the ownership-before-age ordering and the recovery-hold dependency check in each of resume, collect, prune, destroy-admin, checkpoint-request and the recovery-hold verbs, and pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go would lose the only journal format that binds a published capture to the workspace it depends on. The complexity concentrates here rather than spreading, which is what makes it deep.

leverage: A caller gets a workspace that survives the process that created it, a sweep that can prove a workspace is unused rather than guess, and a capture that can refuse to be forgotten while something depends on it — all from one directory of JSON files and a set of flock files, with no daemon and no network registry.
locality: The registry's on-disk shape, its policy document, its recovery-hold journal and all three lock files are here. The one coupling that crosses a boundary is the session lock, whose file lives inside the workspace's own .stow subtree (internal/storage/workspace/session.go:63) while the capture and mutation locks live inside the registry; a change to either location is a change to this package, and pkg/stow resolves the registry path once and records it (pkg/stow/workspace.go:189-193).
risks: Liveness is only as good as the flock. Two processes on a host where flock is not honoured would both see 'not live'; nothing in this package cross-checks the session lock against the registry's LastUsed, so a stale LastUsed is never a reason to remove and never a reason to keep.

The registry stores the workspace path exactly as the caller supplied it in Entry.Dir (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:28) and this package never normalises it to an absolute path — the 'absolute' wording is only a doc comment on Store.Root (internal/storage/workspace/workspace.go:166-167) and Workspace.Dir (pkg/stow/workspace.go:201) — so a registry copied between machines, or one whose caller passed a relative path, points at directories that do not exist or resolve elsewhere. The failure is visible — Prune classifies a missing directory as gone (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:348-363) and All still lists it — but the entry is not self-describing enough to detect the move.

Registry.Collect removes a workspace by opening it and calling Destroy, which routes the removal through the ownership and protected-path checks (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:388-403); a workspace whose directory is replaced between the liveness probe and the destroy is refused by the root-identity check, and the sweep reports it under the shared 'unreadable: ' prefix (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:300-302), so a caller must read the appended error text to tell a lost root identity from a permission failure.

The recovery-hold journal is one file for the whole registry, and a corrupt journal makes every hold query and every forget fail, because a missing identity file beside an existing journal is corruption rather than absence (internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_journal.go:33-38). There is no repair path and no quarantine path.

Registry.All silently skips an entry it cannot decode (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:238-243), so a workspace whose entry is corrupted disappears from a listing and from a sweep's view without anything reporting it. AllStrict is the reader that surfaces the failure (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:87-110), and it is used by RegisterWithLimit's cap check (internal/storage/workspace/admission.go:134), countRegistryEntries (pkg/stow/workspace_limit.go:55) and SetRegistryPolicy (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:37). Prune is not among them: Prune reads through All (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:320), so it also skips a corrupt entry silently.

priority.rationale: The registry is what makes a workspace outlive its process, and its refusals — live workspace, adopted workspace, recovery hold — are the last thing between an unattended sweep and somebody's work. Its blast radius is every workspace verb in pkg/stow (open, resume, list, collect, prune, destroy, checkpoint, request replay, recovery hold) plus internal/capacity's lock. The journal's corruption mode is registry-wide, and All's silent skip means a corrupted entry disappears from the operator's view rather than failing loudly. It is not P0 because each of the three destructive guards is independently implemented and directly tested.

next_action: State the registry's on-disk contract in docs/workspace-contract.md the way the workspace's own contract is stated — the entry file name, the team partition path, the three lock files, the policy document and the recovery-hold journal — because today only the code says any of it, and the code is the only place a caller can learn it. The interface that should change is Registry's: it exposes All, AllStrict, Lookup, Register and the hold verbs but nothing that names the layout, so add an exported description of the registry's on-disk shape rather than another accessor. Pair that with making All report the entries it skipped rather than dropping them, so a corrupt entry is visible to the operator who can act on it.

title: The storage.ConditionalCopyStore optional seam: five production adapters and one observable behaviour difference
summary: internal/storage/store.go:98 declares storage.ConditionalCopyStore, the optional interface that lets a copy refuse to publish anything unless the source version satisfies the caller's conditions. It has five production implementations - storage.MemoryStore (internal/storage/memory_copy.go:32), fs.FilesystemStore (internal/storage/fs/fs_copy.go:25), workspace.Store (internal/storage/workspace/objects.go:223), runthrough.Adapter (internal/runthrough/mutations_adapter.go:227) and runtime.StoreAdapter (internal/runtime/adapter.go:155) - so it is a real seam, not a hypothetical one. What varies across it is observable and documented: an implementation evaluates the conditions against the version whose bytes it copies, under one lock, while a store that does not implement it can only promise an internally coherent copy; internal/s3api/copy.go:85 and internal/runtime/objects.go:320 both fall back to a head-then-copy in that case. The one production adapter that lacks the guarantee is the embedded adapter for caller-supplied stores (internal/embedded/store.go:291-308), so the public library path silently gets the weaker behaviour.

trace.scope: handleCopyObject: the S3 copy request handler; the COPY metadata directive dispatches to copyVerbatim at :354
copyVerbatim reads the source conditions off the request at :84 and type-asserts the store to storage.ConditionalCopyStore at :85
the filesystem backend takes its lock, settles the save journal, opens the source record and evaluates the conditions against that captured version
CheckCopySourceConditions returns storage.ErrPreconditionFailed (at :49) - the refusal a caller sees

evidence.detail: the interface, one method, with the doc comment at :86-97 stating exactly what an implementation must do differently and why a store that does not implement it can only promise an internally coherent copy.
MemoryStore's implementation: it captures the source and commits the destination under one lock, so the bytes that arrive are paired with the metadata that was read.
the filesystem implementation: it settles the save journal before the copy, refuses when a recovery hold covers the destination (:76-78) and streams the source bytes into the new record.
the workspace implementation: it resolves the source path, reads the file and publishes the destination under one lock, so a source overwritten in between cannot be copied as one version.
the run-through implementation: it decides whether the destination propagates upstream, prepares an outbox entry, then delegates the copy to the local store.

the runtime implementation: it routes the request through runtime.Instance.CopyObjectCond so quota and authority are enforced, and its doc comment at :150-154 states that without it the S3 layer would fall back to checking a version it observed and then copying whatever is current.
the fallback path: when the local store is not a ConditionalCopyStore the adapter checks an observed source version and then copies, which is the weaker guarantee the interface documents.
the runtime's own fallback: the same type assertion, and :329 uses it to decide whether the runtime itself has to evaluate the conditions (the check at :284).

the contract suite requires every backing store registered in backendFactories to implement the interface and fails with 'a conditional copy cannot be evaluated on the version it copies' if one does not.

the embedded adapter's CopyObject is get-then-put when the caller's store does not implement the public embedded.CopyStore (and delegates to it when it does), and in neither case does it implement storage.ConditionalCopyStore; the file's comment at :273-277 states that this is a real semantic difference from a native store.
the real request entry point for the copy behaviour: the handler parses the copy source and dispatches to copyVerbatim (COPY) or replaceMetadata (REPLACE).

interface.types: storage.ConditionalCopyStore is a single method: CopyObjectCond(ctx context.Context, req storage.CopyRequest) (*storage.ObjectMeta, error). storage.CopyRequest (internal/storage/store.go:78) names the source and destination as separate bucket and key pairs - deliberately a struct, because a signature taking two adjacent string pairs invites swapping them - and carries storage.CopyOptions (SourceIfMatch, SourceIfNoneMatch, SourceIfModifiedSince, SourceIfUnmodifiedSince, internal/storage/store.go:65). A substituter must evaluate those four conditions against the source version whose bytes it is about to copy, and must publish the destination from that same captured version, or the copy is not atomic.
