The format depends on the checkpoint manifest and on the path rules the checkpoint store owns (pkg/stow/delta_validation.go:49), and the conflict vocabulary deliberately matches the run-through propagation refusal rather than inventing a second one (pkg/stow/delta.go:67). The file-only form is the only one the transport supports, which is stated in both directions (pkg/stow/delta.go:183, pkg/stow/delta_apply.go:57).
risks: The digest check is optional: VerifyDeltaDigest returns nil for an empty expected digest (pkg/stow/delta.go:378), so a receiver that does not pass one gets no change-list binding at all, and the per-file digests alone do not cover the paths a document names.

The transport does not support the portable object form, and the refusal is in both directions (pkg/stow/delta.go:183, pkg/stow/delta_apply.go:57); a caller that keeps one checkpoint in the portable form and one in the file form gets a transport error rather than a partial delta.

The document's own ceiling is 16 MiB (MaxDeltaBytes) while the default caller cap is 1 GiB (defaultDeltaBytes) (pkg/stow/delta.go:57, pkg/stow/delta.go:65), so a delta between two large checkpoints cannot be described even when the caller's own cap allows it, and the refusal arrives inside CreateDelta (pkg/stow/delta.go:292, pkg/stow/delta.go:323), before EncodeDelta is reached.

A delta carries the bytes of every changed path in memory as a map (pkg/stow/delta.go:143), and DecodeDelta bounds the raw read at 32 MiB before parsing (pkg/stow/delta.go:396). The read bound does not bind a valid document: 16 MiB of content encodes to roughly 21 MiB, under the 32 MiB bound, so the effective ceiling remains the declared content bound (MaxDeltaBytes, 16 MiB) and the read bound only guards the parse.

priority.rationale: Impact is P2 because the module has one production caller pair — the CLI's delta and apply verbs — and its blast radius is the exchange of working sets between machines, which is a narrow but consequential path. Overall is P2 because the risks are all about a caller that does not use an option it could, and about a format ceiling that is a deliberate limit rather than a defect.

next_action: Make the digest check the default path rather than an option: VerifyDeltaDigest treats an empty expected digest as a pass (pkg/stow/delta.go:378) and DeltaOptions carries the pair as an optional field (pkg/stow/delta.go:123), so a receiver that forgets it gets no change-list binding. The interface that should change is DeltaOptions: Encoded and ExpectSHA256 are two fields that must be set together and mean nothing apart, and a caller that sets only one gets a silent no-op rather than a refusal.

title: Embedded runtime re-export barrel in pkg/stow
claimed_root_cause: A candidate public module in pkg/stow wrapping the embedded runtime: the object-model types (Backend, Options, Capabilities, Usage, Bucket, Object, ObjectPage, PutOptions, ListOptions), the store interfaces (Store, ConditionalWriteStore, MultipartStore and the multipart types), the runtime handle, the authority vocabulary, the guarded-save, save-request, staged-write, streaming and object-recovery surfaces, and the error set.

trace.scope: Backend = embedded.Backend and the object-model aliases that follow it: the public surface the barrel exposes to an embedder.
Open delegates to embedded.Open and returns its result unchanged; the barrel contributes no step of its own.
embedded.Open branches on options.Store and maps errors, so the behaviour is emitted here rather than in pkg/stow.
runtime.Open normalises options and constructs the Instance that owns the usage, authority and policy state the barrel's surface only names.

evidence.detail: The file is a single type block of Go type aliases onto embedded, followed by a constant block and a var block that alias the embedded values.
Six aliases onto the embedded store interfaces and multipart types; the file owns nothing else.
Runtime = embedded.Runtime plus a one-line Open that delegates.
Nine error values aliased from embedded, so the public error set is the embedded one.
AllowAll, AllowNone, ReadOnly and ReadWrite are one-line delegations to internal/authority; the file's own comment states that the vocabulary is re-exported rather than left behind an internal path.
SaveOutcome, SaveCondition, SaveResult and SaveOptions are aliases, the three outcome constants are embedded constants, and ReplacementCondition delegates.
Two type aliases and two error aliases onto the embedded object-recovery surface.
Seven error aliases onto the embedded save-request surface.
Two aliases onto the embedded staged-write surface.
Six aliases onto the embedded streaming, range and copy surfaces plus the storage object range type.
The embedded Open, and the Runtime methods the barrel's callers actually use, live here and in the other embedded files.

reason: A re-export barrel, not a module. Ten files in pkg/stow — types.go, store.go, runtime.go, errors.go, authority.go, guarded_save.go, object_recovery.go, save_requests.go, staged.go and streams.go — contain nothing but Go type aliases, constant aliases, error aliases and one-line delegations to internal/embedded, which is unimportable outside this module. The ten files total 191 lines; there is no branch, no validation, no state and no decision in any of them, and the only function bodies are the one-line delegations at pkg/stow/runtime.go:9, pkg/stow/authority.go:37-50 and pkg/stow/guarded_save.go:27. The deletion test went the 'vanishes' way: removing these files removes no complexity from anywhere in the tree, because none of the behaviour ever lived in pkg/stow — it lives in internal/embedded (internal/embedded/runtime.go:19, internal/embedded/store.go:15) and, behind it, internal/runtime (internal/runtime/instance.go:34), which have their own Module units in this run. The layer does a real job (pkg/stow/doc.go:1 and pkg/stow/authority.go:5 both say the vocabulary is re-exported so a public API does not force an internal path on an embedder), but a purpose is not behaviour, and the catalogue (Validation rules #8) lists a re-export barrel as something to record so a later run does not search for it again. The workspace, checkpoint, delta, handoff and registry-policy files in the same package are the ones that own behaviour — verified by branching in pkg/stow/delta_apply.go:31-84 and pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:24-88 — and they are recorded separately.

title: Filesystem backend entry point
summary: OpenFilesystem is the public entry point for the durable filesystem backend: it opens one exclusively locked directory, wraps it in a runtime with the filesystem backend and no reset, and refuses an injected store, a different backend, and every platform that is not Linux or Darwin. It is the smaller sibling of OpenWorkspace, and the two differ in what they are: a filesystem store is a durable object store with its own record layout, while a workspace's objects are the directory itself. It is also the only public path to a durable filesystem runtime, because pkg/stow.Open refuses BackendFilesystem (pkg/stow/save_requests_test.go:285).

trace.scope: OpenFilesystem is the public entry point for the durable filesystem backend.
An empty directory and an injected Store are both refused, so the backend owns its own storage.
openFilesystemStore opens the one exclusively locked durable directory, optionally bound to a capacity namespace.
The runtime instance is wrapped and returned as a *stow.Runtime, with the store closed if the runtime could not be opened.

evidence.detail: FilesystemOptions carries the directory, the runtime options and an optional capacity namespace; it is the only public type this module declares.
A non-empty backend other than BackendFilesystem is refused with ErrUnsupportedBackend, so the constant cannot be used to request a workspace here.
The runtime is opened with BackendFilesystem and a nil reset hook, which is what makes Reset unavailable for this backend.
The store is closed when the runtime cannot be opened, so a failed open does not leave a lock behind.

The module records that a previously bound directory refuses an unbound reopen, so opening first and binding afterward fails on that directory; the refusal itself is enforced in internal/storage/fs/fs.go:55-56 (capacity.ErrConflict).
On every platform other than Linux and Darwin the same call returns ErrUnsupportedBackend, so the symbol exists everywhere and the behaviour does not.
The MCP object host opens its configured directory with stow.OpenFilesystem and its authority, so the public entry point is how a host gets a durable object runtime.
The dogfood example opens its store the same way and drives a guarded save through the returned runtime.
stow.Open(Options{Backend: BackendFilesystem}) returns ErrUnsupportedBackend, so OpenFilesystem is the only public way to obtain a durable filesystem runtime.

interface.types: stow.FilesystemOptions{Dir, Options, Namespace} is the input; Dir is required, Options carries the runtime's MaxBytes, MaxObjects, MaxMultipartUploads and Authority, and Namespace optionally binds the store to a capacity namespace. Namespace is a *stow.CapacityNamespace, a public wrapper declared in the same package (pkg/stow/capacity.go:26) around internal/capacity.Namespace; a caller cannot construct one directly and must go through OpenCapacityHost (pkg/stow/capacity.go:28) and (*CapacityHost).BindNamespace (pkg/stow/capacity.go:36). The result is a *stow.Runtime, the same handle type the memory backend returns, so the two are interchangeable to a caller that only uses the object API.
invariants: The store owns its storage: an injected Store is refused (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:15).

The directory is required and is opened with an exclusive lock; a previously bound directory refuses an unbound reopen, enforced in internal/storage/fs/fs.go:55-56 and recorded by the module's own comment (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:15, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:40).
The backend is fixed: a non-empty requested backend other than BackendFilesystem is refused with ErrUnsupportedBackend (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:21).
Reset is unavailable for this backend, because the runtime is opened with no reset hook (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:28, internal/runtime/instance.go:226).
The store is closed if the runtime cannot be opened (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:34).
The capability is platform-specific: the function exists on every platform but returns ErrUnsupportedBackend outside Linux and Darwin (pkg/stow/filesystem_unsupported.go:5).
error_modes: "stow: filesystem directory required and Store must be unset" when Dir is empty or a store was injected (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:16).

stow.ErrUnsupportedBackend when a non-empty different backend was requested, and on every platform that is not Linux or Darwin (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:22, pkg/stow/filesystem_unsupported.go:6).
stow.ErrCapacityInvalid when a capacity namespace was supplied with no inner namespace behind it (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:19).
stow.ErrCapacityConflict when an unbound open targets a directory that already carries a capacity binding (internal/storage/fs/fs.go:55-56); it passes through embedded.MapSaveError unchanged.
The store's own open error, mapped through embedded.MapSaveError so the caller sees the package's error vocabulary (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:26).
ordering: The options are validated before anything is created, so a bad request costs nothing (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:15).

The store is opened before the runtime, and the runtime is opened before the store is handed over, so a failure at either step closes the one that succeeded (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:24, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:34).
The capacity namespace is bound while the store is opened, not after, because a directory already bound cannot be bound again (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:42).
configuration: Dir names the durable directory; the store takes an exclusive lock on it (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:15).
Options.MaxBytes, MaxObjects and MaxMultipartUploads bound the runtime, and Options.Authority is the grant the runtime enforces (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:30).
Namespace binds the store to a capacity namespace, which is how a caller gives a project its own byte budget inside a shared host (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:46).

The backend constant is the only non-empty backend this entry point accepts; an empty Backend is accepted and defaults to BackendFilesystem (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:21, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:29).

implementation: OpenFilesystem (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:14) validates that a directory was named and that no store was injected, rejects a capacity namespace that has no namespace behind it, rejects a non-empty requested backend that is not the filesystem backend, and then opens the store through openFilesystemStore, which takes the plain constructor when no namespace was given and the namespace-bound constructor when one was. The store is opened before the runtime because the runtime is what enforces the quotas, and the store is closed again if the runtime refuses to open. The runtime is opened with the filesystem backend and a nil reset hook, so the reset operation that the memory and workspace backends offer is not available here, and the resulting instance is wrapped for the caller. The whole file is behind a linux-or-darwin build tag, and the counterpart file returns ErrUnsupportedBackend everywhere else, so the public symbol is stable across platforms while its behaviour is not.

callers.scope: The MCP object host opens its configured directory through stow.OpenFilesystem with a read-write or read-only authority, which is how a host gets a durable, bounded object runtime.
The dogfood example opens its store through stow.OpenFilesystem and drives a guarded save and a replay through the returned runtime.
The Go benchmark opens the same directory through stow.OpenFilesystem to measure it against the memory backend.
The managed-save benchmark opens a filesystem runtime the same way.
The in-package performance benchmark opens a filesystem runtime through stow.OpenFilesystem.
The durable-save-request tests open the directory through stow.OpenFilesystem (and exercise the refusal paths at lines 255, 259, 272 and 281).
The filesystem recovery test reopens the same directory through stow.OpenFilesystem to assert recovery holds survive a reopen.
The object recovery test opens the directory through stow.OpenFilesystem with a capacity namespace.
The MCP browser process test opens the served directory through stow.OpenFilesystem.
The MCP objects process test reacquires the directory through stow.OpenFilesystem to prove the lock was released on shutdown.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: The complexity concentrates, so the module is not a pass-through, but a substantial part of it is delegation. Deleting OpenFilesystem would push real work into each of its ten callers: the refusal of an injected store, the refusal of a different backend, the store-before-runtime ordering with the store closed on failure, the nil reset hook, the error mapping, and the linux-or-darwin build-tag split with its refusal stub. That is not trivial: pkg/stow.Open refuses BackendFilesystem (pkg/stow/save_requests_test.go:285), so OpenFilesystem is the only public path to a durable filesystem runtime, and the internal packages it wires (internal/embedded, internal/runtime, internal/storage/fs) are not importable by an external consumer of pkg/stow, so for those callers the complexity would not merely move, it would be unachievable. On the other side, the body is thin and partly pure delegation: a three-item validation list, a four-line two-branch delegation to the fs constructors (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:42-47), a delegation to OpenWithStore, and WrapInstance, with no transformation or state of its own, and the behaviour it configures (record layout, locking, quotas, authority) is owned by internal/storage/fs and internal/runtime, which have their own units in this run. Genuine concentration on one side and thin delegation on the other is why the verdict is mixed rather than deep or shallow.

leverage: A caller gets a durable, bounded, authority-checked object runtime in one call, with the exclusive lock, the platform rule, the error vocabulary and the reset unavailability settled rather than re-derived. The MCP object host and both benchmarks reach the same behaviour through the same call, and the two backends return the same handle type, so a caller can swap them without changing its code.
locality: The whole module is three small files: pkg/stow/filesystem.go for the options type, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go for the linux-and-darwin implementation, and pkg/stow/filesystem_unsupported.go for the refusal elsewhere. The behaviour it configures lives in internal/storage/fs, which has its own module unit in this run, and the runtime it opens is internal/runtime. The one thing worth keeping in mind is that the platform split is by build tag rather than by a runtime check, so the decision to support a platform is made when the file is written.
risks: The public symbol exists on every platform but only works on Linux and Darwin, and the refusal is a runtime error rather than a build-time one (pkg/stow/filesystem_unsupported.go:5), so a caller discovers the platform limit when it calls rather than when it compiles.

The module's own comment records that a previously bound directory refuses an unbound reopen (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:40), which is a rule a caller cannot see from the signature and has to learn from the error (stow.ErrCapacityConflict).

The runtime is opened with a nil reset hook, so Reset is unavailable for this backend (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:28); a caller that treats Reset as part of the runtime interface will find out at the call rather than at compile time, because the handle type is the same as the memory backend's.

pkg/stow reaches into internal/storage/fs and internal/runtime to build the store (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:9, pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:10), so the public package carries the construction of a backend that has its own unit in this run.

priority.rationale: Impact is P3 because the module has ten calling files but only one production caller (the MCP object host at internal/mcpstorage/object_server.go:51); the rest are one example, two benchmarks and six test files, and its behaviour is a thin construction over a backend that is separately mapped. Overall is P3 because the risks found are ones a caller discovers at the call — a platform refusal, a reset that is not there, a directory that is already bound — rather than defects in the construction itself.

next_action: Make the platform rule visible where a caller looks: the build-tagged split (pkg/stow/filesystem_native.go:1, pkg/stow/filesystem_unsupported.go:1) means the capability differs by target while the symbol does not. The interface that should change is FilesystemOptions, whose Namespace field is a *stow.CapacityNamespace — a public wrapper declared in the same package (pkg/stow/capacity.go:26) around internal/capacity.Namespace — so a caller has to build a capacity host and call BindNamespace before it can even express the option (pkg/stow/capacity.go:28, pkg/stow/capacity.go:36).

title: Registry policy and recovery holds
summary: The standing-limits slice of the public package over a trusted registry: a policy of workspace-count, checkpoint-count and checkpoint-byte caps that a registry enforces, the admission check that applies those caps to a new checkpoint on every publish path, the deletion of a retained checkpoint under its descendant and hold rules, and the recovery-hold verbs that pin a workspace and its checkpoints while a recovery is in progress. It owns the rule that a cap refuses rather than evicts, that a policy which existing usage already exceeds is refused, and that a checkpoint with a retained descendant or an open hold cannot be deleted. The admission arithmetic is the load-bearing half: three production publish paths call it. The exported hold verbs are the other half: they delegate to the registry's own hold journal and, as written, nothing in the tree calls them at all.

trace.scope: SetRegistryPolicy is the public entry point for putting standing limits on a registry.
The registry mutation lock is taken, so the policy is validated against a stable view of the registry.
Existing workspaces are counted strictly (line 37) and retained checkpoints are counted with their bytes (line 44); a policy the current usage already exceeds is refused (lines 41 and 48).
WritePolicy persists the policy in the registry's .stow/policy.json, where every later admission check reads it.

evidence.detail: SetRegistryPolicy refuses a workspace cap that the registry's current entry count already exceeds.
The checkpoint caps are checked against the retained checkpoints' count and their payload bytes, and the same condition has a single refusal message.
registryCheckpointUsage skips the .checkpoint- and .import- staging directories, so a capture in flight is not counted as a retained checkpoint.
checkpointRetentionUsage repeats the same staging-prefix skip (.checkpoint- and .import-), so the skip rule is written twice in the package.
The admission check applies the standing cap and then the per-workspace cap, and refuses a new checkpoint whose bytes would exceed the remaining byte budget.
DeleteCheckpoint refuses a checkpoint that has a recovery hold, so a recovery in progress cannot lose the checkpoint it depends on.
checkCheckpointDescendants refuses to delete a checkpoint that a retained checkpoint names as its parent, so the retained chain is not broken from the middle.
mutateRecoveryHold takes the registry mutation lock and re-checks the context before and after taking it, so a hold is admitted and finished under the same lock.
validateRecoveryReferences checks that every referenced workspace exists and that a referenced checkpoint belongs to the referenced workspace.
ListRecoveryHolds bounds the serialised page to 256 KiB and refuses a larger one rather than returning it.

TestRegistryPolicyPersistsAndCannotBeWidenedByPrepare asserts that a standing cap cannot be widened by a prepare; the last-workspace-slot serialisation is asserted separately by TestRegistryAdmissionSerializesLastWorkspaceSlot at registry_policy_test.go:44.

interface.types: stow.RegistryPolicy is an alias for workspace.RegistryPolicy and carries Version, MaxWorkspaces, MaxCheckpoints and MaxCheckpointBytes, where zero means unlimited. The recovery-hold surface is stow.RecoveryHoldRequest{ID, Owner, References []stow.RecoveryReference{WorkspaceID, CheckpointID}, ExpiresAt}, stow.RecoveryHold (the request plus Meaning, State, Created, FinishedAt), stow.RecoveryHoldQuery and stow.RecoveryHoldPage, with the bounds stow.MaxRecoveryHolds, stow.MaxRecoveryReferences, stow.MaxRecoveryHoldBytes and stow.MaxRecoveryHoldPeakBytes. The entry points are stow.GetRegistryPolicy, stow.SetRegistryPolicy, stow.DeleteCheckpoint, stow.AddRecoveryHold, stow.ReleaseRecoveryHold, stow.DiscardRecoveryHold and stow.ListRecoveryHolds.
invariants: A cap refuses; it never evicts. Collecting the oldest idle workspace destroys a task nobody said was finished, and an adopted entry is somebody's project (pkg/stow/workspace_limit.go:12).
A policy that the registry's current usage already exceeds is refused rather than applied (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:41, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:48).
A standing cap and a per-workspace cap both apply to a new checkpoint, and the standing one is checked first (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:90, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:104).
Only published checkpoints count towards the retention caps; the staging directories of a capture in flight are skipped (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:64, pkg/stow/checkpoint.go:127).
A checkpoint with a recovery hold cannot be deleted, and a checkpoint with a retained descendant cannot be deleted (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:136, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:164).
A recovery hold's references must name an existing workspace, and a named checkpoint must belong to that workspace (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:84, pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:94).

A hold may be released or discarded only by its owner, and the finished state is one of released or discarded (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:47, pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:53; the owner check itself is workspace.FinishRecoveryHold at internal/storage/workspace/recovery_hold_mutation.go:91).

The hold mutations take the registry mutation lock and re-check the context after taking it (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:68, pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:73); DeleteCheckpoint checks the context after its mutation-capture lock (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:142). SetRegistryPolicy is the exception: it takes no context and so cannot re-check one.
error_modes: "stow: existing workspaces exceed registry policy" and "stow: existing checkpoints exceed registry policy" (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:42, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:49).

"stow: invalid retained checkpoint %s: %w" when a retained checkpoint cannot be loaded, which is reported rather than skipped because the count would otherwise be wrong (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:69).
"stow: retained checkpoint accounting overflow" on an arithmetic overflow (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:73).
"registry checkpoint retention limit exceeded" as a capacity_exceeded CheckpointError from the admission check (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:96).
"stow: checkpoint has retained descendant %s" (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:165).
"stow: invalid recovery dependency count" and "stow: recovery checkpoint workspace mismatch" (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:81, pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:95).
"stow: recovery hold page exceeds response bound" when the serialised page is larger than 256 KiB (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:118).
stow.ErrRecoveryHoldConflict, stow.ErrRecoveryHoldNotFound, stow.ErrRecoveryHoldFull and stow.ErrRecoveryHoldCorrupt, re-exported from the registry's own hold journal (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:23).
ordering: The policy is validated, then the registry is opened, then the mutation lock is taken, then the usage is counted, and only then is the policy written (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:25, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:28, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:32, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:37, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:51).
The context is checked before the lock and again after it, so a cancelled call does not hold the registry (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:61, pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:73).

Deletion takes the mutation-capture lock, reloads the manifest, then checks the holds and the descendants, then removes the directory, then fsyncs the parent (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:124, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:129, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:136, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:139, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:145, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:148).

A hold that admitted a prepared checkpoint is admitted with that checkpoint's id, and a hold that admits afterwards validates its references (pkg/stow/checkpoint_recovery_hold.go:48, pkg/stow/checkpoint_recovery_hold.go:54).
configuration: The registry directory selects which registry the policy applies to. It is the same resolution rule the workspace lifecycle uses, but these functions pass an empty team (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:16, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:28), so the team partition is not composed in and a caller must pass the already-resolved directory it means.
Every cap of zero means unlimited (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:23).
The policy's own Version field must be accepted by workspace.RegistryPolicy.Validate, which accepts only version 1 (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:25).
A recovery hold's ExpiresAt is an expiry for the hold itself, not for the checkpoint it references (pkg/stow/checkpoint_recovery_hold.go:46).

implementation: SetRegistryPolicy (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:24) validates the policy, opens the registry, takes the registry mutation lock, reads the entries strictly, counts the retained checkpoints and their bytes, and refuses a policy that the current usage already exceeds before writing it. registryCheckpointUsage (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:54) walks the registry's checkpoint directory, skipping the .checkpoint- and .import- staging directories, loading each retained manifest and summing its manifest bytes with an overflow check. checkRegistryCheckpointAdmission (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:81) applies the standing policy's count and byte caps, including the case where the new checkpoint's bytes would exceed the remaining byte budget, and then falls through to the per-workspace cap the registry entry records. DeleteCheckpoint (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:111) resolves the checkpoint's directory, loads the manifest, takes the mutation-capture lock for the checkpoint's workspace, reloads the manifest, refuses a checkpoint with a recovery hold, refuses one with a retained descendant, removes the directory and fsyncs its parent. The recovery-hold surface (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:30) is host administration over a trusted registry rather than a grant from an owner: AddRecoveryHold admits a hold, validating its references when the hold is not already present, ReleaseRecoveryHold and DiscardRecoveryHold finish one by owner, and ListRecoveryHolds reads the page and refuses a page whose serialised form exceeds 256 KiB. The checkpoint capture path uses the same machinery: captureWithRecoveryHold (pkg/stow/checkpoint_recovery_hold.go:18) admits the hold before the capture, refuses to reactivate an aborted hold, and discards the hold when the capture fails with a known outcome while leaving it in place when the outcome is unknown.

callers.scope: The package's own test calls stow.SetRegistryPolicy (line 19) and stow.GetRegistryPolicy (line 22), and asserts at lines 38-41 that a standing cap cannot be widened by a later prepare.

The package's own test calls stow.DeleteCheckpoint after a successful import; the refusals for a retained descendant and for a checkpoint held by a reader are asserted in TestDeleteCheckpointRespectsReaderGateAndLineage at registry_policy_test.go:124 and registry_policy_test.go:133.
The checkpoint capture path calls checkRegistryCheckpointAdmission through captureTarget.checkRetention, so a standing registry cap is enforced on every capture.
Publishing an applied delta runs the same admission check, so a delta cannot be used to slip past a retention cap.
Publishing an imported checkpoint runs the same admission check.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: The deletion test went both ways, which is why the verdict is mixed. The part that concentrates is the admission arithmetic: checkRegistryCheckpointAdmission (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:81) and registryCheckpointUsage (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:54) are called from three separate publish paths — the capture, the applied delta and the imported archive (pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture_core.go:92, pkg/stow/delta_apply.go:280, pkg/stow/checkpoint_import.go:227) — and each of them would otherwise have to re-derive which checkpoints count and how their bytes are measured. The parts that vanish are the wrappers: GetRegistryPolicy and SetRegistryPolicy delegate to the registry's policy file, and AddRecoveryHold, ReleaseRecoveryHold, DiscardRecoveryHold and ListRecoveryHolds (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:30) delegate to the registry's own hold journal; deleting them moves no complexity into any caller because the policy get/set and DeleteCheckpoint are called only by the package's own test and the four hold verbs are called by nothing at all. The module is therefore a real module for the admission arithmetic and a set of pass-throughs for the exported hold verbs.

leverage: A caller gets one place where a retention cap is decided, and the answer is the same whether the checkpoint came from a capture, from an applied delta or from an imported archive. A host that wants a registry bounded sets one policy and every publish path respects it, including the ones a user drives indirectly. A caller holding a recovery can pin the checkpoints it depends on and know they cannot be deleted underneath it — once a caller exists that uses the hold verbs at all.
locality: The policy and admission rules live in pkg/stow/registry_policy.go and the hold surface in pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go, with the checkpoint-side hold handling in pkg/stow/checkpoint_recovery_hold.go. The persistent policy, the hold journal and the locks live in internal/storage/workspace, which has its own module unit in this run, so the two halves of the behaviour are described in two places. The staging-prefix skip that decides which directories are retained checkpoints is written twice, once in pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:64 and once in pkg/stow/checkpoint.go:127, and the two spellings have to agree.
risks: The public surface of this module has no production caller in the tree. SetRegistryPolicy, GetRegistryPolicy and DeleteCheckpoint are called only by the package's own test (pkg/stow/registry_policy_test.go:19, pkg/stow/registry_policy_test.go:99), and AddRecoveryHold, ReleaseRecoveryHold, DiscardRecoveryHold and ListRecoveryHolds are called by nothing at all — no test, no CLI, no MCP server, only their own definitions (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:30). They are exported for embedders of the public package, but the host-administrative path is documented by a doc comment and one test, not exercised by any caller.

The standing policy is scoped to one registry directory, and the team partition is not composed in: these functions resolve the registry with an empty team (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:16, pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:28), so a policy set at the root does not govern a team partition's admissions, and one set on a partition's directory does not govern the root's. A caller has to know which directory the policy was set on, and the exported verbs cannot express a team at all.

The staging-prefix skip for retained checkpoints is written twice — pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:64 and pkg/stow/checkpoint.go:127 — and each copy has to skip the same .checkpoint- and .import- prefixes. A change to the staging layout would have to change both, and the two are not adjacent in the package.

The admission check loads every retained manifest to count it (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:67), so the cost of admitting a checkpoint grows with the number of retained checkpoints whenever a standing checkpoint cap is configured (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:90), and a single unreadable retained manifest makes the check fail rather than be skipped (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:69).

priority.rationale: Impact is P3 because the module's blast radius is confined to the registry's retention behaviour: the three publish paths that consult the admission check, and a public surface with no production caller. Overall is P3 because the demonstrated risk is a duplication and a documentation gap rather than a defect — the staging-skip rule is written twice, and the policy is scoped per directory with no team composition — neither of which threatens data.

next_action: Decide whether the registry-policy and recovery-hold verbs are part of the public library surface or a leftover, and record the answer where a host author will look: nothing in cmd/stow-s3 or internal/mcpstorage calls them, the hold verbs have no caller at all (pkg/stow/recovery_holds.go:30), and pkg/stow/public_surface_test.go:12 shows the package has already pinned exports with no callers rather than remove them. The interface that should change is the team handling: these verbs take a registry directory and an empty team (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:16), so a caller cannot scope a policy to a partition by name, which is the one thing the partition exists for. The duplicated staging-prefix skip (pkg/stow/registry_policy.go:64, pkg/stow/checkpoint.go:127) should collapse into one predicate before the layout changes.

title: Workspace lifecycle and registry
summary: The stow.Workspace handle and the registry-scoped verbs around it: OpenWorkspace, Resume, ResumeIn, ResumeWith, List, Collect, Prune, Touch, Close, Destroy and DestroyRegisteredWorkspace. This module owns the rules that decide where a workspace's metadata lives, that a team is a directory partition inside that directory rather than a label, that a workspace outlives the handle that opened it, that reopening may only narrow the authority and the limits a workspace was created with, and the close-versus-destroy split. It delegates the object operations to the embedded *Runtime so quotas and accounting have a single choke point, and it delegates the adopted-workspace refusal and the collector's liveness/ownership classification to the workspace store and registry below it. The embedded *Runtime supplies the object operations, so quotas and accounting have a single choke point and a workspace is not a second implementation of PutObject.

trace.scope: OpenWorkspace is the public constructor; every other lifecycle verb reopens or reuses what it creates.
The workspace store is wrapped in a runtime instance so quota and usage accounting has one choke point.
An advisory session lock is claimed for the lifetime of the handle; that lock is what lets a collector establish that nobody is using the workspace rather than guess.
The durable registry entry is written with the id, directory, bucket, authority mask and retention caps.
RegisterWithLimit persists that entry in the registry directory on disk, which is where the next process reads it from.

evidence.detail: The Workspace struct embeds *Runtime, so the object API, the usage accounting and the authority all come from the one runtime instance.
The workspace bucket is bootstrapped through the store rather than the runtime, so a read-only authority that withholds bucket.create can still open a workspace.

The workspace store's CreateBucket returns early for the workspace bucket, so the construction call materialises nothing and never reaches the runtime's authority check (internal/runtime/buckets.go:37 checks authority.BucketCreate).
Destroy requires both the EnvironmentDestroy authority and a policy grant on the workspace root; a subtree selector does not match, so the destroy is refused rather than narrowed.
The adopted-workspace refusal is enforced here: assertDestructible refuses when the manifest is not Owned, and Destroy delegates to store.Destroy.
The collector's adopted skip is enforced here: classify checks liveness first, then returns "adopted" and declines before age is consulted, so Collect can never remove a caller's project.
resumeWith resolves the registry directory once and hands the resolved path down, because a team workspace re-registered at the registry root is a workspace two sweeps can both reach.
resumeLimit refuses a requested limit that would widen the persisted one; the same rule is applied to the authority mask at :110.
Touch records the last-used timestamp a TTL is measured from, and returns nil when the registry entry is not found.
List opens the registry read-only so that listing a registry does not create the thing it lists.
DestroyRegisteredWorkspace refuses a directory whose workspace identity does not match the registered entry.
The workspace count cap refuses a prepare rather than evicting an older workspace.
The CLI's seventeen workspace verbs are a table mapping each verb name to one command function; every registry-scoped verb reaches this module through that function.

interface.types: stow.Workspace is a struct that embeds *stow.Runtime, so a workspace handle is simultaneously a workspace lifecycle handle and an object-runtime handle. stow.WorkspaceOptions is the constructor input: Dir (required), Bucket, MaxBytes, MaxObjects, MaxMultipartUploads, MaxCheckpointBytes, MaxCheckpoints, Authority (*Authority, nil permits everything), Policy (policy.Source, nil consults no policy), TTL, RegistryDir, Team, Adopted and Now. The verbs take stow.CollectOptions{RegistryDir, Team, Now}, stow.PruneOptions{RegistryDir, Team, IncludeAdopted}, stow.ListWorkspacesOptions{RegistryDir, Team, Now} and return stow.CollectResult, stow.PruneResult and stow.WorkspaceListing (which carries the resolved Registry directory, the Team partition, and a []stow.WorkspaceSummary with a Readable flag per entry).
invariants: The registry directory is resolved once, at the point the workspace is opened or registered, and the resolved absolute path is what is recorded; a team is composed into that path as a directory partition, so the root and the team compose rather than compete (pkg/stow/resume.go:45, pkg/stow/resume.go:348).
Closing a workspace releases the handle and the session lock and deletes nothing; removal is an explicit Destroy (pkg/stow/workspace.go:243).

A workspace stow adopted is never destroyed and never collected, because its contents are the caller's; the refusal is enforced below this module, in the workspace store's destructibility check (internal/storage/workspace/destroy.go:43) and in the registry's collect classifier (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:376), which Destroy and Collect delegate to (pkg/stow/workspace.go:266).

A live session's advisory lock is what establishes that a workspace is unused; the collector acts on that fact and never on a directory's age alone (pkg/stow/workspace.go:156, pkg/stow/resume.go:212).
Reopening a workspace may only narrow the persisted authority mask and the persisted limits; a wider request is refused (pkg/stow/resume.go:110, pkg/stow/resume.go:141).

The directory is authoritative for a workspace's identity: if the reopened workspace's id does not match the requested id, the resume fails rather than handing back a different workspace (pkg/stow/resume.go:79).
The registered working directory must exist and must stay inside the workspace root, both lexically and after symlink resolution (pkg/stow/resume.go:157, pkg/stow/resume.go:169).
Touch updates the last-used timestamp a TTL is measured from and is a no-op on a workspace with no registry entry (pkg/stow/resume.go:428).
error_modes: stow.ErrClosed for any operation on a closed or closing handle (pkg/stow/workspace.go:254).
"stow: workspace Dir is required" when Dir is empty (pkg/stow/workspace.go:118).
"stow: no workspace with id %s" when the registry has no such entry (pkg/stow/resume.go:99).
"stow: workspace %s does not match the workspace registered at %s" when the directory and the registry disagree about identity (pkg/stow/resume.go:84, pkg/stow/workspace_admin.go:49).
"stow: resume authority would widen the workspace policy" and "stow: resume %s would widen the workspace limit" (pkg/stow/resume.go:111, pkg/stow/resume.go:142).

"stow: workspace %s has no supported persisted access policy; reopen it explicitly with OpenWorkspace or recreate it before resuming" when the entry's policy version is not 1 (pkg/stow/resume.go:106).
"stow: registered working directory is invalid or outside the workspace" and "stow: registered working directory resolves outside the workspace" (pkg/stow/resume.go:158, pkg/stow/resume.go:170).
stow.ErrNotAuthorized from the authority check and the policy narrowing in Destroy (pkg/stow/workspace.go:278, pkg/stow/workspace.go:281).
"stow: cannot collect on this host: %w" when the platform has no file locking (pkg/stow/resume.go:218).
"stow: workspace count limit reached (%d of %d)" with a message naming the two commands and the config key that can relieve it (pkg/stow/workspace_limit.go:32).
ordering: OpenWorkspace resolves the registry directory before it registers, and both happen before the handle is returned; a caller that reads the registry after OpenWorkspace always sees the entry (pkg/stow/workspace.go:189, pkg/stow/workspace.go:194).
Close and Destroy are idempotent: closing twice is not an error, and destroying a workspace whose directory is already gone is not an error (pkg/stow/workspace.go:242, pkg/stow/workspace.go:266).

Destroy takes the lifecycle lock and closes the runtime before removing the directory, so a facade serving that runtime is shut down before its bytes go (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:109, pkg/stow/workspace.go:296).
Collect and Prune open the registry themselves and take their own locks; they must not be called while holding a workspace handle's lifecycle lock.
Resume re-opens through OpenWorkspace, so the registry entry is re-registered and the last-used timestamp moves as a side effect of a resume.
configuration: RegistryDir places the machine's workspace registry; empty takes the default under the user's configuration directory (pkg/stow/workspace.go:91, pkg/stow/resume.go:370).
Team selects a directory partition inside the registry directory; it is a directory boundary, not a label (pkg/stow/resume.go:364, pkg/stow/resume.go:367).
TTL is the collection window the workspace records for itself; recording a TTL does not schedule a sweep (pkg/stow/workspace.go:85).
Authority and Policy are enforced below every interface, so the filesystem surface and the S3 surface cannot be granted different things (pkg/stow/workspace.go:72, pkg/stow/workspace.go:80).
Now is an injectable clock, so the TTL behaviour is testable without sleeping (pkg/stow/workspace.go:104).
Adopted marks a workspace the caller is taking over rather than scratch space, and it is what keeps Destroy's refusal honest (pkg/stow/workspace.go:100).

implementation: OpenWorkspace (pkg/stow/workspace.go:116) validates its input (Dir required, non-negative checkpoint caps), generates a bucket name when none is given (pkg/stow/workspace.go:319), opens a workspace store rooted at Dir (pkg/stow/workspace.go:128), wraps that store in a runtime instance carrying the caller's Authority, Policy and quota caps (pkg/stow/workspace.go:140), claims an advisory session lock on the directory (pkg/stow/workspace.go:156), bootstraps the workspace bucket through the store rather than the runtime so a read-only authority can still open the workspace (pkg/stow/workspace.go:181), resolves the registry directory once (pkg/stow/workspace.go:189) and registers a durable entry carrying the id, directory, working directory, bucket, TTL, policy version, authority mask, byte and object caps and checkpoint caps (pkg/stow/resume.go:400). resumeWith (pkg/stow/resume.go:39) resolves the registry once more and then reopens through OpenWorkspace, refusing a workspace whose persisted policy version it does not understand, refusing a request that would widen the authority or a limit, and refusing a registry entry whose directory holds a different workspace; the working directory is re-confined to the workspace root, both lexically and after symlink resolution, and the corrected value is written back to the registry (pkg/stow/resume.go:147). Collect delegates the sweep to the registry and reports every decision, not only the removals, so a caller can tell 'nothing was collected' from 'three were skipped because they are in use' (pkg/stow/resume.go:212). Prune removes registry entries whose directory is gone and never touches data (pkg/stow/resume.go:287). List opens the registry read-only, stats each directory for existence without opening it, computes age and idle from one clock and sorts quietest first (pkg/stow/list.go:92). DestroyRegisteredWorkspace is the host-administrative counterpart to Destroy: it goes through the registry, takes a session lock of its own, re-checks the identity and lets the store refuse a live, adopted, protected or mismatched directory (pkg/stow/workspace_admin.go:14). Touch records the last-used timestamp a TTL is measured from (pkg/stow/resume.go:428). The registry layout, the entry schema, the session lock and the ownership classification that these verbs delegate to live in internal/storage/workspace.

callers.scope: The CLI's `workspace resume` verb calls stow.ResumeWith with the registry directory it resolved, and then reports the workspace's capabilities and authority.
The `workspace list` verb calls stow.List and serialises the resolved registry directory and the summaries.
The `workspace collect` verb calls stow.Collect and reports every decision the sweep made.
The `workspace prune` verb calls stow.Prune and counts the entries it forgot.
The `workspace destroy` verb calls stow.DestroyRegisteredWorkspace, the administrative path that does not need a workspace handle.
The `workspace serve` verb resumes a workspace by id and then attaches the S3 facade to that handle.
The `workspace handoff` verb reads a registry entry with stow.LookupWorkspace, because naming a workspace must not claim its session.
The MCP workspace tools read a registry entry with stow.LookupWorkspace so a capture can be scoped without claiming the workspace's session.
MCP construction validates the configured workspace with stow.LookupWorkspace before any tool is registered.
openPreparedWorkspace, the task preparer, opens the prepared workspace through the same OpenWorkspace constructor after reserving the destination directory.
Checkpoint handoff import resolves its destination registry through ResolveRegistryDir before restoring the archive.

The dogfood example opens a workspace, injects a committed-mutation failure in the object index, checks that the reported commitment matches the host bytes, then closes and reopens the workspace to read the object back.
The package's own test asserts that a workspace survives its process, resumes by id, and is collected on a TTL without a live one being touched.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: The complexity concentrates in the callers rather than vanishing. Deleting this module would push six distinct decisions back out into cmd/stow-s3, internal/mcpstorage and every embedder: how a registry directory and a team partition compose into one absolute path (pkg/stow/resume.go:348), the session lock that makes 'nobody is using this workspace' a fact a collector can act on (pkg/stow/workspace.go:156), the delegation that makes an adopted workspace undestroyable and uncollectable (pkg/stow/workspace.go:266), the rule that a resume may only narrow a persisted authority or limit (pkg/stow/resume.go:141), the confinement check on the registered working directory (pkg/stow/resume.go:169) and the close-versus-destroy split (pkg/stow/workspace.go:243). Each of those is a rule the callers currently get for free by calling one function, and each is the kind of rule that a caller re-implements slightly differently, which is what the module's own comments say happened.

leverage: Callers get one place to learn where a workspace's metadata lives and one place to learn what a workspace may be asked to do. The CLI's seventeen workspace verbs (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:119) each reach the module through one command function, and the MCP workspace tools inherit the same rules without restating them. A caller that wants a workspace to outlive its process gets durability, an identity, a session lock and a retention policy from one call; a caller that wants to destroy one gets the adopted-workspace refusal without knowing it exists.
locality: Change, bugs and knowledge concentrate in pkg/stow/workspace.go, pkg/stow/resume.go and pkg/stow/list.go, and in the registry they write into. The registry layout, the entry schema, the lock discipline and the ownership classification live in internal/storage/workspace, so a change to the persisted entry shape is felt in both places, and the resume path is the one that has to understand the older shape. The rules a caller must know are stated in prose at the call sites, which is the one place where they are not enforced.
risks: Workspace.Touch returns nil when the registry entry is missing: Registry.Lookup returns (Entry{}, false, nil) for a missing entry (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:176), and Touch returns that nil error on the !found branch (pkg/stow/resume.go:436), so a caller cannot tell a recorded touch from a silently dropped one.

The resolve-then-open composition is repeated rather than centralised, and the copies differ: ResolveRegistryDir is defined once (pkg/stow/resume.go:348) and every path calls it, but openRegistry (pkg/stow/resume.go:329) opens with workspace.OpenRegistry, which creates the directory (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:117), while openRegistryReadOnly (pkg/stow/resume.go:246) and List (pkg/stow/list.go:93) open with workspace.OpenRegistryReadOnly, which does not (internal/storage/workspace/registry.go:134). A fourth copy has to know which of the two behaviours it wants, and the CLI already carries its own thin wrapper (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:76) that delegates to the package.

OpenWorkspace exempts the workspace bucket from the runtime's authority check by creating it through the store (pkg/stow/workspace.go:181, internal/storage/workspace/buckets.go:142). A caller that assumes every bucket creation is subject to the grant has to know about this one exemption.

Collect opens the registry with openRegistry, which creates the directory (pkg/stow/resume.go:213), while List and Prune open it read-only (pkg/stow/list.go:100, pkg/stow/resume.go:288). A sweep against a machine with no registry therefore brings one into existence, which is the opposite of what a listing does.

A registry entry whose policy version is not 1 cannot be resumed at all (pkg/stow/resume.go:106); the only way forward is to reopen the directory explicitly, which loses the persisted policy and caps.

priority.rationale: Impact is P1 because the blast radius is the whole workspace surface: seventeen CLI verbs, the MCP workspace tools and every embedder of the public package depend on the resolution, session-lock and close-versus-destroy rules, and the rules are stated in prose at the call sites rather than enforced by a single entry point. Overall is P2 because the defects the map exposed are contained — one silently swallowed error return, one repeated resolve-then-open composition and one inconsistent registry-creation behaviour — and the action the map implies is a documentation and interface-tightening change rather than a redesign.

next_action: Make the registry-opening behaviour a property of the verb rather than of the copy: keep ResolveRegistryDir (pkg/stow/resume.go:348) as the one resolution rule and give the package a single resolve-and-open helper parameterised by create/read-only, so openRegistry (pkg/stow/resume.go:329), openRegistryReadOnly (pkg/stow/resume.go:246) and List (pkg/stow/list.go:93) cannot drift. The interface that should change is Workspace.Touch, which should return a named error when the registry entry is absent rather than nil (pkg/stow/resume.go:436), and Collect should open the registry read-only the way List and Prune do (pkg/stow/resume.go:213).

title: Workspace preparation and seeding
summary: PrepareWorkspace creates a Stow-owned workspace directory, copies declared local files and directories and shallow Git commits into it, checks the seed against the workspace's effective limits, records the Git provenance and returns a fingerprint of exactly what was seeded. It owns the rules about where a seeded path may land (never outside the workspace, never inside the reserved .stow directory, never with a non-portable segment), which inputs are refused unless the caller explicitly opts in (credential-looking filenames and locations), and that a failed prepare removes only the root this call created.

trace.scope: PrepareWorkspace is the public entry point for creating a seeded workspace.
The registry retention check runs before anything is created, so a refusal costs a command rather than a half-made workspace and a cleanup.
openPreparedWorkspace creates the destination root and opens the workspace that will own it, removing a partially created root if the open fails.
seedPreparedWorkspace copies the declared inputs and clones the selected Git commits, accumulating bytes and objects into one budget.
Each seeded file is written into the workspace directory with O_EXCL, so a seed cannot overwrite an existing file.
workspaceFingerprint hashes the seeded tree into BaseIdentity, the durable identity of what was seeded.

evidence.detail: A deferred discardOnFailure rolls back a prepare that did not commit, folding a cleanup failure into the error that caused it so the caller can tell which of the two happened.
checkSeedLimits compares the seeded totals with the workspace's effective capabilities, which were read from the opened workspace rather than from the requested options.
safeDestination refuses an absolute destination, a parent-directory traversal, a non-portable segment and the reserved .stow directory.
sensitiveSeedPath is the single definition of a credential-looking path, used by the seed, the checkpoint scan and the delta path.
seedGitCommand neutralises system and global Git configuration, disables terminal prompts and skips LFS smudge, so a prepare reads no credential store.
admitGitTree reserves the selected immutable tree before the payload is fetched, so a large commit is refused against the budget before it is downloaded.
workspaceFingerprint skips the .stow metadata directory and any .git directory and refuses a non-regular file, so the identity covers the seeded content only.
The package's own test asserts that a prepared workspace is persistent, inherited no upstream authority, and holds the seeded file at the requested destination.

interface.types: stow.PrepareOptions embeds stow.WorkspaceOptions and adds WorkingDirectory (relative to the workspace root), Inputs ([]stow.WorkspaceInput{Source, Destination}), Repositories ([]stow.GitRepositoryInput{Source, Destination, Ref}), IncludeSensitiveInputs and MaxWorkspaces (a call-specific narrowing of the standing registry cap). The result is stow.PreparedWorkspace{Workspace, WorkingDirectory, SeededBytes, SeededObjects, BaseIdentity, Repositories, RegistryEntries, MaxWorkspaces}. stow.WorkspaceTaskManifest is the version-1 JSON document the CLI reads and hands to PrepareWorkspace.
invariants: The destination root must not already exist and its parent must be an existing directory (pkg/stow/prepare.go:216, pkg/stow/prepare.go:226).
At least one input or one repository is required (pkg/stow/prepare.go:127).
A seeded destination is always relative to the workspace root; a directory input copies its contents beneath the destination (pkg/stow/prepare.go:16).
Symlinks are refused as inputs, at the top level and inside a copied directory (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:88, pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:132).
Credential-looking paths are refused unless IncludeSensitiveInputs is set, and the refusal names the file (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:94, pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:138).

The Git tree is admitted against the seed budget before it is fetched, and the checkout is verified to have resolved to the requested commit (pkg/stow/prepare_git_budget.go:13, pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:112).
A failed prepare removes only the root this call created; the deferred rollback is skipped once the prepare has committed (pkg/stow/prepare.go:107, pkg/stow/prepare.go:179).
The prepared workspace is owned by stow unless the caller marked it Adopted, and the ownership decision is what Destroy will later act on (pkg/stow/prepare.go:205).
error_modes: "stow: prepare requires a workspace Dir" and "stow: prepare requires at least one input" (pkg/stow/prepare.go:125, pkg/stow/prepare.go:128).
"stow: prepare destination already exists: %s" and "stow: prepare destination parent must be an existing directory" (pkg/stow/prepare.go:222, pkg/stow/prepare.go:228).
"stow: seeded bytes %d exceed workspace limit %d" and the object equivalent, raised by checkSeedLimits after the seed (pkg/stow/prepare.go:285).
"stow: seeded totals exceed supported limits" on an arithmetic overflow of the running totals (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:70).
"sensitive-looking input %s is excluded by default (set include_sensitive_inputs explicitly to include it)" (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:95).
"symbolic link inputs are not supported" and "only regular files and directories are supported: %s" (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:89, pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:175).
"stow: Git checkout did not resolve to requested commit %s" (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:114).
"stow: fingerprint prepared inputs: %w" when the tree contains a non-regular file (pkg/stow/prepare.go:177).
ordering: The registry retention check precedes any creation, so a refused prepare leaves nothing behind (pkg/stow/prepare.go:136).
The root is created before the workspace is opened, and the root is removed if the open fails (pkg/stow/prepare.go:201, pkg/stow/prepare.go:210).
The seed happens before the limits are checked, because the effective limits are only known once the workspace is open (pkg/stow/prepare.go:152, pkg/stow/prepare.go:166).

The usage is refreshed after the limits are checked and before provenance is written, so a workspace whose seed overflows its quota never records a provenance file (pkg/stow/prepare.go:169, pkg/stow/prepare.go:172).
The working directory is created and persisted to the registry entry before the seed limits are checked (pkg/stow/prepare.go:158, pkg/stow/prepare.go:163).
configuration: IncludeSensitiveInputs is the opt-in that lets a credential-looking path be seeded; it is off by default (pkg/stow/prepare.go:49).

MaxWorkspaces narrows the standing registry cap for this prepare only, and is reported back as PreparedWorkspace.MaxWorkspaces so a caller can see which policy produced the headroom count (pkg/stow/prepare.go:51, pkg/stow/prepare.go:96).
The Git ref is always explicit: a repository input names a ref that is resolved to an immutable commit before anything is fetched (pkg/stow/prepare.go:30, pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:75).
The seed budget is the workspace's effective MaxBytes and MaxObjects, read from the opened workspace's capabilities rather than from the request (pkg/stow/prepare.go:152).

implementation: PrepareWorkspace (pkg/stow/prepare.go:123) validates the request, refuses a destination that already exists, checks the registry's standing workspace count before creating anything, defaults the authority to ReadWrite when the caller named none (pkg/stow/prepare.go:140), and opens the workspace through openPreparedWorkspace, which creates the root and removes it again if the open fails (pkg/stow/prepare.go:200). It then seeds: seedWorkspaceInputs copies each declared file or directory through copySeed, which refuses symlinks, refuses non-regular files, refuses a credential-looking path unless IncludeSensitiveInputs is set, and copies the bytes with O_EXCL so an existing file cannot be overwritten (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:83, pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:201). cloneGitRepositories resolves each input's ref to an immutable commit, admits the tree against the seed budget before fetching (pkg/stow/prepare_git_budget.go:13), initialises a fresh repository under the workspace, fetches the single commit with depth one and no submodules, disables hooks by pointing core.hooksPath at an empty directory, checks out the commit detached, and re-reads HEAD to confirm it resolved to the requested commit (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:95). All git invocations run with GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM, an empty GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, terminal prompts off and LFS smudge skipped (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:175), so a prepare reads no credential store. After the seed, the effective capabilities are read from the opened workspace and the totals are checked against them, the usage is refreshed, the Git provenance is written to .stow/provenance.json (pkg/stow/checkpoint_provenance.go:24), and the tree is fingerprinted into a sha256 over relative paths and content (pkg/stow/prepare.go:293). A deferred discard closes and destroys the workspace if the prepare did not commit (pkg/stow/prepare.go:107).

callers.scope: The CLI's `workspace prepare` verb builds a PrepareOptions from a version-1 task manifest and calls stow.PrepareWorkspace, then reports the headroom the registry cap left.
restoreCheckpointFiles restores a checkpoint by seeding the checkpoint's files through PrepareWorkspace, so a restore and a prepare obey the same path and quota rules.
The package's own test asserts the seeded file lands in the requested working directory and that the prepared workspace is persistent and local.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: The complexity concentrates rather than vanishes. Deleting this module would push five separate rules into every caller: where a seeded path may land (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:16), which inputs are refused as sensitive (pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go:144), that a Git input names an explicit immutable commit rather than a branch (pkg/stow/prepare.go:30), that a failed prepare removes only the root it created (pkg/stow/prepare.go:107), and that the seed is checked against the opened workspace's effective limits rather than the requested ones (pkg/stow/prepare.go:152). A caller re-implementing any of them would get a subtly different answer, and the same rules are shared with the checkpoint and delta paths, which is why they live here rather than at each call site.

leverage: One call gives a caller a directory, a bucket, a working directory, a fingerprint of the seed and a base identity, with the path, sensitivity and quota rules already applied. A caller that wants to seed from Git does not have to know that a ref must be resolved to a commit before it can be fetched, that hooks are disabled, or that the tree is admitted against the budget before the download. The same safeDestination and sensitiveSeedPath rules then serve the checkpoint and delta paths, so the rule is stated once.
locality: The rules live in pkg/stow/prepare.go, pkg/stow/prepare_seed.go, pkg/stow/prepare_git.go and pkg/stow/prepare_git_budget.go. The sensitive-path list in prepare_seed.go is shared with the checkpoint scan (pkg/stow/checkpoint_capture.go:79) and the delta path (pkg/stow/delta.go:289), so a change to it moves three features at once. The Git behaviour depends on the host's git binary and its version, and on the host's ability to fetch from a local path, which is the one part of this module that is not decided by this repository's source.
risks: The Git seed is the only part of preparation that depends on an external program rather than on this repository's code, and the module's own comment (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:12) records that the source repository is left untouched; a caller that expects a worktree registration in the source will not get one.

The seed budget is charged once per Git input, but it is admitted twice through two different accumulators. Before the fetch, a copy of the running totals (checkoutBudget, pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:42) is charged with the tree's blob sizes (pkg/stow/prepare_git_budget.go:13) and then with the fetched metadata (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:102), and that copy is discarded. After the checkout the input is measured again and charged once to the shared totals (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:56, pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:60). Because the pre-fetch projection and the post-checkout measurement are different quantities, passing the admission does not by itself guarantee the checkout fits; the post-checkout charge is what decides, and a near-limit input can still fail after the fetch has already run.

The Git input is pinned by the commit that resolveGitInput computes before any read (pkg/stow/prepare_git.go:75), and that same commit drives ls-tree, fetch, checkout and the HEAD check, so a moving ref cannot change the tree between admission and checkout. The module does not, however, re-derive the admitted tree's digests and compare them against the checkout, so content integrity rests on Git's own object verification rather than on a comparison this module performs.

priority.rationale: Impact is P2 because the module has two production callers (cmd/stow-s3/workspace.go:287, pkg/stow/checkpoint_restore.go:87) and its path and sensitivity rules are shared with the checkpoint and delta paths, so a mistake in either would surface in three features rather than one. Overall is P2 because the module is well covered by its own tests and the risks the map found are narrow: the Git path is the only externally dependent behaviour, and the seed budget is charged once per input even though it is admitted twice.

next_action: Document the two rules a caller cannot infer from the signature: that a Git input must name a ref that resolves to an immutable commit, and that the seed is charged against the opened workspace's effective limits rather than the requested ones. The interface that should change is PrepareOptions.MaxWorkspaces: it is assigned into the unexported WorkspaceOptions.maxRegistryWorkspaces (pkg/stow/prepare.go:144) and echoed back as PreparedWorkspace.MaxWorkspaces (pkg/stow/prepare.go:184), so a caller reading PreparedWorkspace.RegistryEntries has to know which bound produced the count (pkg/stow/prepare.go:89).

title: Workspace S3 facade
summary: The opt-in loopback S3 endpoint a workspace can expose: Workspace.Facade and Workspace.FacadeWithOptions start an authenticated HTTP S3 server on 127.0.0.1 that is bound to the workspace's own runtime instance, so the object store has one implementation and two surfaces. The design is deliberate that a facade with its own storage is rejected, and the module is where that composition is actually made: the server is handed an adapter over the same runtime the workspace already uses, and the handle's close path shuts the server down before the runtime it borrows.

trace.scope: Workspace.Facade is the entry point for the opt-in loopback endpoint.
The facade is built from embedded.UnwrapInstance(w.Runtime), which is the workspace's own runtime instance and no other.
runtime.NewStoreAdapter wraps that same instance in the store interface the S3 server speaks, so the server is a second surface over one store.
s3api.New is configured with Host 127.0.0.1, SigV4 authentication over freshly generated credentials and Mode local.
The server goroutine starts listening on the loopback interface and the descriptor — endpoint, region and keys — is handed back to the caller.

evidence.detail: startWorkspaceFacade adapts the workspace's own runtime instance; there is no path in this function by which a facade could be given storage of its own.
borrowedWorkspaceStore embeds the runtime's store adapter and overrides Close to do nothing, so closing the HTTP server cannot close the storage the workspace still owns.
A second FacadeWithOptions call with different limits is refused; the facade already running keeps its limits.
closeRuntimeLocked shuts the facade down with a ten-second timeout and waits for the listener to finish before closing the runtime the facade borrowed.
The package's own test writes through the S3 facade and then reads the workspace's usage, which is the assertion that the facade and the handle share one store and one accounting.
A file the host wrote directly into the workspace directory is counted against the quota on the next write through the facade, which is the same-bytes claim of ADR 0007 reached through the facade.
A read-only authority is enforced through the facade: a read succeeds and a write is refused.

The product glossary states the facade as an opt-in loopback endpoint bound to the same runtime instance, and that a facade with its own storage is rejected because that would be two stores and a synchronization problem.
The decision record states that a workspace that speaks S3 and one that does not are the same object store, and that any design giving the facade its own storage is rejected.

interface.types: stow.WorkspaceFacade is the descriptor returned to the caller: Endpoint, Region, AccessKeyID, SecretAccessKey, MaxMultipartUploads, MaxConcurrentRequests and MaxRequestBytes, all JSON-tagged because the CLI serialises it as the readiness record. stow.WorkspaceFacadeOptions{MaxRequestBytes, MaxConcurrentRequests} is the input. The methods are (*Workspace).Facade() and (*Workspace).FacadeWithOptions(WorkspaceFacadeOptions).
invariants: The facade serves the workspace's own runtime instance, so a write through the facade and a write through the handle are the same bytes and the same accounting (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:83, pkg/stow/workspace_facade_test.go:42).
The endpoint binds to 127.0.0.1 only and is authenticated with SigV4 over freshly generated credentials (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:90, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:91).
The facade is opt-in: no listener exists until Facade or FacadeWithOptions is called (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:42).
A facade is created at most once per workspace handle, and a second call with the same options returns the same descriptor (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:64, pkg/stow/workspace_facade_test.go:29).
The facade borrows the runtime's store: closing the server does not close the storage the workspace still owns (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:32).
The workspace's authority is enforced through the facade, because the facade is the same runtime (pkg/stow/workspace_facade_test.go:137).
The facade is shut down before the runtime it borrows is closed (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:114, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:126).
error_modes: stow.ErrClosed when the workspace is closed or closing (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:62).
"stow: maximum concurrent requests must not be negative" and "stow: maximum request bytes must not be negative" (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:48, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:54).
"stow: existing workspace facade has a different request limit" when a second call asks for different limits (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:72).
The error from s3api.New when the server cannot be constructed, and the server's own error when the listener fails to start (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:95, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:102).
The shutdown error from the S3 server, which aborts the close before the runtime is closed (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:117).
ordering: The facade must be requested before the workspace is closed; a facade on a closed workspace is refused (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:61).
The server is started and the caller waits for its readiness before the descriptor is returned, so the endpoint is usable when the call returns (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:100).
The facade is shut down as part of closing the workspace, before the runtime is closed and before the session lock is released (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:109, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:132).
The limits must be decided on the first call, because a later call with different limits is refused rather than applied (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:71).
configuration: MaxRequestBytes and MaxConcurrentRequests bound the HTTP surface; zero takes the s3api defaults (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:50, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:56).
The region is fixed to us-east-1 and the host to 127.0.0.1; the caller cannot move the facade off the loopback interface (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:87, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:90).
The credentials are generated per facade and returned in the descriptor; the admin token is the secret key (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:79, pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:93).
The write policy is fixed to local-only and the cache policy to none (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:92).

implementation: FacadeWithOptions (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:46) rejects negative limits and fills the zero ones from the s3api defaults, takes the workspace's lifecycle lock so a concurrent close cannot race the start, refuses a closed handle, and then starts the facade once and remembers it. startWorkspaceFacade (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:78) generates a credential pair, adapts the workspace's own runtime instance with runtime.NewStoreAdapter, and constructs the S3 server with that adapter wrapped in borrowedWorkspaceStore, whose Close is a no-op so the server's own shutdown cannot close the storage the workspace still owns. The server is configured for the loopback interface, for SigV4 authentication against the generated credentials, for local mode, for no cache and for a local-only write policy, and the admin token is the generated secret. The server is started in a goroutine and the caller waits for its readiness before reading the address, so the endpoint is live when the call returns. The descriptor carries the endpoint, the region, the credentials and the multipart limit read from the instance's capabilities. The close path (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:109) shuts the server down with a ten-second timeout, waits for the listener goroutine to report, and only then closes the runtime the facade borrowed and releases the session lock, so the listener never outlives the storage it was serving.

callers.scope: The CLI's `workspace serve` verb calls stow.Workspace.FacadeWithOptions and writes the descriptor as the readiness record the client packages read from an inherited file descriptor.
The package's own test drives a real S3 client against the facade and asserts that the facade and the handle share one store, one accounting and one authority.
A second package test starts the same facade to assert that a multipart write racing a host edit is refused through the shared runtime.

depth_assessment.deletion_test: The complexity concentrates rather than vanishes. Deleting this module would push the composition itself into the callers: the rule that the facade must be bound to the same runtime instance (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:83), the rule that the server must not close the storage it borrows (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:34), the ordering that the listener is stopped before the runtime it serves is closed (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:114), and the fact that the limits are decided once. A caller re-implementing those would build a second store over the same directory, which is exactly the arrangement ADR 0007 rejects (docs/adr/0007-workspace-is-the-default.md:136) and exactly the synchronization problem CONTEXT.md names.

leverage: A caller that needs S3 wire compatibility for a workspace it already holds gets it from one call, with no second store to keep in step, no separate credential store and no process. The caller receives everything a client needs to connect — endpoint, region, keys and limits — in one JSON-serialisable descriptor, which is what lets the CLI publish it as a readiness record. The module also carries the burden of proving the composition is real, which its test does by writing through the facade and reading the workspace's usage.
locality: The whole module is pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go, with the S3 server itself in internal/s3api and the runtime adapter in internal/runtime. The changes that would matter are the composition at pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:83 and the close ordering at pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:109; everything else is configuration of a server that has its own unit. The one coupling worth naming is that pkg/stow imports internal/s3api, so the public library surface now depends on the HTTP layer, and a change to the s3api configuration shape reaches the library.
risks: pkg/stow, the public library surface, now imports internal/s3api (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:12), so a Go embedder that wants only the in-process runtime links the HTTP server's dependency tree. The facade is opt-in at runtime but not at link time.

The facade's credentials are generated per workspace and returned in the descriptor, which the CLI then writes to a readiness record. A caller that logs the descriptor leaks the secret; nothing in the module redacts it.

A second FacadeWithOptions call with different limits is refused with a plain error rather than by re-configuring the running server (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:71), so a caller that wants different limits must close the workspace and open a new one, which changes the workspace's identity path.

The facade is shut down with a ten-second timeout during close (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:115); a shutdown that exceeds it fails the close and leaves the runtime open, and the caller sees a close error rather than a partial close.

priority.rationale: Impact is P2 because the facade is the bridge between the in-process library and the S3 wire protocol: the CLI's `workspace serve` verb and the TypeScript and Python client packages' readiness handshake both depend on the descriptor and on the composition holding (cmd/stow-s3/workspace_serve.go:58, packages/stow-s3/src/workspace-serve.ts:74, packages/stow-s3-py/src/stow_s3/workspace_serve.py:95). Overall is P2 because the risks are about link-time coupling and credential handling in the descriptor rather than about a defect in the composition, which the module's own test demonstrates.

next_action: Split the public package so that a Go embedder that never asks for S3 does not link internal/s3api: the facade is one file (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go) and its dependency is the whole HTTP surface (pkg/stow/workspace_facade.go:12). The interface that should change is WorkspaceFacade, whose SecretAccessKey is serialised into the readiness record without any indication that it must be treated as a secret.
